The use of electrical muscle stimulation as a shortcut to improving physical fitness was first commercialized sometime in the early 19th century, and while EMS has waxed and waned in popularity over the years, it’s never gone away. Today it is widely used across rehabilitative medical applications but also to boost strength and stamina.
The promise is simple: Stimulate the muscles with pulses of electricity while you’re working out and you can create thousands of muscle contractions in a short amount of time, far more than you can achieve through standard reps. You still have to activate the muscles through flexing and the like—you can’t just lay on the ground and zap your way into shape—but you can accomplish more with a lot less if you’re using EMS as part of your workout.
Studios like Body20 and Manduu now outfit clients with electrodes and pair them with trainers to guide them through EMS sessions. Both companies promise complete body workouts in 20 minutes or less.
The latest spin on EMS is even more appealing: Rather than requiring a studio visit, why not give consumers an EMS suit they can wear at home and use on their own schedule? To that end, German EMS suit maker Pepper offered to let me try out one of its fancy electro-suits to gauge its long-term impact. The company claims that working out while wearing the suit for 20 minutes gives you the equivalent caloric burn and muscle activation of an hour-long traditional workout, all with less strain on the joints.
At least five companies occupy this space at present, ranging from Apeborn’s $4,000 offering to Pepper’s $1,400 suit, which is the cheapest one I’ve found. And even though the idea of getting ripped with minimal effort tickled my lazy bone, it took me a while to come around to the idea of zapping myself on purpose. Could this possibly do any good?
It turns out EMS has been exhaustively studied—dozens of research papers have been published in the past 20 years—and while results vary, researchers seem optimistic on the whole. One 2021 meta-study determined there is “significant evidence for significant, large-sized effects of [whole body]-EMS on muscle mass and strength parameters, but not on body fat mass.” A 2012 study on trained athletes measured the benefits of using EMS for three to six weeks directly: Vertical jump height increased by up to 25 percent, and sprint times got faster by as much as 4.8 percent.
Another meta-analytical study from 2023 offered perhaps the most compelling commentary, concluding that “eight weeks of continuous resistance training combined with daily upper body, lower body, and abdominal EMS training can significantly improve muscle mass and upper body muscle strength performance, as well as significantly reduce body fat percentage in healthy subjects.”
It all sounds promising, yet despite the extensive research into EMS, there’s no general medical consensus about the tech.
I spoke to a half-dozen physicians about EMS for this story, and opinions varied along quite a wide spectrum. At one end, Andrew Mock, a primary care physician in Newport Beach and five-time winner of the California’s Strongest Man competition, lightweight division, said that EMS had proven beneficial for rehab or critical care situations in patients with severe mobility restrictions, but healthy patients were unlikely to see much value. “If you go outside and start shivering, those are muscle contractions,” he says. “But shivering doesn’t make you stronger.”
At the other end, I heard from Ethan Kellum, the team doctor for the NFL’s Tennessee Titans, who said he uses a form of EMS not just for rehab but to supplement his own workouts. “It’s really a function of the nervous system,” he says, noting that in older patients, muscles can become unresponsive and “go to sleep,” requiring significant effort to reawaken them. “When used appropriately, EMS can help improve the efficiency of communication between the nervous system and the body. Add it to what you’re doing. It can be really helpful.”
Across the board, everyone I spoke to hedged by saying that EMS could, at least for some users, provide some benefit. Perhaps the most representative comments came from Joseph R. Hribick, a professor of physical therapy at Lebanon Valley College. “Current research does not suggest that EMS alone is superior to strength training for developing strength,” he says, “Instead, it should be looked at as a tool to complement strength training and not replace it.”
Suiting Up
After speaking to Pepper founder Emilia von Keyserlingk at length, I relented. To mimic the aforementioned 2023 study, I would work out with the Pepper suit regularly for two months, three times a week—in addition to maintaining my regular cardio and strength-training workouts and keeping my diet and daily routines the same—and see what transpired.
The suit is a lot like a spring-weather wetsuit that stops at the knees and the elbows. Like with a wetsuit, putting it on can require some effort. Twenty electrodes cover the abs, pecs, glutes, thighs, pecs, biceps, and multiple parts of the back. These are dry electrodes, so you don’t have to wet Pepper’s suit down before you put it on (a common requirement for older gear), but your sweat will improve the conduction of electricity. Of course, if you’re pregnant or need a pacemaker, you shouldn’t use an EMS suit.
Pepper’s suit, available in sizes from XXXS to XXXL, is designed to be very tight so that the electrodes won’t slip into places you don’t want them. Since the suit is intended to be worn with nothing underneath it, that’s a particularly important consideration. And based on the way certain body parts are situated beneath the fabric, it is definitively not something I felt I could wear in public without a cover-up layer.
The only removable part of the suit is a small box that connects at your hip. This is the brains of the operation and its power source. Charge it with a USB-C cable and it’s good for at least 10 training sessions.
Pepper’s app divides workouts into three categories: strength, cardio, and relax, each with a different electrode firing pattern. (Oddly, I discovered that a few workouts were available only in German.) I tried workouts across all of the categories but spent nearly all of my time in strength, as my goal was to build muscle. Strength sessions all involve electricity pulsing through the suit for four seconds, then pausing for four seconds, then repeating for up to 24 minutes.
The workouts—there are dozens, I rarely repeated any—are tuned to the pulses so that you’re activating muscles across your body while the pulse is on, then usually resting while it’s off. Again, Pepper’s approach is that EMS only works if you are using your muscles while they are being energized, so many of the workouts involve entire body flexes, stretches, and crunches, four seconds at a time.
Plugging In
I’ve experienced isolated EMS for a back injury once before, so I had an inkling of what Pepper might feel like, but the full-body experience is on another level entirely. Fortunately, Pepper eases you in, starting off with soft pulses you can’t even feel. Each of Pepper’s 10 workout zones can be individually controlled, with the power level ranging from 1 to 100. My first video-based trainer said she starts to feel the pulses at level 25, so I slowly ratcheted my way up, bit by bit, until I had all regions hitting around 20.
The shocks on the lower settings don’t really hurt, but you can definitely feel them; powerful, rapid vibrations that shake your insides and sometimes burn a little on the skin. No pain, no gain, right? As I continued to push the levels up, I discovered there was a fine line—really 1 or 2 points on Pepper’s 100-point scale—between tolerable and painful. Those vibrations turned into racy shocks that could be almost paralytic at times, and I spent the rest of my initial 12-minute session dialing the power level back down.
One key discovery is that sweat really matters. When you start your workout, presumably with dry skin, the shocks aren’t as powerful because conductivity is minimal. Start sweating and the shocks increase, even without adjusting the power level in the app. One pulse could be manageable, the next debilitating, just based on how much I was sweating.
My abdominal muscles were the most sensitive to the shocks. Bent over in a crunch position, the contractions could be so powerful in the stomach that I sometimes got a bit nauseous. I was constantly adjusting the levels and ended up with most of my levels around the 30s. To be sure, many of the workouts would be tough even if I weren’t getting zapped.
I asked von Keyserlingk for guidance on the appropriate power level. “The intensity should be high but not too high that you cannot do the exercises in the correct form,” she says. “Being able to breathe normally is key.” Von Keyserlingk says that her levels range from 40s in the lower body to 20s in the back and abdominals—pretty close to my own settings. She notes however that Pepper’s internal EMS expert regularly works out with levels in the 90s. Masochist.
After my first workout, I felt good but was happy to peel off the suit, which was sweaty and unpleasant to linger in. (The suit can be machine washed.) If Pepper’s app was to be believed, my short workout burned a whopping 306 calories and earned me 182 “Pepper points,” which are used as the currency for gamified leaderboards across the Pepper user base. By the end of my testing, I could regularly accrue over 1,000 Pepper points per session and have even earned a few top-10 positions on those leaderboards, which are specific for each workout.
After three sessions, I found myself getting more comfortable with the EMS pulses. I also felt soreness visiting different body parts almost at random. On one day my left hamstring was achy. On another, my right biceps was in so much pain I could barely use it. I figured these were all signs that Pepper was doing something—though, again, I alternated standard workouts with Pepper workouts, taking only Mondays off from disciplined exercise.
Considering Gains
Two months went by. The only workouts I missed were during a weeklong vacation, and I made up the extra time afterward.
The experience was marked by a few problems. After an update, Pepper’s app began glitching and failed to record several of my workouts, costing me thousands of hard-earned Pepper points. Midway through the experience, Pepper released a new, thinner version of its suit with the zipper in front, which the company sent to me. I was excited to give it a try until a piece of the electrical connector snapped off, leaving me unable to connect the battery. The battery pack of suit number three disconnected from the app on two occasions, aborting the workout but at least recording my progress, and it came with an unexpected power boost that left my entire body aching the next day.
Regardless, I muddled through. When the experiment was finished, I’d accumulated 24,000 Pepper points and, purportedly, burned a total of more than 11,000 calories across more than 9 hours of EMS workouts.
To measure my progress, I captured physical data with a tape measure before and after the experience, and I used three different smart scales to further evaluate my stats. All of the scales agreed that the trend line was good: muscle up by 2.7 pounds, fat down by 1.6 pounds—and that’s with smoothed data, since all of these numbers can vary considerably day to day. I added a half-inch or more to my measurements of biceps, thigh, and chest circumference, and my strength was slightly improved, as I’ve been able to add a plate or a few reps to most of my resistance exercises at the gym. Qualitatively, I would say that my physique looks slightly more toned, and I did receive one unsolicited opinion that my arms had better definition. Gains, folks.
What didn’t change? My waistline, which I had hoped to improve, didn’t budge at all. While my abdominal muscles feel noticeably stronger, they remain covered by a layer of blubber that is apparently impervious to electricity. That said, the research predicted as much.
Is EMS responsible for my gains, however modest? While there’s no way to say whether my stats improved due to EMS training, my regular workouts, or dietary changes, I think it’s reasonable to conclude that shock tech did have some impact on my fitness level, since my results are in line with what the 2023 study found. I can’t say whether EMS is responsible for 80 percent or 10 percent of those gains, but I think it’s fair to deduce that some good has been happening.
Going forward, I plan to keep using the suit, though perhaps dropping down from three sessions a week to two. If for no other reason than, while it’s great that my level of fitness is improving, the suit has become quite the topic of conversation at social gatherings. I may be able to slack on my personal fitness, but I can’t let down my people.

Actor Hayden Panettiere has died at 36, her representative told ABC News on Monday.
"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden. She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen," her father, Skip Panettiere, said in a statement to the outlet.
The family did not immediately provide any other details about her death.
Panettiere began her acting career as a child, with one of her earliest major roles as Sarah Roberts on the ABC soap opera "One Life to Live," on which she appeared from 1994 to 1997.
She later became widely known for playing Claire Bennet in the hit series "Heroes" and Juliette Barnes in the musical drama "Nashville."
In her memoir, released on May 19, Panettiere wrote about her struggles with postpartum depression after giving birth to her daughter in 2014.
"It wasn't panic that was sitting in my chest. It was nothing. A total blackout of emotion, like my soul was dead," she wrote.
To deal with her symptoms, she turned to alcohol to get "those happy hormones," she wrote.
"The first thing I'd thought of when I woke up was alcohol. Not my child, not my job, and not the rest of my life. I needed a drink to function — at 6 a.m.," Panettiere wrote.
In 2018, Panettiere signed over full custody of her daughter to the child's father, Wladimir Klitschko, saying she believed it was best for her daughter.

Haemophilia, a genetic bleeding disorder where blood doesn’t clot properly, is usually hereditary and can be passed down from parent to child. The condition is caused by a lack of, or improper functioning of certain clotting factors. This can lead to uncontrolled bleeding after injuries, or even without a clear trigger.
India has the world’s second-largest haemophilia burden. A 2025 review in the Journal of the Association of Physicians of India put prevalence of diagnosed and registered haemophilia cases in India at 0.9 per 1,00,000. However, statistical modelling puts the true disease burden much higher, at around 1,36,000.
Diagnostic challenges
The challenge is to reach those who have not been formally diagnosed. Low awareness and the concentration of labs that can diagnose haemophilia in a handful of metros are some of the reasons for the gap in both timely diagnosis and access to care.
Usually when this gap is discussed, the focus is on the orthopaedic impact on patients - repeated joint bleeds, arthropathy, a young man with the knees of a seventy-year-old. While this is an important aspect of the condition, it leads to lesser conversations on the other effects of haemophilia on the body – the effect on the eyes and vision. This is irreversible when it happens, and can cost patients with undiagnosed haemophilia their sight.
The vision problem
A retrospective study of haemophilia patients at a government hospital in India found that bleeding in and around the eye accounted for 13% of all bleeds recorded. The types of bleeding included anterior segment bleeding (part of the eye in front of the lens), subconjunctival haemorrhage (under the conjunctiva), periorbital ecchymoses (bruising of the skin around the eye), and hyphaema (pooling of blood inside the front chamber of the eye). Posterior segment bleeding in the part of eye behind the lens occurred in around 1.8% of patients. This is a critical matter and led to permanent loss of vision in the affected eye.
The onset can be sudden. One of the patients in the study was a 45-year-old man with moderate haemophilia and no other illness. He came with a sudden one-sided headache. There was no eye pain and no injury that would have made him consult an ophthalmologist. The headache was eventually attributed to an intraorbital haemorrhage, by which point the eye was lost.
That is the challenge faced. While bleeding that threatens vision is a rare occurrence in the eye, the diagnosis is usually delayed due to ambiguous symptoms, with a very short window to take action and correct the clotting factor levels in the blood.
Missing elements
A common scenario is a patient with undiagnosed haemophilia being taken into an operating theatre in an emergency. Traumatic hyphaema or pooling of blood inside the front chamber of the eye due to an injury is quite common in a child. The usual pre-operative panel that includes a complete blood count, a chest radiograph and a urinalysis, does not detect a clotting factor deficiency. In such a case, surgery may result in bleeding in the eye after the procedure, with resultant complications.
Two more factors make the risk harder to tackle. About a third of people born with haemophilia have no family history at all, so an unremarkable family tree is not reassurance. And mild haemophilia frequently goes undetected until adulthood, surfacing only after a dental extraction, an accident or surgery.
The clinical baselines are well established. For ocular surgery, clotting factor levels are recommended at 70% to 80%, with a minimum of 50% in emergencies. Blood in the anterior chamber or vitreous is treated as an emergency requiring immediate treatment. None of this is achievable if the diagnosis is unknown, and is difficult if the clotting factors are not readily available.
The solution
This can be fixed. Pre-operative checklists must have a bleeding history line that asks specifically about prolonged bleeding after tooth extraction, easy bruising and heavy menstrual periods. An APTT (Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time) and factor assay must be done whenever ocular bleeding looks disproportionate to the trauma that caused it. Referral links between district eye units and the nearest haemophilia treatment centre must be established.
Damage to joints takes place over years and can be partly rehabilitated. An eye does not get a second chance. We must work to prevent vision loss due to India’s haemophilia diagnosis gap.
(Dr. Anusha Venkataraman is senior consultant & surgeon - vitreo retina and ocular oncology, ASG Vasan Eye Care, Coimbatore. anushavenkat262@gmail.com)

India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party has lost a byelection in a seat it had held for three decades, after the Cockroach movement student protests that have shaken Narendra Modi’s government.
Prashant Kishor, a high-profile electoral strategist turned politician, scored a breakthrough win for his fledgling Jan Suraaj (Good Governance) party in the Bankipur constituency in Patna, the capital of the eastern state of Bihar.
The byelection, in what had been considered a BJP stronghold, was closely watched because it came in the aftermath of nationwide student protests over exam paper leaks that forced the resignation of the education minister, a rare retreat by a government that prides itself on not yielding to public pressure.
Kishor said his victory was a wake-up call for Modi to improve education and create jobs.
The BJP lost two of three byelection contests this week, with the opposition Congress retaining the Datia constituency in central Madhya Pradesh. The BJP comfortably held Manjalpur in Gujarat, Modi’s home state.
Kishor’s supporters said his campaign had succeeded by focusing on issues that resonated with younger voters, particularly education, exams scandals and unemployment.
Deepak Sharma, a former BJP supporter, told the Hindu newspaper: “Unlike other political leaders who make lofty promises, he raised the simple slogan: vote for the future of your children.”
The opposition have said the student protest movement is beginning to dent BJP support among younger voters. Nearly two-thirds of India’s population is under 35. While the official youth unemployment rate is 16%, nearly 40% of graduates aged 15-25 and 20% of those aged 25-29 are jobless, far higher proportions than among the less educated, according to the latest State of Working India report by Azim Premji University.
The BJP’s president, Nitin Nabin, who previously represented Bankipur, described the largely gen Z protesters as “a virus and a cockroach gang devoted to breaking the country” during the byelection campaign.
After he lost the election, he said the party would “undertake a thorough introspection”. Senior BJP sources quoted in the Indian media said the loss has shown that even core supporters could change their minds.
A significant victory for the BJP in West Bengal last year expanded the party’s reach into one of the last major regions outside its control, but that triumph has been followed by a string of political headaches, including the student protests.
The Cockroach Janata party began as an online joke after a senior judge described unemployed young Indians as cockroaches and parasites. It has since morphed into a nationwide movement with 26.6 million Instagram followers, more than the BJP and Congress combined.
The government has also become embroiled in a separate confrontation with the social media company Meta after a video featuring Modi in which he promised to crack down on exam fraud briefly disappeared from Facebook.
The parliamentary committee on communications and information technology has demanded Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, apologise personally and explain how the video vanished. According to local media, Meta executives have already apologised and blamed automated systems designed to detect fake content.
The row has highlighted broader government unease about the influence of foreign technology companies over political discourse. Nishikant Dubey, the chair of the committee, said large parties such as the BJP and Congress often received less visibility online than movements with no formal political status.
“The country needs to understand what Meta, X and YouTube are doing through their algorithms,” Dubey said.
Ajoy Bose, a Delhi-based political analyst, said the Bankipur defeat carried symbolic weight far beyond a single constituency. “Coming as it does after the student protests, the optics look very bad for the BJP. I would not directly connect the result to the protests, but Bihar was one of the main centres of the student agitation, so the two will inevitably be linked in public perception.”
But he cautioned against reading the outcome as evidence of a nationwide shift in voter sentiment. “What’s changing is the perceived invincibility of the BJP’s election machine,” Bose said. “There was a widespread belief the party had every election sewn up.”

Secondhand book sales are booming. Is it because of AI?
- Published
Something mysterious has been happening in the world of secondhand books.
Over the last few months independent booksellers have been observing a strange pattern of purchases which have seen scores of their novels being shipped to far-off warehouses.
In a typical week, Stuart Manley, from Barter Books, in Northumberland, would sell two or three thousand books. But one recent single bulk order from a Canadian company equalled what he would expect to move in seven days.
He says he has "never seen the like of this after 30 years in the second-hand book trade".
Mr Manley is not alone. Booksellers from around the world have been reporting similarly unusual mega orders.
They aren't sure what the final destination for their books is.
But the suspicion is that they are not being bought for avid overseas readers but instead something else with a voracious appetite for new information: AI.
The court battle over books
The idea that the secondhand sales boom is being driven by the explosive growth of AI can be traced back to a court ruling in the US.
In 2025, a judge ruled using books purchased in this way to train AI software was not a violation of US copyright law.
The decision was the result of a lawsuit brought against AI firm Anthropic by three authors. In his ruling, Judge William Alsup said Anthropic's use of the authors' books was "exceedingly transformative" and therefore allowed under US law.
When court documents were unsealed last month it also emerged books were being destroyed in the process of training Anthropic's AI chatbot, Claude.
"Claude is trained on a mix of publicly available web data, commercially acquired datasets, and data we generate ourselves," a spokesperson said.
They insisted sourcing books for training was a widely used approach across the AI industry.
"None of our data acquisition programs buy and destroy rare or antiquarian books," they added.
Nonetheless, the idea that books are being pulped is causing unease.
David Tobin, runs Walden Books in north London, has also had unusual sales.
"In some ways it's very nice to sell some of these titles which haven't been sold for many years, but it would be sad if they are ultimately destroyed," he says.
Destructive scanning
The court documents relating to the Anthropic case revealed the project of ingesting old books was referred to in internal company communications as "Project Panama."
The documents indicated the company's aim was to "destructively scan all the books in the world".
Destructive scanning is the process of shipping books to locations where they can be digitised at an industrial scale.
It includes removing a book's spine so all the pages can be scanned rapidly - and the remains recycled.
"A lot of mystery surrounds Project Panama," Manley, from Barter Books, says.
"The name is new to me, but the reality of the project is not, and has been the subject of much discussion on the bookseller forums."
He does not know that his books are being bought for it or similar projects by other AI firms.
But he says it's also difficult to account for the sales, which appear random with "no rhyme or reason."
They have varied from obscure Latin texts to cowboy novels.
Experts say the diverse subject matter also points to AI, as unusual and rare texts could provide fresh material to improve the training of large language models, the tech which underpins generative AI tools like chatbots.
Professor Emily Hudson, intellectual property specialist at Oxford University, says copyright laws in the UK are different to those in the US.
"The starting point in the UK is that all these acts of copying - creating the training library and doing the training – require the permission of the copyright owner," she says.
Ethical concerns
For the booksellers, it poses a dilemma.
They are uncomfortable with the idea of books being destroyed - even if they admit not every title needs to be saved.
"A recent academic text published in only 100 copies, 75 of which are already in libraries, may be very rare on the market - but it is perhaps not such a great loss if one copy is destroyed," says Derek Walker, owner of Edinburgh bookshop McNaughtan's.
"But we have, and have sold, books which are for example the only known surviving example of an edition from the 18th century.
"It would be a much more significant problem if one like that were to be bought for destruction, having survived this long."
And Manley says recycling books is a good solution for many titles which the public no longer want on their shelves - especially when it comes with a bump in trade.
"Some may have ethical concerns about where the books end up and if they're destroyed," he says.
"But the world no longer needs five million copies of The Da Vinci Code.
"I've had books advertised for 20 years on the web which haven't sold until now".

Attractive design, now with more color options. Extremely easy to set up and maintain. Can grow whatever you want. New, less intrusive light with an optional app and vacation mode. Tomato-and-pepper kit with longer dowels available as an add-on.
TIRED
Lack of pump means potentially stagnant water (but also one less failure point).
When Auk’s originalMini 1 herb garden hit the market in 2024, it touched on something that many tabletop gardens had until that point failed to consider: If you’re going to give up that much counter or table space, you don’t want it to be for something ugly.
Aerogardens and similar models look … fine, but you’re probably not going to see one in the background of an Architectural Digest shoot. The Auk Mini filled that marketplace gap with its pairing of sleek Scandinavian design and utility, transforming the run-of-the-mill herb-growing operation into a conversation piece.
When I reviewed the original Auk Mini last fall, I loved that it allowed users to plant their own seeds in widely available coco coir, an alternative to peat moss made from coconut husks. No proprietary pods, no subscriptions, no fussy app.
When I started testing the brand-new Auk 2 earlier this summer, I wondered what new features could possibly justify a new model. Turns out, there was more room for improvement than I thought.
Same but Different
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
For the uninitiated, Auk (pronounced “owk”) is a Norwegian company that released its first garden, the Auk 1, in 2021. Essentially a larger version of the Mini 1, the Auk 1 received mixed reviews online for its tower water reservoir and inconsistent light and watering cycles. (In fact, a former WIRED director tested it and became so frustrated that he threw it in the trash.)
The Mini 1 was a simplified version of the Auk system, with four oval pots set over a 3-liter reservoir. Users could grow the included herb seeds or anything else they wanted in the pots using coco coir. It was simple, stylish, and effective.
The Auk Mini 2 features a handful of updates, but perhaps the most visible is that it comes in new color variations, rather than just black and white. There are still the oak and walnut wood bottoms, but Mini 2 offers beech and ash instead of the Mini 1's cork. Espresso, sage, and terra-cotta colored tops now join the menu of offerings.
The Mini 2 also sports bigger plant pots and a 25 percent larger water capacity, despite its overall footprint being 12 percent smaller than the original.
Auk Mini 1
Photograph: Kat Merck
Auk Mini 2
Photograph: Kat Merck
There is now also—and I admittedly had mixed feelings about this—an app. Using the Auk Connect app isn’t mandatory; you can still control the light schedule manually using a button on the light bar, as with the Auk Mini 1. The app doesn’t add much, but to its credit, it’s easy to set up. You don’t even need to make an account. Just download it; open it; and choose your garden, which the app should already recognize. You’ll access a page where you can turn the light on or off, dim it, set a time schedule, or swap grow mode from “Herbs & Salads” to “Fruits & Veggies.”
Though the stock dowels for the light bar on the Mini 2 are, as on the Mini 1, too low at a maximum of 15 inches to easily accommodate taller fruiting plants like peppers, Auk now offers a $39 Chili & Tomato Kit with longer dowels and a tray with larger pots (two instead of three). I have not tried it, but I’d be surprised if it didn’t result in substantially increased success rates.
The app also allows you to select the Mini 2’s brand-new vacation mode feature, which it calls Slow Mode. On Slow Mode, the Mini 2’s lights dim to slow down growth and water absorption so that, if you need to step away, you’re not left with a mess of overgrown parsley and bolting basil, as happened when I tested the Mini 1.
Let There Be (Better) Light
For comparison purposes, I grew the same herbs in the Mini 2 as I did in the Mini 1: Italian parsley and Genovese basil. I also used only the included nutrients. However, once the parsley and basil got to harvestable size, I noticed something different: These herbs were not leggy. In fact, they were lush and bushy, just like the marketing photos, with almost none of the floppiness that plagued my plants when I tested the earlier model.
Mini 1 on the top, Mini 2 on the bottom
Photograph: Kat Merck
This result was, I learned, due in part to the Mini 2’s new light bar incorporating an optical lens system that allows the light to not only appear less bright, but also focus more light directly on the plants. Because the plants now get enough light, they don’t have to stretch toward it—which caused overly tall, weak stems in the Mini 1.
I also noticed that less of the light spills over into the surrounding area—I kept the Auk Mini 2 on a console table behind the couch in my living room, and unlike the lights on most gardens I test, it wasn’t visually disruptive while I watched TV. In fact, the light was so visibly dim (in a good way) that I nearly forgot it was on.
Auk Mini 1 herbs
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
Another possible contributing factor to the plants’ ability to stay upright was the starter kit’s new addition of a topper: a bag of fine gravel that forms a sort of crust over the top of the coco coir as the substrate absorbs water. None of the herb stems struggled to pop through, though some wore a little gravel hat for quite a while. Once they were big enough to stand upright, they stayed that way. The gravel was a little bit of a mess to apply, but I don’t advise skipping this step.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Best to Buy Now
Otherwise, the Mini Auk 1 and Mini Auk 2 are quite similar. They have an identical tension assembly for the light bar; the same little dot-studded water-level indicator wheel (seen above), where the red dot means the reservoir is empty; and they have the same nutrient schedule. (Two pumps of each bottle, “Grow” and “Flavour," per liter of new water added.) There’s still no pump, meaning the water in the reservoir is stagnant, but it’s absorbed so quickly, within a few days when the plants are full-sized, that there’s not much risk of mold.
The Mini 1 retails for $259, and for now, the Auk Mini 2 is $229 ($249 for the espresso-and-walnut combination I tested). The Mini 2’s current price is a limited-time launch deal not likely to last past the end of the month. If you’ve been in the market for the Auk specifically, or just an easy-to-maintain indoor herb garden, this is too good a deal to pass up.

I used Claude Cowork to organize my downloaded courses and build a local offline course player with progress tracking, autoplay, subtitles, a Pomodoro timer, mobile access, and custom study plans. It runs on Mac or Windows and keeps everything on your device.
There are plenty of course streaming platforms out there. All of those come with a learning management system where the courses are organized by default and let you keep track of your progress. Some even motivate you to finish the courses on time, while others spam your email inbox because you left on the second day of starting a course.
But I sometimes prefer learning courses offline. I download the entire catalog, whether it’s a YouTube video playlist or courses from third-party websites (if allowed).
Then, I put my phone in silent mode, turn on the Pomodoro timer for 45 minutes to finish as many as possible. This is the most productive way, and the one I recommend to everyone. However, it can get increasingly complex if you have multiple courses and thousands of videos that you need to organize.
Moreover, if you are playing them offline, it’s hard to track your progress, which can quickly create a frustrating experience.
For years, I had no choice except to carefully write a separate note of where my videos are located and how many videos I have finished in each session. But that has changed once I built my own course player. Thanks to Claude, I have built a local course player that organizes all my courses into simple folders and keeps track of my progress. Moreover, since I built it myself, I can add a few features as I want on top of the existing setup.
For instance, I added a native Pomodoro timer, which allows me to focus for 45 min without any distractions, and added the ability to autoplay the next video, which websites lack by default. You need to manually play the next video.
And it doesn’t stop here. Since you are building it on your own using AI, you have complete control to add whatever features you like and can fix all your pain points that you are currently facing while you are learning something offline.
In this guide, you are going to learn how I use Claude Cowork to organize my messy download folders. You will also learn how I created a simple offline course tracker website that organizes files into folders and keeps track of my progress, and also how you can add additional features to it.

How to Build a Local Offline Course Player Using Claude Cowork
This can be done with other co-working agents from OpenAI, such as ChatGPT Work, Codex, and Google’s Antigravity, or using other AI models of your choice. The process is pretty much straightforward and very simple; these AI models will do everything for you and can keep staring at the screen until it’s done and finish your chores.
Before going to the steps, remember that to do this, you need a Claude subscription to access the Claude Cowork feature and a Mac or Windows laptop to create a local course. Now, let’s get started.
Step 1: First, open the Claude app on your Mac or Windows and switch to the Home tab
Step 2: Now switch to Cowork mode.
Step 3: Now select the location of the folder where all your courses are located. Tap on the Add a Folder option.
Step 4: Now enter this prompt and press Enter; this even works if your course files are in zip folders.
Prompt:
“I have a folder of video courses on my computer. Connect to it and help me organize it based on what is actually there. Do not assume any folder structure. First, survey the folder without changing anything. Report the total number of courses, videos, and total storage size. Identify all video formats, including MP4, MKV, WebM, MOV, AVI, and any videos stored inside ZIP or RAR archives. Explain whether the content is stored as a flat folder of videos, one folder per course, nested sub-courses, or a mixture. Identify extra files such as SRT or VTT subtitles, PDFs, slides, exercise files, and code. Look for real problems, including sub-courses buried inside unrelated courses, duplicate content, empty folders, inconsistent or messy names, and filenames that do not sort correctly, such as “Lesson 10” appearing before “Lesson 2.” Then tell me honestly whether the folder is already well organized. If it is, say so and stop. Do not reorganize it unnecessarily. Only propose changes that fix problems you actually found. If changes are needed, show me a detailed plan before touching anything. Specify exactly which folders will be moved, renamed, or set aside, and ask for my approval. If multiple approaches are reasonable, explain them and ask which one I prefer. Never delete anything. Before treating files as duplicates, prove they are identical by comparing filenames and sizes or by calculating checksums, and show me the evidence. Move anything unwanted into a reversible “_removed” folder. After approval, execute the plan and verify that nothing was lost. Reconcile the video count and total size before and after, then show me the final course catalog. Keep subtitles and resources alongside their related videos. Never re-encode, rename, or modify video files themselves. Only reorganize folders. If the folder is very large, work efficiently and avoid reading every file unless necessary”
Step 5: That said, Claude now organizes the course into neat folders, which means 50% of your work is already done.

When I’m asked what to buy if you want to get into making electronic music, I often recommend Elektron’s budget-minded Model:Samples and Model:Cycles grooveboxes. They don’t grab headlines the way Teenage Engineering’s gear or the Telepathic Instruments Orchid do, and even compared to the company’s higher-end and more niche musical offerings like the Digitakt, Octatrack, or Tonverk, they’re often overlooked. But as my collection has grown to include fancier and far more expensive instruments, I still find myself coming back to the Model series.
Don’t overlook Elektron’s budget electronic music instruments
I keep coming back to the criminally slept-on Model:Samples and Model:Cycles.
Those looking to get their first groovebox are often drawn to more familiar brand names like Korg or Roland. And lots of people on Reddit will be quick to recommend the Novation Circuit Tracks (which I personally find confusing and mediocre-sounding). This is probably also partially due to the reputation Elektron gear has for being obtuse. If you’re an established music maker and aren’t deterred by a complicated workflow, you’re probably going to pick up a more powerful Elektron box, like the Digitone or Syntakt. That leaves the Models lineup in a weird no man’s land, and that’s a shame.
The primary difference between the two Models instruments is that the Model:Cycles uses FM synthesis and the Model:Samples, appropriately enough, plays samples. (It is not technically a sampler, however, since it can’t record samples, and instead they have to be loaded over USB.)
The Model:Cycles is built around a streamlined version of the engine found in the Digitone, one of my favorite-sounding synths of all time. This is a modern take on FM that can do the cold bells and icy pads you associate with iconic instruments like the DX7 (the iconic sound of the ’80s). But it also does modern glassy keys and aggressive turn-of-the-millennium EDM bass.
The two are more alike than not, though. They’re both six-track grooveboxes with six velocity-sensitive pads and plenty of knobs for hands-on controls, and they look almost identical. But most importantly, they feature Elektron’s legendary step sequencer without being nearly as intimidating as the company’s more expensive and notoriously complicated offerings.
The sequencer is built around what the company calls “trigs” and “locks.” Trigs are basically just events, typically triggering a note, and locks are just step-specific settings. It seems like a simple enough concept, but it makes these instruments far more capable than they might seem at first blush.
Six tracks isn’t a lot to work with. Once you’ve loaded up a kick, snare, and hi-hat, then you’ve only got three more tracks for bass, any melodic elements, and additional percussion. But sound locks allow you to change samples or presets on a per-step basis. That means, so long as they never play simultaneously, you can have your kick and snare share the same track, then you can put your hi-hats and other percussion on a second track, and leave the four other tracks for everything else. This is just the most obvious example of how locks expand the possibilities of what might seem rather limited on paper.
The sequencer can be treated like a simple step sequencer where you drop a four-on-the-floor kick and a snare on the backbeat. But it also grows with you as your skills improve, and you want to create more complex tracks. Trig conditions, for example, allow you to set rules that govern when certain steps are triggered, like only every third time through the loop, only when you press the fill button, or only if a previous trig condition is met. This means that you can create a huge amount of variety in a single 64-step pattern. And then you can chain several of those patterns together to create complex and evolving arrangements that just aren’t possible on most gear in this price range.
The Models boxes are also just incredibly fun. Where Elektron’s other gear demands a lot of menu diving, the Model:Samples and Model:Cycles are immediately approachable and built for live performance. It’s easy to trigger a drum fill with the push of a button, tweak a knob to open the filter on a bass, or briefly bathe a lead melody in delay.
Control-all might be the most fun feature, which, as you might have guessed, allows you to control all the tracks simultaneously. Bury your entire track in reverb as you start cranking up the distortion and lowering the pitch of all your samples to create a mangled, chaotic breakdown. And then immediately undo it all and drop the beat again by pressing the function and pattern buttons. The Model:Samples and Model:Cycles encourage jamming in a way that frankly a lot of electronic music gear just doesn’t, and it’s an absolute blast.
Now, they’re not without their flaws. The pads are pretty mediocre. Having to load samples via USB rather than recording them directly kinda sucks. And the lack of polyphony (each sequencer track can only play one note at a time) is a bit of a bummer. But at $349, it’s hard to complain. Plus they can be snagged used for as little as $200 on Reverb or Craigslist. Frankly, they’re some of the best bargains in music hardware and a great place to start your journey into producing electronic music.

Multiple people killed and child seriously injured in head-on motorway crash
The motorway is closed in both directions while emergency services attend the scene
A number of people have died and a child is among those seriously injured after a head-on collision between two cars on a motorway in Co Kildare.
A gardaí spokesperson said one of the cars was travelling in the wrong direction on the M9 northbound.
Gardaí said they are investigating the circumstances of the collision at junction 3 at about 3am on Sunday.
Emergency services were alerted to a vehicle travelling southbound on the M9 northbound carriageway.
The vehicle was travelling between junctions 3 and 4 when it collided head-on with another car.
A gardaí spokesperson said: “A number of fatalities have occurred and no further details are available at this time.”
The spokesperson said the female driver and front-seat passenger, both aged in their 30s, of the second car have been taken to Tallaght University Hospital and both remain in critical condition.
A female rear-seat passenger, aged in her 20s, was taken to St Luke’s General Hospital and is in a serious condition.
The third passenger, a child, has been taken to the Children’s Health Ireland at Crumlin and is in a serious condition.
The M9 from junction 3 to junction 4 northbound and southbound remains closed with local diversions in place.
A garda forensic collision examination will take place.
Gardaí are appealing for anyone who may have witnessed the collision to come forward.
Fiosrú, the Office of the Police Ombudsman, has been notified.
A statement from Fiosrú said: “The referral was made following a fatal road traffic incident on the M9.
“One of Fiosrú’s on-call team of investigators attended the scene and its independent investigation is ongoing.
“In line with its statutory remit, Fiosrú’s investigation relates to incidents involving contact with gardaí where a member of the public has died or been seriously injured.”
The statement added: “A referral does not necessarily mean a garda or gardaí have been accused of wrongdoing.
“Instead, it means that Fiosrú should independently investigate the incident to ascertain whether or not the act or omission of a garda or gardaí may have resulted in the death of, or serious harm to, a person.
“As the matter is now under investigation, pursuant to section 208(1)(b) of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, Fiosrú cannot make any further comment.”

Suspect killed a missing North Carolina woman and then stole her dog, cops say
Floyd Morris Long is accused of killing Shaquina Latavia Harris ‘on or around July 5’ and then stealing her dog
A North Carolina man has been accused of killing a 29-year-old woman who was missing for weeks — and then stealing her Yorkie terrier mix dog.
Floyd Morris Long, 45, was arrested by police in Charlotte Saturday in connection to the murder of Shaquina Latavia Harris, who was last seen leaving Atrium Health Carolinas Medical Center on July 2, WSOC-TV reported.
Her sudden disappearance last month was out of character and prompted her friends and family to hang missing persons posters around town in mid-July, just weeks after she was first reported missing.
“I ain’t sleeping. I can’t sleep ‘cause we don’t know if you’re okay, if you’re not,” her aunt, Lakisha Harris, told WSOC in July.
“On July 3, Shaquina goes completely blank. Nobody hears from her, sees her,” she added. “Sigh, it’s just not like her.”
Michaela Carter, Harris’ best friend, told the outlet last month that were “not stopping until we find her.”
Harris’ last known contact with her loved ones was a FaceTime call from a home on Woodford Bridge Drive the night of July 2. Records show that Long’s address is on the same street.
Her friends said that she had been visiting her newborn niece at the hospital the day that she was last seen.
In addition to hanging posters, friends and family searched the greenway near where Harris was last seen.
However, new court documents accuse Long of killing Harris “on or around July 5” and then stealing her dog, described as a white, long-haired Yorkie terrier mix.
The relationship between Long and Harris was not immediately clear. No further details about how police linked him to the alleged murder were released.
He was also charged with concealing or failing to report a death. Prosecutors allege in the court documents that Long secretly disposed of Harris’ body with the intent of concealing her death, according to Queen City News.
Long was booked Saturday in the Mecklenburg County Jail and charged with first-degree murder, felony larceny of a dog and concealing/failure to report death.
He is currently being held without bail.

Athens cleans its all-marble Olympic stadium for the first time in over a century
Athens’ iconic Panathenaic Stadium is undergoing its first systematic cleaning in more than a century
ATHENS, Greece -- It has welcomed marathon runners, rock stars and the first modern Olympic athletes. Now it’s time for a monumental scrub.
Athens’ U-shaped Panathenaic Stadium — made entirely of white marble — is getting its first systematic cleaning in more than a century.
Rebuilt for the first modern Olympics in 1896, the site is the ceremonial send-off point for the Olympic flame, including for Los Angeles 2028.
The stadium is made of the same glittering marble used on the Acropolis, making the cleanup job delicate.
The work is revealing a monument changed by time, weather and millions of visitors. Cleaners in white and blue overalls move across the stadium’s 47 steep tiers with thin spray lances, using clean water at carefully controlled, low pressure. Machines vacuum up the runoff as they go.
“The goal of cleaning is not to make everything white. It’s to remove the dirt and the first layers of organic material that are deposited on the surface,” said Dimitris Selemis, a senior conservator at the site.
“The idea is to clean all the material that (contains) dirt from the surface, so we have a better understanding of the monument,” he said, noting that there is more weed growth and dirt in areas that receive less direct sunlight.
Crews are also using steam to remove blotches of chewing gum, which have turned black over time. Stadium officials say chewing gum, high heels and soft-drink stains are among the main culprits that stain the marble.
Now slowly being revealed, the original gleaming look of the venue earned it the widely used Greek nickname “Kallimarmaro,” or beautiful marble.
“We call it Kallimarmaro because it is made of the finest marble, the best that was ever produced ... We are very proud of it,” Isidoros Kouvelos, president of the Hellenic Olympic Committee, told The Associated Press in an interview.
“It needed to be cleaned of everything that has accumulated over all these years," he said. "This way the Panathenaic Stadium will show all its brilliance and will once again be the foremost monument of humanity for the Olympic Movement.”
Built into a natural ravine, the stadium’s site was used for ancient Greek athletic contests and later Roman spectacles before falling into centuries of disuse.
Since its 1896 revival, it has staged fashion shows, rock concerts, boxing matches and national celebrations — as well as lavish patriotic ceremonies ordered by a military dictatorship in the 1960s.
Today, it’s a popular draw for tourists. Apart from the cleanup, the Kallimarmaro is also getting a new track, upgraded lighting and fresh support facilities. The project is privately funded by a shipping company and overseen by the Hellenic Olympic Committee with guidance from Culture Ministry experts.
The work will continue through 2026 but is currently concentrated on the stadium’s “sling,” or curved end, in time for the next torch-passing ceremony on Sept. 10.
That will be for the Dakar Youth Olympics, scheduled for Oct. 31-Nov. 13 in Senegal, which will be the first Olympic competition ever hosted in Africa.
IOC President Kirsty Coventry, a swimming gold medal winner from Zimbabwe, is due to attend the Sept. 10 ceremony, Kouvelos said.

Boy, 4, among six dead in Indiana after days of storms and record-setting flooding

At least six people have died after days of severe storms and widespread flooding in Indiana, where floodwaters on the White River in Indianapolis reached their peak Sunday.

Battering Indiana over the past week, heavy rain forced local rivers to crest and set new records.
In Anderson and Noblesville, the White River reached over 24 feet (7.32 meters), surpassing records established back in 1913.
Indianapolis Mayor Joe Hogsett said the city is experiencing its worst inundation in more than 30 years.
Gov. Mike Braun’s office confirmed that emergency crews carried out more than 350 evacuations along with numerous welfare and rescue checks elsewhere in the state, including at a senior mobile home community north of Indianapolis.
President Donald Trump on Saturday granted Braun’s request for federal disaster assistance to aid local response and recovery efforts.
The torrential rainfall and destructive floodwaters were among the impacts of severe storm systems that have wreaked havoc across the Midwest and beyond in recent days.
Tornadoes, heavy rain, and flash floods inflicted widespread damage on communities ranging from Illinois to western Pennsylvania.

Where do Canada-U.S. trade negotiations stand? Here's a sector-by-sector breakdown
Canadian and American negotiators remain at impasse with tariff deadline days away
Canada is continuing to negotiate a trade deal with the United States that will allow it to both avoid U.S. President Donald Trump's crippling tariff threat — set to come into effect on Wednesday — and get some additional relief on existing tariffs in key sectors.
But after a flurry of meetings between top Canadian and American negotiators over the last three weeks, the two countries remain at an impasse heading into the home stretch.
Sources have told CBC News that Canadian negotiators fear there may be no way to avert Trump's 50 per cent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian goods, as Washington digs in on its demands while Ottawa tries to persuade provinces to lift restrictions on American alcohol.
The U.S. claims it's imposing the tariffs because of Canadian discrimination toward its automobile, dairy and alcohol sectors.
With two days left to negotiate, here's what sources have told CBC News about where Canada-U.S. trade talks stand on Monday morning, broken down by each key sector.
Automobiles
According to sources, the U.S. is proposing to reduce its existing auto tariffs from the current 25 per cent down to 12.5 per cent, an offer the Canadian side believes is not good enough.
The U.S. has cited issues with Canada's auto trade as one reason why it intends to impose its 50 per cent tariffs. The White House argues Canada imposes tariffs and quotas on vehicles imported to Canada from the U.S. — but not other countries.
Lana Payne, national president of Unifor and a member of Prime Minister Mark Carney's advisory committee on Canada-U.S. economic relations, said on Friday that Trump is missing the fact that his auto tariffs hurt U.S. companies.
"We can't afford to give any more concessions here, and we need a good deal. And that means we've got to grind it out until the very end," Payne said.
Payne has previously warned that agreeing to the levies in writing now could give Washington a path to seeking permanent auto tariffs as part of a renegotiated Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA).
Sources say, however, that Canada will need to concede some ground in any sort of deal.
Dairy
Trump has long lambasted Canada's supply management system, which allows a certain amount of U.S. dairy to enter Canada tariff-free before steep duties are applied.
In announcing its 50 per cent tariff threat, the White House said Canada established tariff-rate quotas on cheese from the U.S. that are "much more restrictive" than the quotas applied on similar imports of cheese from the European Union.
On Friday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer reiterated that argument and said that "we have an uneven dairy treatment."
Sources have told CBC News that Canada will need to concede on dairy in any new deal. It's unclear what Canada has offered on the matter.
But concessions on this front could be politically dangerous for the Carney government.
Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette said on Friday that supply management is a red line for her province and that several thousand farms and jobs depend on Canada's dairy industry.
Alcohol
The federal government has told provinces to be ready as soon as possible to put U.S. alcohol back on store shelves in case a tariff deal is reached, sources have told CBC News. That irritant is another reason behind Trump's 50 per cent tariff threat.
Only Alberta and Saskatchewan, which have privatized alcohol retail systems, have resumed the sale of U.S. booze. Other provinces have maintained their bans, although there has been division among them for months over whether to relent.
Sources have told CBC News that Canadian negotiators fear this is a significant obstacle in avoiding Trump's tariff threat. The bans are entirely provincially controlled, but some provinces have said they'll only relent if they get relief for their sectors.
On Thursday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he will end the province's boycott only if negotiators secure what he describes as a "fair deal" that addresses tariffs on key sectors.
"If we get a fair deal that will protect our steel sector, our auto sector, our forestry sector, agriculture sector, manufacturing sector, then we'd be more than happy to bring booze back on the shelves," Ford said.
Similarly, Fréchette has said she's open to allowing U.S. wine to return to store shelves, but she'll need to see reductions in tariffs on key sectors like aluminum and manufacturing.
Sources have also said the federal government has asked provinces and territories to be prepared to drop retaliatory procurement rules that favour Canadian suppliers in case a deal is made.
Steel and aluminum
Canada is pushing to have the Trump administration lower its existing tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper — which range from 10 to 50 per cent.
The Carney government has announced various measures over the last few months to prop up the sectors, including establishing a $1-billion loan program through the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) so companies most affected by tariffs can get the money they need to stay in business.
Last week, the federal government announced it would pump an additional $100 million into Canada's steel industry with a new program that will pay for half the costs of transporting Canadian-made steel by ship or rail within the country.
The program is slated to operate for one year, or until the $100-million funding envelope runs dry, with a single producer eligible for a maximum rebate of $50 million.
When asked what will happen to the program if it runs out of money before the end of its one-year timeline, Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon hinted that an extension may be considered.
Softwood lumber
According to sources, Canada is pushing for relief on tariffs the U.S. has slapped on Canadian softwood lumber, but Washington is not interested in discussions on this front. The existing total tariff rate is 45 per cent.
The Canada-U.S. fight over softwood lumber predates the Trump administration by decades and was also a point of concern when former U.S. president Joe Biden was in office.
Sources say the Trump administration's view is that the softwood issue should be negotiated separately from the other sectoral tariffs.
Trump's looming 50 per cent tariffs are planned to hit items like charcoal, plywood, wooden doors, wooden fixtures and various lumber products. It's expected to be especially challenging for British Columbia.
Ashlee Cribb, CEO of Gorman Bros. Lumber Ltd. in West Kelowna, told CBC's The House last week lumber tariffs need to be resolved quickly and that it will be difficult for the company to respond to the additional tariffs.
On Friday, B.C. Premier David Eby said U.S. lumber tariffs need to be addressed and that Ottawa is "well aware" they are one of B.C.'s biggest concerns.
Critical minerals, energy and security
The Americans are seeking a deal that would see preferential access to Canadian critical minerals and cover security and energy.
Canada has several projects located across the country that mine and develop many critical minerals the U.S. desires, such as lithium, nickel, cobalt and copper. Ottawa is also working to advance production through its national strategy, released in 2022.
Earlier this month, Trump announced the U.S. government will invest $3 billion in critical minerals and battery projects to increase domestic production and boost national security and industry policy.
The White House needs critical minerals to replenish weapons stockpiles depleted during its ongoing war with Iran and reduce U.S. dependence on Chinese supply chains.
There's also the question of Canada reviewing its F-35 fighter jet purchase from the United States. Carney launched the review in March 2025 in response to diplomatic and trade tensions with the Trump administration.
Last week, National Defence Minister David McGuinty acknowledged the F-35s are "being examined by our negotiating team."
"The question of what is part and parcel of that negotiation continues. And I am hopeful we will come to a successful outcome in due course," he said.

'Neglect, insecurity, or indignity': SC rules senior citizen tribunals can order eviction to protect elderly parents
SC rules senior citizen tribunals can order eviction from property when necessary to protect elderly parents’ maintenance, dignity and security.
The Supreme Court has ruled that tribunals constituted under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 have the power to order eviction of persons from a property when such a measure is necessary to ensure the senior citizen’s maintenance or protection.
A bench of justices PS Narasimha and Alok Aradhe said that the legislation was intended to ensure that advancing age does not become synonymous with “neglect, insecurity, or indignity” and reflects values deeply rooted in the country’s civilisational ethos, which “revere the mother and the father as divine.”
It emphasised that the measure of a civilised society is often reflected in the dignity, respect and security it affords to its elderly. “Across cultures, religions, and civilisations, senior citizens have been regarded not merely as dependents requiring care, but as repositories of wisdom, experience, and collective memory whose guidance enriches families and society alike,” said the bench.
Also Read | SC seeks report from rent controller in Gurugram over tenant’s eviction order
It added that the fundamental right provisions relating to life, dignity and equality envisage a social order that protects the vulnerable and enables every individual to live with dignity throughout the course of life and that “this commitment finds statutory expression in the Act.”
The court said the power to order eviction flows from the statutory scheme itself. While Section 7 provides for constitution of tribunals and Section 8 empowers them to conduct inquiries through a summary procedure with powers of a civil court, Section 27 expressly bars the jurisdiction of civil courts. “On this analogy, we have no hesitation in holding that the tribunal under the Act has power to order eviction in order to ensure the maintenance or protection of a senior citizen,” the bench held in a recent order.
Also Read | Supreme Court directs man to handover properties to 80-year-old father
The judgment came in an appeal filed by Ravi Kant Gupta, whose 81-year-old mother had been forced to leave his residential premises and reside in an old-age facility. Gupta had approached the district magistrate seeking eviction of his son from the property, alleging that his son did not permit his grandmother to stay in the house and had created nuisance.
The sub-divisional magistrate ordered the son’s eviction in November 2022, holding that the premises was Gupta’s self-acquired property. The district magistrate upheld the order and directed the son and his wife to hand over possession of the premises. The Allahabad High Court, however, subsequently quashed the eviction orders, holding that authorities under the 2007 Act did not have the power to order eviction. It reiterated the view while dismissing Gupta’s review petition in January 2024.
The Supreme Court set aside both high court orders and restored the eviction orders passed by the authorities under the Act.
Also Read | SC rues tragedy of elderly, restrains son from parting with ailing mother’s property
SC cites constitutional protections, earlier rulings
The bench emphasised that the Act has to be understood in the context of the constitutional commitment to protect vulnerable persons and enable every individual to live with dignity. It referred to Articles 21 and 41 of the Constitution and said Parliament had enacted the law to provide a speedy remedy to senior citizens.
The court also relied on earlier judgments, including the three-judge bench ruling in S Vanitha Vs Deputy Commissioner (2021), to hold that eviction may be ordered where it is necessary and expedient to ensure the maintenance and protection of a senior citizen or parent. It noted that subsequent two-judge benches had reiterated the same position.

“Breakups are… tough.”
Open Mike Eagle and Kenny Segal crafted a hip hop breakup masterpiece
DOOMED! pairs Eagle’s deeply personal lyrics with some of Segal’s most commanding beats.
Open Mike Eagle and Kenny Segal crafted a hip hop breakup masterpiece
DOOMED! pairs Eagle’s deeply personal lyrics with some of Segal’s most commanding beats.
It’s the opening lines of an interlude towards the end of DOOMED! Called “It Happens in Every Universe.” It’s also basically the thesis of the entire record. It’s no grand revelation, but it’s a well-trodden subject that Open Mike Eagle manages to mine for artistic gold.
Eagle’s subject matter is usually personal, and his productions tinged with nostalgia. But DOOMED! is his most intimate album yet. A lot of that is due to the production from Kenny Segal. The two have traveled in the same orbit and worked together before, but this is the first full-length album release from the two.
These are some of Segal’s most commanding beats since Maps, his 2023 record with Billy Woods. There’s still warbly piano samples, strings, detuned sax melodies, and psychedelic synths, but everything feels more grounded and meaders less. Opener “Out to Lunch” even has fully on-the-grid hi-hats that tick robotically.
That gives way to “Streets of Rage: Public Arguments Edition,” which grooves along with a loose clap, jazzy piano, and confident bassline that recalls the work of Madlib. Over this lowkey funk, Eagle spins an oblique tale of fighting with a significant other. “She cut deep with short barbs, but twist me up with a lil whisper.”
It turns out that Segal and Eagle are a perfect pair. The rapper’s melodrama and eye for microscopic details play off the producer’s woozy and forlorn beats that are occasionally punctuated by a sense of foreboding. On the Billy Woods-featuring “She Swear I’m Colorblind,” Eagle intones on the chorus:
Some reason, shit got twisted,
Told me it was all my fault, she said
“Pay attention when I talk.”
The backing track is stabbed through with bursts of windchimes before ending on a high-pitched whine that feels like the onset of a panic attack.
“Unfinished Concrete Initials” contains some of Eagle’s most vulnerable bits, like, “In my daydreams your name’s curse words so I bleeped it,” and:
My memories like landmines and they heinous
Clicking high pootify collaborative playlists
Agonizing over deletions
Flushing evidence, pain is better in secret
There are still sparks of Open Mike Eagle’s sense of humor, though. “Schrödinger’s Green Room (There but Uninvited)” opens with him awkwardly proclaiming as if he’s trying to be heard over a bad phone connection, “All my thoughts is intrusive, there’s a DJ in my head, and he picks all his own music, it’s so confusing.” And, as you’d expect from the man who penned “Sweatpants Spiderman,” there are countless pop culture references to anime, Kitty Pride, Beanie Babies, Flipmode Squad, and even The Proclaimers.
Open Mike Eagle and Kenny Segal’s DOOMED! is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including YouTube Music, Apple Music, Spotify, Qobuz, and Deezer.

Flesh-eating bacteria sounds like the premise of a bad horror movie, but it’s a growing – and potentially fatal – threat to people in the U.S. and beyond.
Vibrio vulnificus, a type of flesh-eating bacteria that thrives in warm seawater, is once again threatening the safety of beachgoers and raw shellfish enthusiasts. To date, Louisiana has reported nine cases, with five fatalities, and Florida has reported 14 cases, with two fatalities. As of late June, Maryland has reported 72 cases.
I’m a professor at the Indiana University School of Medicine, where my laboratory studies microbiology and infectious disease. Here’s why health officials are so concerned about this deadly infection – and ways to avoid contracting it.
What does ‘flesh-eating’ mean?
There are several types of bacteria that can infect open wounds and cause a rare condition called necrotising fasciitis. These bacteria do not merely damage the surface of the skin – they release toxins that destroy the underlying tissue, including muscles, nerves and blood vessels. Once the bacteria reach the bloodstream, they gain ready access to additional tissues and organ systems. If left untreated, necrotising fasciitis can be fatal, sometimes within 48 hours.
The bacterial species group A Streptococcus, or group A strep, is the most common culprit behind necrotising fasciitis. But the U.S. Centers for Disease Control points to Vibrio vulnificus as an additional suspect. There are only 150 to 200 cases of Vibrio vulnificus infections in the United States each year, but the mortality rate is high, with 1 in 5 people succumbing to the infection. Cases have also increased in Europe.
How do you catch flesh-eating bacteria?
Vibrio vulnificus primarily lives in warm seawater but can also be found in brackish water – areas where the ocean mixes with freshwater. Most infections in the U.S. occur in the warmer months, between May and October. People who swim, fish or wade in these bodies of water can contract the bacteria through an open wound or sore.
Vibrio vulnificus can also get into seafood harvested from these waters, especially shellfish like oysters. Eating such foods raw or undercooked can lead to food poisoning, and handling them while having an open wound can provide an entry point for the bacteria to cause necrotising fasciitis. In the U.S., Vibrio vulnificus is a leading cause of seafood-associated fatalities.
Why are flesh-eating bacteria infections rising?
Vibrio vulnificus is found in warm coastal waters around the world, like those of the southern Gulf Coast states in the U.S. But rising ocean temperatures due to global warming are creating new habitats for this type of bacteria, which can now be found along the East Coast as far north as New York and Connecticut. A recent study noted that Vibrio vulnificus wound infections increased eightfold between 1988 and 2018 in the eastern U.S.
Vibrio vulnificus is also spreading into coastal areas of Northern Europe and the Baltic Sea as a consequence of climate change driving warming water temperatures.
Climate change is also fueling stronger hurricanes and storm surges, which have been associated with spikes in flesh-eating bacteria infection cases due to increasing contact with seawater or brackish water.
The number of people around the world who are most vulnerable to severe infection, including those with diabetes and those taking medications that suppress immunity, is on the rise.
What are symptoms of and treatments for necrotising fasciitis?
Early symptoms of an infected wound include fever, redness, intense pain or swelling at the site of injury. If you have these symptoms, seek medical attention without delay. Necrotising fasciitis can progress quickly, producing ulcers, blisters, skin discoloration and pus.
Treating flesh-eating bacteria is a race against time. Clinicians administer antibiotics directly into the bloodstream to kill the bacteria. In many cases, damaged tissue needs to be surgically removed to stop the rapid spread of the infection. This sometimes means amputating affected limbs.
Researchers are concerned that an increasing number of cases are becoming impossible to treat because Vibrio vulnificus has evolved resistance to certain antibiotics.
How do I protect myself?
The CDC offers several recommendations to help prevent infection.
People who have a fresh cut, including a new piercing or tattoo, are advised to stay out of water that could be home to Vibrio vulnificus. Otherwise, the wound should be completely covered with a waterproof bandage. The tiniest scrape or cut is enough for Vibrio vulnificus to get under your skin. One case was even traced to freshly shaven legs.
People with an open wound should also avoid handling raw seafood or fish. Wounds that occur while fishing, preparing seafood or swimming should be washed immediately and thoroughly with soap and water.
Anyone can contract necrotising fasciitis, but the elderly and people with weakened immune systems are most susceptible to severe disease. This includes people taking immunosuppressive medications or those who have pre-existing conditions such as liver disease, cancer, HIV or diabetes.
It is important to bear in mind that necrotising fasciitis presently remains very rare. But given its severity, it is beneficial to stay informed.
Cases of infection by Vibrio vulnificus are about as rare as shark attacks. While shark bites get more attention, the microscopic shark that is Vibrio vulnificans can also rob you of life or limb.
This is an updated version of an article originally published on Sept. 25, 2023.
(Bill Sullivan, Professor of Microbiology and Immunology, Indiana University)

P.V. Sindhu returns to the World Championships chasing a place in history. With five medals already to her name, the Indian star needs one more podium finish to become the first women’s singles player to win six medals at the showpiece event.
Below is a quick recap of her five BWF Worlds medal-winning performances.
2013 Guangzhou — Bronze
Sindhu claimed her first World Championships medal as an 18-year-old, announcing herself on the global stage. She beat defending champion Wang Yihan of China in the third round and then defeated compatriot Wang Shixian in the quarterfinals before losing to eventual champion Ratchanok Intanon of Thailand in the semifinals.
2014 Copenhagen — Bronze
Sindhu followed her breakthrough with a second successive World Championships bronze, becoming the first Indian to win medals at consecutive editions of the tournament. She beat Wang Shixian again in the quarterfinals before losing to eventual champion Carolina Marin in the semifinals. The same year, she won a Commonwealth Games singles bronze and was part of India’s bronze-medal-winning women’s team at the Asian Games.
2017 Glasgow — Silver
Sindhu reached her first World Championships final, producing an instant classic against Nozomi Okuhara. She lost 19-21, 22-20, 20-22 in a gruelling match that lasted an hour and 50 minutes at the Emirates Arena. Despite the defeat, it remains one of the most celebrated matches in badminton history, and it deepened her rivalry with Okuhara.
2018 Nanjing — Silver
Sindhu made back-to-back finals, this time facing familiar foe Carolina Marin of Spain. She fell to Marin to win her second consecutive silver medal. The result extended her run of near-misses at the top step but reinforced her status as the tournament’s most consistent performer of the era.
2019 Basel — Gold
Sindhu finally broke through in her third straight final, this time avenging her 2017 heartbreak. She beat Japan’s Nozomi Okuhara 21-7, 21-7 in just 36 minutes to become the first Indian to win the BWF World Championships title, capping a remarkable arc from two bronzes to two silvers to gold.
