India is facing a critical nationwide shortage of two key chemotherapy drugs, cisplatin and carboplatin, driven by soaring global platinum raw material costs, West Asia shipping route disruptions, and domestic price caps. While government hospitals in several States have managed to stabilise supplies, private hospitals in many parts are still facing a crunch. For patients, this has meant interruptions or delays in life-saving treatment. In response, the government last month raised temporarily ceiling rates for the two drugs by 50%, to help restart halted domestic manufacturing lines.
What’s happening?
Cisplatin is a chemotherapeutic agent used in the treatment of solid tumors as well as certain blood cancers. Carboplatin is a second generation platinum compound that is also used to treat solid tumours. Both are among the most widely used chemotherapy drugs in India and are indispensable in the treatment of several cancers, including ovarian, head and neck, lung, gall bladder, urinary bladder, breast and testicular cancers.
Prices for platinum—the core raw material used in cisplatin and carboplatin—more than doubled, making old price-controlled manufacturing rates financially unviable for companies. Additionally, geopolitical conflicts and shipping constraints through West Asia have restricted raw material imports from primary global suppliers. This resulted in several generic makers temporarily slowing or stopping production of these drugs, says Sayoni Bhanja, consultant, medical oncology at HCG Cancer Centre, Kolkata.
Impact on hospitals, patients
At the Cancer Institute (WIA), Adyar, in Chennai, Kalpana Balakrishnan, chief executive officer and medical director, said that the shortage has been ongoing for nearly seven months due to the war and has had significant impacts. “The cheapest drug, cisplatin, a first-generation platinum drug, is not available. Carboplatin and oxaliplatin, which are second and third generation platinum drugs, are considerably more expensive.”
Sujith Kumar Mullapally, senior consultant - medical oncology, Apollo Proton Cancer Centre, Chennai said that the hospital has not received cisplatin and carboplatin from its regular companies for a long time now and was depending on companies which are Indian generic companies. He added that they have managed up until now with available stocks, and that through medical oncology forums, significant efforts have been made to inform the necessary authorities.
In Karnataka, some hospitals reported stocks sufficient for only six to eight weeks.
Amit Rauthan, head of medical oncology, immunotherapy and precision medicine at Manipal Hospital, Old Airport Road, Bengaluru, said cisplatin and carboplatin are also critical in treating childhood cancers such as neuroblastoma, hepatoblastoma, germ cell tumours and retinoblastoma, and that their therapeutic role cannot be easily replaced by alternative medicines.
Vijay Kumar Srinivasalu, senior consultant in medical oncology at Sakra World Hospital, Bengaluru, said platinum-based chemotherapy continues to be the backbone of treatment for several solid tumours despite advances in targeted therapies and immunotherapy. Treatment delays or substitution with less effective regimens could compromise outcomes, particularly in curative-intent cancers. This is especially significant in concurrent chemoradiation for cervical and head and neck cancers, where weekly cisplatin plays a vital role in enhancing the effectiveness of radiation therapy, he noted.
For patients, this has meant delays and interruptions in treatment, additional stress, as well as increased costs.
The immediate fallout, said, Sandeep Nayak, chairman of oncology, MACS-Renova Oncology Institute, KIMS Hospital, Bengaluru lands directly on cancer patients: while alternative treatment regimens exist, they are generally less effective, non-standard, and can carry higher costs or different toxicity profiles.
The disruptions are leading to treatment delays, changes in chemotherapy regimens and additional financial and psychological stress for patients and their families, warned Smitha Saldanha, consultant in medical oncology at HCG Cancer Hospital, K.R. Road, Bengaluru.
Bhawna Sirohi, medical oncologist and medical director of Vedanta Medical Research Foundation, Raipur, Chhattisgarh, said for patients this may mean a compromise on curative cancer treatment.
How the government sector is faring
The government sector seems to be doing better in several States.
At the Regional Cancer Centre, Kerala in Thiruvananthapuram, treatment was not disrupted as the hospital had adequate stock of platinum-based drugs to tide over a few months, said director, R Rejnishkumar. “We were beginning to get worried too, as we could not get any response for the purchase tenders we floated. But now that the government has revised the prices, our purchase process is going forward and I am told that we will get new stock soon,” Dr. Rejnish said.
The Karnataka government-run Kidwai Memorial Institute of Oncology in Bengaluru has said it currently has adequate stocks and multiple procurement channels to ensure continuity of care. “We have annual tenders in place and procure medicines through the Central Medical Store as well as the Kidwai Cancer Drug Foundation (KCDF). We also have multiple vendors, and non-governmental organisations support us by supplying these drugs,” said KMIO director (in charge), R. Krishnappa.
At the Delhi State Cancer Institute, both cisplatin and carboplatin injections are currently available and chemotherapy services are continuing as per clinical schedules, said Pragya Shukla, head of clinical oncology.
Sources in the T.N. government said that cisplatin was in the essential drugs list of the Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation and hence, its supply was ensured. However, carboplatin, a speciality drug, was unavailable for bulk purchases but hospitals were managing through local purchases.
In Telangana, however, the Mehdi Nawaz Jung Institute of Oncology and Regional Cancer Centre in Hyderabad, the State’s largest and only government tertiary cancer care hospital, has been grappling with a shortage of both cisplatin and carboplatin for the past two months, with supplies falling well short of its monthly requirement. Sadashivudu Gundeti, Director of MNJ Institute of Oncology, said the institute requires thousands of vials of the two chemotherapy drugs every month but is currently able to procure only a few hundred vials. Suppliers have informed the hospital that they were currently unable to meet its full requirement, he said. He expressed hope that supplies could become adequate by the end of August.
What the government has done
On June 12, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) invoked special clauses to raise the price cap of cisplatin from ₹7.26 to ₹10.89 per mL, and carboplatin from ₹60.49 rupees to ₹90.74 per mL, citing public interest. The increase is a one-time revision and will be reviewed after six months, the NPPA said. India is heavily dependent on imported platinum, and the measure was aimed at boosting domestic manufacture to restock depleted supply chains.
Boben Thomas, a consultant medical and paediatric oncologist in Thiruvananthapuram said companies have now resumed manufacturing these drugs. However, doctors have pointed out that short-term measures are not a permanent solution.
Long-term strategies
With more than 1.5 million new cancer cases diagnosed annually in India, Dr. Saldanha said uninterrupted access to essential oncology medicines must be treated as a national healthcare priority.
While describing the recent revision of ceiling prices as a useful short-term measure, Dr. Srinivasalu said India requires a long-term oncology drug security framework, including strategic reserves of essential cancer medicines, diversified domestic manufacturing, stronger active pharmaceutical ingredient supply chains, centralised procurement and an early-warning system for anticipated shortages.
Dr. Saldanha called for coordinated action involving manufacturers, regulators, healthcare providers and policymakers to strengthen domestic production, build strategic buffer stocks and ensure equitable distribution of essential chemotherapy drugs across the country.
A Union Health Ministry official said the Central government has taken all steps to ensure that the supply chain stays stable. In case any State or patient faces any issue regarding availability or access to the drug, they may approach the concerned department, the official said.
(With inputs from Afshan Yasmeen in Bengaluru, Shrabana Chatterjee in Kolkata, Serena Josephine M. in Chennai, C. Maya in Thiruvananthapuram, Bindu Shajan Perappadan in Delhi and Siddharth Kumar Singh in Hyderabad.)

12 more bodies are recovered in Zimbabwe's ferry disaster, bringing death toll to 84
Authorities in Zimbabwe continue searching for bodies after an overloaded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba last week, killing more than 80 people
HARARE, Zimbabwe -- Authorities on Sunday searched for more bodies from an over loaded ferry that capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe last week as the death toll in the disaster rose to more than 80 people.
The ferry capsized in strong waves on Tuesday. Police on Sunday said the death toll had risen to 84, from 72 the previous day as more bodies were recovered. Zimbabwe’s disaster management agency has said 77 people were rescued.
Estimates had put the number of passengers as high as 153 on a ferry authorized to carry 90 people, but the latest official figures now suggest the number of passengers could be even higher.
Police in the southern African country said “search efforts are still underway in a bid to recover victims identified as missing.”
The aging ferry was traveling from the town of Kariba to rural and fishing communities in the country’s northwest, where roads are damaged and public transportation is scarce.
Among the dead are 18 children, with the youngest just 1 year old. According to police, 16 of the victims were aged 10 or younger.
Kariba is the world’s largest human-made lake by volume, created by damming the mighty Zambezi River in the late 1950s and early 1960s. It stretches more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) and is up to 40 kilometers (25 miles) wide in places.
Zimbabwe and Zambia share the lake, with their border running through its middle.

In a whitewashed basement in a village south of Kabul, a dozen young women bustle about, stirring cauldrons of bubbling cherries and plums, and sticking labels on glass jam jars. Ventures like this are one of the rare spaces where women are still able to gain skills and employment in Taliban-ruled Afghanistan.
It is run by Najia, a 47-year-old Afghan entrepreneur and mother of nine children who was married at the age of 14.
If the authorities hadn't barred girls and young women from secondary schools and universities, many of the women in this workshop, including Naija's daughters, would be studying for a different kind of future.
But now, even this is being squeezed too. Recent rules say women have to ask men to take their products to market, and only men can sit at their stalls to show their wares at trade fairs. The Taliban gives various reasons for this, including claiming that women aren't wearing proper hijab or head covering.
"The world has to talk to the Taliban in a different way because it's just not working," says Najia. "The lives of Afghan women have to change because we're losing hope."
Five years after this ultra-conservative Islamist movement took charge, women are banned from much of the public sphere and girls are prohibited from going to school over the age of 12. Many inside and outside Afghanistan are asking the same pressing question: what's the best way to engage the Taliban to try to achieve meaningful change?
The issue is deeply divisive. There are fissures between many groups, with a huge array of conflicting issues at stake. These include women's rights, unpredictable Taliban edicts, international sanctions and aid cuts during a spiralling humanitarian crisis. The international response is split between Western countries often focused on human rights and others more interested in investment opportunities. And the West itself is divided on the best response.
Many now accept that whatever they're doing, it's not working.
Engage, not isolate
Few voices call for absolute isolation, not when the United Nations warns that 22 million Afghans – nearly half the of the population – rely on some form of foreign assistance to help them survive.
The country has been battered by multiple shocks: an agonising economic crisis; devastating natural disasters; clashes with neighbouring Pakistan, and the influx of millions of Afghans deported from countries near and far into this impoverished land.
And there's no avoiding it – the Taliban are in charge now.
In the years since their fighters swept into Kabul on 15 August 2021, they've grown in confidence and consolidated control despite intermittent attacks by armed opposition groups based abroad, as well as Islamic State fighters.
The Taliban are collecting tax revenues and signing deals in mining, energy and more with Beijing, Moscow, Abu Dhabi, and Tashkent, along with other neighbours.
But they're still strangled by international sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights. Russia is the only country to formally recognise their rule, and they haven't been allowed to take up what they see as their rightful seat at the UN in New York.
But formal diplomatic recognition is no longer the focal point.
"The West is losing the argument over recognition," says a former senior UN official who requested anonymity because they continue to work in Afghanistan. They point to the growing number of countries which have conferred de facto recognition by clinching deals, accrediting diplomats, operating embassies, and more.
"There's no doubt the Taliban would like to be recognised at the UN but it's no longer as potent a bargaining chip as it was at the beginning," they assess.
Behind the soaring blast walls of the foreign ministry in Kabul, in the sprawling compound of manicured lawns and graceful historic buildings, Taliban diplomats keep adding names and flags to the growing collection of Afghan embassies worldwide which are now under their control, rather than the last holdouts of the government they ousted. The current tally is more than 40.
"We need to come closer diplomatically rather than talking from a distance if we want to make progress in our relationship," says Zabihullah Mujahid, the main Taliban spokesman.
We meet in Kandahar in southern Afghanistan, the real seat of power. This is where the Taliban's reclusive emir, Hibatullah Akhundzada, has been steadily building his political and military base and issuing hundreds of edicts, many of them focused on erasing women and girls from public life – what he portrays as an Islamic obligation to protect them.
This five-year mark is widely seen as an inflection point.
"An unstable and potentially dangerous equilibrium," is how the situation was described in closed-door remarks by a senior UN official at a recent international gathering.
And, yet, Afghanistan has fallen far under the world's radar. Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East absorb international attention, and Europe's burning issue is how to stop so many Afghans fleeing towards their shores. It's a startling reversal.
"It's extraordinary given the scale of Western effort from 2001-2021 how ignored Afghanistan is now," remarks a Western diplomat who recently served as an envoy to the country. They did not want to be named because they're still in the diplomatic service.
"The real diplomatic gap is the US," they added, in reference to the current US administration's decision to eliminate their special envoy position and dismantle many agencies, including the US Agency for International Development (USAID), which once led the world's approach on almost every Afghan issue.
Even within Taliban ranks, especially among those known to differ with some of the strictest edicts handed down by their emir, there is frustration that the world doesn't seem willing or able to forge a different kind of relationship.
"We want to be part of the international community," emphasises Mullah Abdul Salam Zaeef, a founding member of the Taliban who now runs a madrasa for boys and girls on the outskirts of Kabul. Unlike mainstream schools, madrasas take girls of all ages and some, especially those run privately, are teaching more than religious classes.
"Just putting pressure won't work," he tells us. He takes the long view of Afghanistan's history of resisting foreign invaders. "We didn't surrender to the Russians, to the Americans, so why would the Taliban surrender now?"
Open dialogue
UN officials believe their presence in Afghanistan makes a difference, however limited. They point to progress on issues such as the treatment of prisoners, their detailed discussions on the harsh implementation of the morality code known as the Propagation of Virtue and Prevention of Vice, as well as efforts to improve humanitarian access.
"Engagement is slow, progress is incremental, and reversals are frequent," is the UN's sober summary of the past five years of on-off dialogue.
But it still insists it needs to stay the course.
"A stalled process is better than no process," emphasises Georgette Gagnon, a deputy special representative of the secretary-general for Afghanistan, who is now the acting head of the UN mission in Kabul.
The UN has been criticised for not pushing back enough against the Taliban, including for holding forums such as the so-called Doha Process, in which a Taliban delegation travelled to the Qatari capital in 2024 to discuss a range of issues, on condition that no Afghan women's representatives were at the table. UN officials insist all issues were discussed, and that subsequent meetings included their participation.
A new process called Mosaic approaches negotiations in a more structured format, on six core issues. On one side there are human rights including women's rights, inclusive governance, and counterterrorism. On the other, there are Taliban demands – sanctions relief, unfreezing assets, diplomatic representation.
"Confidence and reciprocity are beginning to take shape to open the door to engagement on the most difficult issues," says Gagnon whom we meet inside the UN's vast, heavily fortified compound. She calls them "small steps on the long road".
She insists it has to be done through a collective effort, not only through discussions by individual governments. "Pressure has not worked so far, threats have not worked; our best chance lies in consistent and common messaging and action."
For some sceptics, even inside the UN, there's worry that the Mosaic approach isn't going to work either.
But just keeping the lights on, preventing a slide into isolation, and continuing protection work with vulnerable communities, especially women, is seen as essential.
Talk quietly
In dusty provincial capitals and farmers' fields, where international and Afghan aid agencies wrestle with ways to work on the ground, the conversations continue day in day out.
It's there that edicts handed down by the reclusive emir are translated into what are known as workarounds. These workarounds can mean women are able to work in some agency sectors from home, or in different rooms, on different floors, or even in different buildings to men.
"Everything in Afghanistan is relationships, and day-to-day that can help make things easier," says Chris Kinder, the chairman of Afghanaid, a British charity which has been working in Afghanistan for more than 40 years. He emphasises that most of these conversations on access and implementation are conducted by experienced Afghan staff.
My own visits to provincial cities and towns in recent years have underscored how some local Taliban officials try to find pragmatic solutions. But others remain deeply suspicious of any foreign assistance.
Local agreements were described by another charity as "verbal and fragile".
Kinder rejects criticism that aid agencies have had to compromise on principles to keep their projects in place.
"The Taliban have their red lines and we, and our donors, have ours. We discuss approaches so both sides understand where they are coming from."
Here too, many aid officials call for a more unified approach.
Talk tougher
"We need to keep talking, but now we need to set conditions," is the view of Najia the jam maker. It's a stance also taken by women activists in the diaspora and human rights groups who say dialogue has been a one-way street, with the Taliban not offering any significant changes in return.
They insist discussion should not go beyond aid issues until they do.
A recent flashpoint was the decision by EU officials in June to host a Taliban foreign ministry delegation in Brussels for the first time since the Taliban returned to power. Representatives of 15 member states joined this one-day meeting to discuss processes to send back Afghan nationals who had no legal right to remain in the EU.
The EU called them "technical-level" talks. The Taliban saw them differently. A spokesperson described the agenda as including possible consular presence in Europe and the "need for trust-building measures".
"The diplomatic community is well aware that there are already existing channels through which technical issues can be discussed with the Taliban," says Rina Amiri, an Afghan-born former American diplomat who served as the US special envoy for Afghan women, girls and human rights from 2022 to 2025 and also grappled with the terms under which to meet the Taliban.
"Meeting in Brussels was clearly a decision that was about politics, not logistics," she says.
The critics call it "creeping normalisation".
Will it work?
"After these last five years I spent in Afghanistan, what do I have to show?" asks Mahbouba Seraj, an Afghan activist who runs a shelter, when we visit her in Kabul. When the Taliban took over in 2021, Seraj made headlines when she announced that she would stay in her country to fight for women's rights.
Seraj, 78, now says she's preparing to leave.
Her last shelter, which provided a life-saving refuge for more than 30 Afghan women fleeing domestic abuse, was shut down in December. Her repeated appeals to Taliban leaders to re-open classrooms for women and girls have been ignored.
"These small windows that the world sees, the little openings here and there including secret schools for girls, are just meant to fool everybody," she laments with visible sadness.
But Seraj calls on the international community to keep talking.
"They have to talk, but they have to make sure that when they sit down and talk, it's not just a lot of people just filling the air."
There are others who say the same.
"Only more capable diplomacy through quiet and confidential engagement can deliver the change," says a former Afghan official who's been involved in discreet discussions with Taliban officials. He hopes whoever is chosen as the new UN Secretary General and takes office at the start of next year will engage more effectively.
But, in the end, it's not the international community which is in the driving seat of any change.
"I don't think the answer is the world finding the right language to talk to the Taliban," says a Western analyst who's long been involved in Afghanistan and like others interviewed for this article asked to remain anonymous. "Five years on, it's very clear that real change can only come from within."
Some senior Taliban officials have occasionally spoken out about the emir's harshest orders, in particular the closure of girls' schools, and there've been rare instances when some were able to find ways to roll back his rules. One such case was last year's nation-wide internet shutdown which paralysed daily life and was later reversed.

The emir's edicts are regarded as absolute. The movement has shown it values unity, and power, above all else. Even the entreaties of Islamic scholars and officials of Islamic countries the world over have not bent the iron will of the emir and his enforcers, especially on the most sensitive issue of education.
Five years on, there are no simple or swift solutions.
At Najia's jam workshop, a table bristling with her framed training certificates – from local Afghan institutes to the now defunct USAID – attests to her efforts to become a bigger and better entrepreneur in the face of cascading restrictions.
Year on year, a new society starts to take shape. But many Afghans still keep pushing and praying for a different future – and hope the world won't forget them.

As cancer treatments have advanced and outcomes have improved, one aspect of cancer care in the US has consistently worsened over the last decade: the wait time for surgery.
According to a study in JAMA Surgery, patients with one of six types of cancer—breast, colon, lung, pancreatic, gastric, and esophageal—have faced longer wait times for surgery than in 2012. Timeliness is considered a core metric of healthcare quality, and delays in cancer surgery have been linked to poorer outcomes, including reduced survival rates and increased patient anxiety and distress.
The findings of the new study are based on data from over 2.7 million patients who had been diagnosed with non-metastatic stage I–III cancers requiring surgery between 2012 and 2023. Researchers led by cancer expert Timothy Donahue at the University of California, Los Angeles, broke that time frame up into four groups: 2012–2015, 2016–2019, 2020–2021, and 2022–2023 to see how wait times have changed over the period.
Wait times for all six cancer types increased over the entire period and incrementally between each of the time groups. For breast cancer, wait times went from 34 days in 2012–2015 to 45 days in 2022–2023. For colon cancer, they went from 20 days to 31 days. For lung cancer, they went from 41 to 53 days. For pancreatic cancer, they went from 23 days to 32 days. For gastric cancer, they went from 35 days to 49 days. And for esophageal cancers, they went from 38 days to 48 days.
Healthcare system changes
The study also found that the proportions of patients with hefty wait times increased across all the cancer types. Rates of patients having prolonged waits of 30 or more days increased across all the cancer types, as did rates for patients having “extreme” waits of 60 or more days.

Two dead and evacuation under way as fires break out on Greek island
- Published
Two people have died and an evacuation is under way after two fires broke out within minutes of each other on a Greek island near Athens.
Fire officials said nearly 200 firefighters were working to extinguish the flames on the island of Salamina and keep them from converging, Greek media report.
The first blaze was reported at 14:40 local time (12:40 GMT) and spread rapidly due to high winds, according to officials on the island - which was under a high wildfire risk on Sunday.
Some 90 people have so far been evacuated by sea, a coastguard spokesman told Greek broadcaster ERT.
Five patrol boats have been sent to the area and several other private vessels are being made available for assistance, he added.
A number of aircraft and 50 fire engines have been deployed to the blaze.
Salamina Deputy Mayor Thodoris Zannis said firefighters were trying to keep the fires from burning over a mountain on the island and forming one major wildfire.
Salamina sits just west of Athens and has some 37,000 residents, many of them elderly.
Firefighters across Europe have been facing a series of wildfires this weekend, fuelled by high heat.

- The claim that some sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier are facing mental health crises and have attempted to jump overboard is still under investigation.
- The claim stemmed from reporting by the U.S. military news outlets Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, which interviewed families of various sailors.
- The reports, citing second- and thirdhand accounts from military spouses , claim at least two sailors tried to jump overboard as the aircraft carrier logged more than 250 consecutive days at sea amid the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. Military families say they have had limited communication with sailors facing mental health crises while at sea.
- We are unable to independently confirm the conditions onboard the aircraft carrier or the mental health of the sailors. As such, we have left this claim unrated until we receive more information.
- A Navy official said there had not been "an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship," but noted that one sailor had gone overboard. The spokesperson declined to provide further details, including whether the sailor jumped.
In August 2026, a rumor spread online that numerous sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln had attempted to jump overboard. The aircraft carrier had logged nine months at sea amid the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
Numerous reports claimed multiple sailors tried to jump overboard from the aircraft carrier due to mental health crises and poor conditions.
The reports originated from military news outlets such as Navy Times, which reported that a sailor's spouse said her husband attempted to jump overboard:
Annabelle Loma has spoken with her husband only a few times since he attempted to jump overboard from the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln during his current deployment.
Communication has been difficult to come by, and he is now on medical hold.
Loma, who lives in San Diego, said her husband had been repeatedly overextended before he tried to jump from the carrier.
"He's scared," Loma said. "He thinks he'll get a dishonorable discharge, and just because he was burnt out, his 13-year career is ruined, just like that. That's not fair, that's not right. That's not what he should be worrying about right now."
Loma said she initially received a call from the ship's ombudsman after the incident but has not heard from anyone with the Navy in recent weeks.
Star and Stripes, another news outlet covering the U.S. military, spoke to family members of sailors — whom it did not identify — who expressed their worries over the crew's mental health amid long months at sea.
As of this writing, we were unable to independently confirm the conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln or the mental health of its sailors. All the available media coverage relies on anonymous sources or secondhand reporting from sailors' families who say they have sporadic communication with their deployed family members. Snopes does not rely on anonymous sources for its fact-checking and instead seeks out primary evidence, such as verified documentation or communications, to rate claims.
Short of going onboard the aircraft carrier or speaking to sailors directly, it is impossible for us to confirm firsthand the conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln. As such, we've left this claim unrated and will update our report if new information emerges.
In an email to Snopes, a Navy official said there had not been "an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship." According to the official, one sailor had gone overboard but had recovered after treatment. The official did not confirm the circumstances in which the sailor went overboard, making it unclear whether the sailor had jumped.
According to the Navy Times, one woman said her husband was "overextended" and burned out when he tried to jump overboard, but was rescued. In a separate incident, another sailor's wife said her husband saw his shipmate try to go overboard before he intervened.
In August 2026, around 200 military family members gathered in San Diego to meet with Navy leadership to express their concerns about the sailors' mental health. According to Stars and Stripes, a military spouse told Navy officials she received a message from her husband saying "he hopes he doesn't wake up tomorrow."
According to U.S. officials, the crew of the USS Lincoln has supported 40 days of continuous combat operations and logged 250 days at sea. A Navy spokesperson told Snopes via email:
We have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship. We take every service member's well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise. USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN 72) has five Navy Chaplains, one clinical psychologist, one clinical social worker, three behavioral health technicians and an embedded integrated prevention coordination (EIPC) counselor. The ship also has an expeditionary facility dog, CAPT Fathom, to support crew morale and emotional welfare. These resources are available to Sailors and Marines throughout the Strike Group 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
Sailors go through normal transitions throughout a deployment cycle. Adapting to life at sea can be difficult, so we've learned how to provide resources and help Sailors with these transitions. We are not experiencing an uptick in mental health issues aboard Abraham Lincoln.
The spokesperson said a crew member had gone overboard but declined to provide further details, including whether the sailor jumped:
A Sailor assigned to the air wing attached to USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN 72) went overboard from the ship in early August. The Sailor was quickly recovered by an air wing search and rescue helicopter, treated by Abraham Lincoln's medical department, and transferred off ship for follow-on care. The Sailor's family was notified according to standing notification policies.
Numerous media reports also addressed purported food and supply shortages and low morale among the crew. We previously reported on the alleged deteriorating conditions aboard the aircraft carrier, including low supplies of toothpaste, deodorant and soap. In response to those claims, a Navy spokesperson said:
Lincoln is operating in a highly contested environment where traditional supply hubs in the Middle East were disrupted by combat actions. In response, leadership prioritized mission-critical supplies: first food, then hygiene items, then mail. Current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional AC, and healthy meal options.
For further reading, Snopes has covered Iranian media outlets' claim that seven Navy personnel died in a brawl onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.
If you or someone you know is experiencing a mental health, suicide or substance use crisis or emotional distress, reach out 24/7 to the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline (formerly known as the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline) by dialing or texting 988 or using chat services at to connect to a trained crisis counselor.

Chokepoints and the cost of cutting off access
The most dangerous chokepoint may not be the narrowest strait or rarest tech but where the final decision rests with the fewest people
It exposed a question hidden inside every chokepoint. We usually ask where dependence is concentrated: a strait, mineral, technology, network. But three simpler questions matter. How much depends on it? What does it take to use it? Who decides?
The threshold of a chokepoint lies in the second question: what someone must risk, in blood, money, law or reputation, before leverage becomes action.
China has lived with the first question for more than two decades. In 2003, then president Hu Jintao warned that “certain major powers” could control the Strait of Malacca, exposing China’s dependence on imported energy. Beijing gave the anxiety a name: the “Malacca dilemma”.
Twenty years on, that fear has bought a navy. Malacca did not by itself drive Beijing’s naval build-up; Taiwan, territorial disputes and great-power competition all mattered. But vulnerability at sea helped define the problem. If you cannot control the passage, build enough capability to make anyone contemplating its closure think harder about the consequences.

Twenty-eight-year-old Jacob Fortinsky has been busy. “I was a groomsman at two weddings this weekend,” he tells me over Zoom. Also, the sports trading company he runs, Novig, launched its prediction market last week, facilitating $18 million in trading volume on its first day. Today, Novig launches a “responsible trading framework” in its exchange rulebook, codifying its guardrails as part of its effort to be seen as a kinder, gentler prediction market player.
Unlike industry leaders like Polymarket and Kalshi, which allow people 18 and older to participate, you have to be at least 21 to use Novig. Fortinsky says that decision was made in response to “valid concerns” put forth about the susceptibility of younger participants to risky behavior, including lobbying from the NCAA and other professional groups. Fortinsky sees this move as staying ahead of the curve as concerns grow about the negative impact that prediction markets can have on teens. “There’s a broader reckoning coming with the younger traders,” he says. “That group is particularly susceptible to irresponsible behavior and financial ruin.”
Novig’s rulebook also prohibits marketing to minors, and lays out guidelines banning other marketing practices, like ads that claim there’s no risk or ads that try to appeal to a prospective participant’s money troubles. That means when it advertises on TikTok, for example, it uses a setting that allows targeting only people over 21. Fortinsky positions these restrictions as part of Novig’s push to be seen as a “serious, legitimate financial product” as it comes onto the scene. “Some of our competitors, I think, have been seen as being a little bit more cavalier in certain regards,” he says. (He declined to name specific rivals.)
Because Novig only offers sports-themed markets, it doesn’t wade into some of the more hotly contested topics, like US elections and the Iran war. That doesn’t mean it’s avoiding controversy. As a sports-centered platform, the types of speculation opportunities it offers are at the center of an ongoing regulatory war, with prediction markets and federal regulators on one side and state regulators, tribal authorities, and occasionally traditional sportsbooks and casino operators on the other. Dozens of messy legal battles are raging across the US. States are suing Kalshi and other platforms, alleging that they illegally offer gambling; Kalshi is suing right back; the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which oversees the industry, is suing several states, arguing that it alone has jurisdiction over these markets.
Also, Novig isn’t immune to the general cultural distaste for prediction markets; when the New York Mets announced a recent partnership with Novig, the baseball team received a flood of criticism on social media. Sample post: “This is vile.”
If sports-related event contracts offered by prediction markets are banned, big players like Kalshi and Polymarket will be in deep trouble, with the majority of the action on their services gone. But Novig’s position is even shakier, since that’s all it does.
Fortinsky is betting it all on a win, and Novig wasted no time jumping into the legal fray. Within three days of launching, the startup sued New York, Massachusetts, New Mexico, and Washington, all states that have taken an aggressive approach to curbing prediction markets. It is trying to block these states from attempting to apply their gambling laws to federally regulated exchanges, which is what it’s licensed as. Sports betting attorney Daniel Wallach tells WIRED that these complaints are a “great marketing strategy” and a way to announce that Novig has arrived on the scene.
Whether they'll be successful is another matter. Recent court decisions have largely swung toward state attorneys general. A judge in New York denied Novig’s efforts to get a temporary restraining order, on the grounds that doing so would undermine another decision already reached in a case against Kalshi. “It’s increasingly looking more positive for the states,” Wallach notes. But that could change; Wallach and other onlookers expect the fight to get kicked up to the US Supreme Court before anything is definitively resolved.
Until then, Novig is plowing ahead. One of Novig’s appeals to customers is that it offers a different kind of sports speculation experience, one without a house that takes a “vig,” the fee that bookies take for arranging a bet. (“No vig,” get it?) Fortinsky has harsh words for many of the dominant sports gambling players, calling sportsbooks “inefficient, exploitative, and predatory.” He sees the peer-to-peer model that prediction markets facilitate as distinct, since it’s two parties on equal footing going up directly against each other. But if Novig goes how he’d like it to go, those parties won’t always be two average sports fans squaring off. The company is actively courting financial institutions to take sides of wagers, and Fortinsky says Novig is currently onboarding proprietary trading firms and banks. The company is taking steps to make it easier to “trade programmatically,” using algorithms to automate placing money on which team will win the Super Bowl or how many times the Mets will lose, for example.
“Something that's really cool to see,” he says, “is that you have hundreds of these small shops with a couple guys with $100,000 that are now competing against some of the largest Wall Street trading firms in the world and doing quite well.” Good thing the teens aren’t allowed in.

Trump pushes Congress to end ‘RIDICULOUSLY CHANGING CLOCKS’ - could it actually happen?
Trump wants to see the sun later. But just like his ballroom, voter ID and his ‘slush fund’, the Senate isn’t playing ball, writes John Bowden
Donald Trump spent part of his Sunday urging the Senate to vote for a bill that would make daylight saving time permanent — putting an end to what he called the “ridiculous” and “disruptive” practice of resetting clocks twice per year.
“The Senate must vote on the NO MORE CHANGING THE CLOCKS ACT as soon as possible. More sun later in the day is better (including for fighting crime!), but, even more importantly, NO MORE RIDICULOUSLY CHANGING CLOCKS AND WATCHES TWICE YEARLY, with all of the disruption and chaos it causes. FINALLY, GET IT DONE!!!” he wrote on Truth Social.
Proponents say the changing clocks will provide more sunlight later in the day; however, that means less light in the morning when children head to school.
But the bill championed by Trump twice in one week seems doomed in the Senate, at least for now, as the chamber stares down the midterms with a number of priorities still at hand.
The push to eliminate the biannual resetting of clocks isn’t new. Congress once passed a law permanently setting clocks back by an hour, and the result was unpopular at the time, causing the law to be repealed less than a year after it took effect in 1974. Under permanent daylight saving time, the sun’s highest point would fall around 1:00 p.m., while sunrise would occur much later during the winter in some states and regions.
For that reason, Senate Majority Leader John Thune has warned that members of both parties oppose the bill in the upper chamber, including himself. Thune voted against the bill in committee and hasn’t scheduled a floor vote, meaning that the legislation passed by the House earlier this year remains in limbo.
But that hasn’t stopped Trump from increasing calls to end the practice of “spring forward” and “fall back.”
This isn’t the first issue on which Thune has bucked the president and his opposition comes as the Senate is separately ignoring Trump’s calls to pass the SAVE America Act, a piece of voter ID legislation.
The Hill reported that Senate GOP sources estimated the bill to end changing clocks would take up several weeks of the upper chamber’s time were it to be brought to the floor, and that Republicans were unsure of its passage. But the legislation hasn’t undergone a formal whipping of the votes by either party in the Senate, and it passed the House with overwhelming bipartisan support. In 2022, the Senate passed a bill to make the change permanent via unanimous consent — but at least one GOP senator has said that he’d halt that from occurring once more. Others have been cagey about their views on the subject.
One Republican who hasn’t been shy about his opposition to the bill is Sen. Tom Cotton, who represents a Southern state and trashed the idea in a recent interview with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt.
“If you live in Bentonville, Ark., the sun wouldn’t come up in the depths of winter until well after 8 o’clock, maybe even 8:30,” said Cotton. “There are places throughout the Midwest and the Rocky Mountain states that wouldn’t see the sun until 9, 9:30, almost 10 o’clock in some cases. That would be very dangerous, especially for kids who are walking to school, biking to school, being left at bus stops.”
Two states, Hawaii and Arizona, already refuse to participate in daylight saving time.
Dozens of countries do besides the U.S., but neighboring Mexico abandoned it — mostly — in 2022. Canada and much of Europe practice setting the clocks back, but most of Africa and Asia do not. Legislation to do away with the changing of the clocks was proposed in the European Union in 2018, but stalled before final passage and implementation.
The New York Times reports that 19 states have passed efforts to make the time change permanent, though those laws are superseded by federal policy.
If nothing else, the main reason for the bill’s unlikely future in the Senate may be Trump’s fraying relationship with Thune and the Senate GOP caucus. A “peacemaking” meeting on Capitol Hill between Trump and members of the Senate GOP was described as tense and combative at times, and the president has not seen his relationship improve with the two GOP senators he forced out of office, Bill Cassidy and John Cornyn.
His support for their primary opponents similarly damaged Trump’s ties with Thune, and the caucus has grown frustrated with the White House over its repeated support for issues and policy pushes that are viewed as widely unpopular, such as money for Trump’s ballroom or a fund that would reward January 6 rioters.
For now, the legislation seems stuck. The Senate is now out on recess until September, leaving it low on a list of priorities for the chamber upon its return. Trump’s dream of seeing that bipartisan unity come to pass in the Senate may end up being the latest casualty of the divide increasingly eating away at Republican leadership.

A Green Light for Crooks
The Treasury has made the American economy a safe space for corruption.
Ever since Donald Trump returned to the White House, his administration has taken a sledgehammer to anti-corruption efforts, destroying policy after policy dedicated to preventing bribery and money laundering in the country. But this week brought the biggest blow yet: The Treasury has obliterated a recent rule to deter devious shell companies, handily reopening the American economy to anyone looking to hide their illicit wealth.
On Tuesday, the Department of the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) announced that businesses formed in the United States would no longer need to disclose their actual owners, and that nearly all the data already gathered on such companies would be destroyed. This move, which Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called “a victory for common sense and American small businesses,” effectively undoes years of progress in curbing devious financial networks, both domestic and foreign. It also delivers a new shelter for wealthy Americans who wish to dodge taxes and move money around undetected. Corporate entities that allow owners to stay anonymous are handy vehicles for corruption—they enable dodgy characters from around the world to stash their proceeds in an otherwise legal American business. After a brief experiment cracking down on these black boxes, the U.S. has decided to let them multiply instead.
Technically, this company registry will still exist, but as a mockery of its former self. When the registry was created a few years ago, it was heralded by many (including me) as the single greatest anti-corruption step the United States had taken in decades. The U.S. had long been the primary provider of anonymous shell companies to anyone and everyone around the world. For as little as $100 and in as little as 15 minutes, any cartel head, human trafficker, oligarch, autocrat, kleptocrat, fentanyl dealer, or corrupt politician in America or overseas could create a shell company in states such as Delaware, Nevada, and Wyoming. Perfectly untraceable and perfectly legal, American shell companies became by the late 2010s the go-to tools for anyone looking to hide their financial tracks for any reason.
These companies weren’t just the preserve of foreign crooks. The industry in the U.S. has long served wealthy Americans looking to hide their assets and enrich themselves and their families. American shells provided all of the secrecy protections they could want and, after the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United decision eliminated corporate-spending limits in American politics, they became an ideal tool for covertly bankrolling American politicians, saturating U.S. elections in billions of dark, untraceable dollars.
Efforts to end the scourge of American shells finally broke through just as Trump’s first term was coming to a close. The bipartisan Corporate Transparency Act—which passed in early 2021, over Trump’s veto—would finally force these companies to divulge their owners. The legislation wasn’t perfect; unlike the company registries in the United Kingdom and elsewhere, the proposed U.S. shell-company database was to remain private, accessible only to federal officials and investigators. The rule also failed to tackle all of the ways trusts and other vehicles provide impenetrable secrecy for the wealthy and the crooked alike. But the CTA, which took effect in 2024, was deceptively simple: Corporate owners simply had to disclose who was in control. America’s reign of corporate anonymity was finally coming to an end.
Now that’s all gone. The Trump administration has gutted the legislation and is torching nearly all of the gathered data. This cannot all be blamed on Trump or Bessent. Republican allies in Congress are busy trying to pass legislation that will formally repeal the CTA, thus preventing any future administration from restarting the database.
The American economy is now open for business again for all kinds of mischief. “The United States Treasury has taken a step that enables criminals to continue financing and profiting from their crimes by using anonymous companies formed in the United States as their ‘getaway vehicles,’” Scott Greytak, the deputy executive director of the advocacy group Transparency International U.S., said in a statement. Anyone with dirty money can once more turn to the U.S. to launder it clean. Now anyone, domestic or foreign, can secretly barrel as much money into American elections as they want.
We have no idea how many businesses formed in the United States are sieves for foreign financing—for elections and otherwise. As Michael Sozan of the Center for American Progress wrote in 2019, these corporations allow foreign entities to “exert influence on the nation’s domestic political process.” The anonymity at play ensures that the scope of this threat will stay unknown too.
All of this is in keeping with what has become the most corrupt administration in American history. Not only has Trump and his family watched their net worths balloon by the billion since he returned to office last year, but his administration has also worked relentlessly to topple America’s anti-corruption infrastructure, eliminating task forces dedicated to combatting dirty money, killing the enforcement of anti-bribery statutes, and gutting efforts to force the wealthiest Americans to pay their fair share of taxes, among countless other measures. The demolition of the Corporate Transparency Act is just the latest and most dramatic move to cater to the president’s deep-pocketed buddies and fellow cronies. But it surely won’t be the last.

Jammu, Aug 16: Veteran Congress leader from Jammu and Kashmir and former Member Parliament (MP) Dharampal Sharma passed away at his residence in Jammu on Sunday.
Being nonagenarian, he was not keeping good health for the past some time, due to age-related ailments.
Dharampal Sharma also served as an MLA in J&K Legislative Assembly from Akhnoor segment for four terms. He represented Congress in Rajya Sabha from 1988 to 1994.
His last rites will take place today at Shastri Nagar cremation ground at 1 pm.
Jammu and Kashmir Pradesh Congress Committee (JKPCC) chief spokesperson Ravinder Sharma, on behalf of the party, expressed profound grief and sorrow over the sad demise of veteran Congress leader and prayed for courage to the bereaved family to bear an irreparable loss.
“Entire rank and file of the Congress party deeply condoles the sad demise and prays for peace to the departed soul,” Ravinder Sharma said, in a condolence message.

A Commercial Tax Officer (CTO) was killed by his first wife after a quarrel over his retirement funds and assets in Husnabad town of Siddipet district.
The deceased, 60-year-old Venkatesham, worked as a Commercial Tax Officer in Asifabad and was due to retire from service this month. His wife, Rajamani works as an Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM).

Venkatesham was shifted to hospital for treatment but succumbed to his injuries while undergoing treatment.

The Problem With Child-Led Potty Training
Many Americans are waiting for their kid to be “ready” to use the toilet—and waiting, and waiting, and waiting.
The time has come to admit it: The United States has a potty-training problem. In Utah, a law came into effect last year mandating that, with some exceptions, children will not be allowed to enroll in public school without first being toilet trained. Kansas lawmakers introduced a similar bill in January, and at least one district in Florida is considering a policy change that could force kindergartners to stay home until they are out of diapers.
These directives have come about because growing numbers of children are showing up to school unprepared to use the toilet. And U.S. schools aren’t the only ones confronting this issue. In the United Kingdom, the nationally representative School Readiness Survey found that last year, more than a quarter of children were not toilet trained when they began primary school (which most children do the September after they turn 4). Felicity Gillespie, the chief executive of Kindred Squared, the organization that commissions the annual survey, told me this means that teachers “can never really get into the curriculum, because they’re constantly having to take kids out and change their nappies.”
The shift toward delayed potty training, I learned while reporting this article, has been under way for quite a long time. And the sources I spoke with pointed to a few factors driving it. One is that easy access to disposable diapers—which reduce the mess involved in having a child who can’t reliably make it to the toilet—has made the need for training less pressing. Another is that many families with working parents are short on the considerable time needed for monitoring trips to the bathroom. But from Gillespie’s perspective, the root of the issue is that parents are taking a child-led approach to what should be a “100 percent parent-led activity,” she said. “You don’t sit and wait for a child to say, ‘Do you know what? I think I’d like to try wearing pants today.’”
A desire to empower children as decision makers in their own lives, as well as an underlying wariness about parental authority, manifests in many trending parenting philosophies—and is perhaps most recognizable in “gentle” or “respectful” parenting, which emphasizes guidance and persuasion over rules and instruction. Broadly, this approach is rooted in an admirable desire to respect children as humans. The author of The Sovereign Child, a 2025 book that advocates for rules-free parenting, describes a general philosophy of “taking children seriously.” What it amounts to, though, is going to great lengths to avoid just telling your kid what to do.
Potty training offers a strong case study in how easily the child-led approach can break down amid the realities of modern life.
In the United States, official guidance on toilet training has been through a huge evolution over the past century. In a 1938 guide to infant care, the U.S. Children’s Bureau advised that bowel training should begin at six months or earlier and be completed by the child’s first birthday; bladder training should start at 10 months, and daytime dryness should be achieved by age 2.
Things shifted in the mid-20th century, particularly after the pediatrician T. Berry Brazelton published a paper titled “A Child-Oriented Approach to Toilet Training,” in which he argued that a child needed to reach certain physiological and psychological milestones before their training could begin. Brazelton’s emphasis wasn’t really on starting at a particular age but on allowing the child to direct the process. “Don’t rush your toddler into toilet training or let anyone else tell you it’s time,” he said years later, in a 1998 Pampers commercial. “It’s got to be his choice.”
The child-led approach has had formal backing from established experts, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, since the 1960s. To this day, many American parents are coached to wait for signs of their child’s readiness before kick-starting the potty-training process. (Readiness is a fuzzy term, but it essentially means that a child will, in addition to hitting specific physical and cognitive milestones, ideally give indications that they’re motivated to use the toilet, such as expressing discomfort in soiled diapers and a desire to wear “big-kid” underwear.) A University of Michigan poll last year, of a national sample of parents, found that 75 percent reported initiating training when their child “seemed ready.” Other motivations for beginning—preparation for day care or preschool, the high cost of diapers—weren’t as influential.
All of this waiting for readiness has coincided with the emergence of delayed potty training. According to data from the 1950s, a large majority of kids, 80 percent, had completed bowel training by 24 months; only 5 percent were still bowel training after 34 months. Even within a sample of 1950s children whose parents were advised by Brazelton to use his child-oriented approach, 98 percent were daytime potty trained by age 3. Over the next few decades, this timeline was pushed back. A 2001 study found that close to zero percent of kids had completed potty training by 24 months, and only about half had done so by 36 months. Still, that study found that almost all kids had started training before their third birthday. These days, only 21 percent of kids begin potty training before they hit 2—and about a quarter do not begin until after they turn 3.
In parents’ defense, the readiness framework can be hard to follow. Tinne Van Aggelpoel, a Belgian pelvic-floor physiotherapist who has conducted research aimed at understanding the causes and consequences of delayed toilet training, told me that no consensus exists regarding what ought to count as a sign of readiness or when parents can expect signs to manifest. Some, such as the ability to stably sit on a potty, tend to emerge very young. Others, such as the capacity to walk or dress oneself, develop far later. And some seem unlikely to develop until potty training has begun: A child probably won’t start asking to use a potty chair or demonstrate the ability to sit on it for long stretches unless a potty chair is already in the picture. “If you don’t give your child a bicycle,” Van Aggelpoel said, “then they don’t learn to ride the bicycle, right?”
The deeper issue, though, is that readiness does not develop in a vacuum. It is influenced by all sorts of social and environmental factors, including diapers, Van Aggelpoel said. Bodily cues—expressions that a child needs relief—are one common sign that a kid is ready to toilet train. But research by Van Aggelpoel and her colleagues suggests that disposable diapers reduce these signals. Without a diaper on, kids squirm and touch themselves when they need to use the toilet. Kids wearing a disposable diaper mostly carry on playing. And of course, to a great extent, readiness boils down to a child’s dissatisfaction with the diapered status quo—the discomfort of which today’s diapers have been explicitly designed to mitigate.
From Van Aggelpoel’s perspective, there’s no such thing as training too early. Continence, like crawling or walking, is a motor skill that develops over time. Its development relies on sensory feedback acquired through a messy trial-and-error process of exercise and repetition. “You do something, and something goes wrong,” Van Aggelpoel said, “and then you know, This was wrong; I need to do it in another way.” Just as children learning to roll, crawl, and walk need plenty of opportunities to lie on the floor, pull up on chairs, and tumble around, children learning to control their bowels need plenty of opportunities to experience all of the bodily sensations that go along with failing to hold it. Disposable diapers directly inhibit this feedback loop.
In the United Kingdom, experts have lately been departing from the readiness-centric paradigm. This past spring, when I was living in England, a health-care provider examining my then-10-month-old told me that there was no need to put off potty training, and then texted me a link to a site offering parents guidance on how to get started. “Should we wait for ‘signs of readiness’?” the FAQs read. “No!” the answer said. “The idea of readiness is not based on good research evidence.”
In the United States, too, experts seem to be subtly backing away from recommending that parents delay. In 2008, guidance from the American Academy of Family Physicians stated in no uncertain terms that the skills required for toilet training do not emerge until after age 2; it cited research suggesting that children benefit little from starting training earlier than 27 months, because the earlier training begins, the longer it takes. But an updated version of the guidance, published in 2019, acknowledged that kids in a lot of countries are trained much earlier—89 percent of Vietnamese children begin training by six months, and 98 percent are trained by 2, for example—and that normally developing children seemed to experience “no harms from early training.”
As recently as 2022, the American Academy of Pediatrics’ webpage outlining the right age to potty train stated that “child-development experts now believe that toilet training works best for most families if it can be delayed until the child is ready to control much of the process herself.” The current page is far less heavy-handed about children calling the shots, advising parents to “expect hesitancy.”
Dorota Talalay, a Polish writer who has pointed out how odd the delayed approach to potty training looks to many people outside the Anglosphere, acknowledged that training can indeed take longer the earlier that you start. But she told me that this doesn’t necessarily mean the training is harder. When she began plopping her child, at six months old, on the potty every 90 minutes or so, she received little resistance. “You just sit them on the potty,” she said, “and because they can’t walk, they just sit there, they do their thing, and then everybody moves on with their lives.”
By contrast, the current U.S. norm of waiting until kids are at least 2 means that potty training is aligned with a child’s “peak defiance,” Talalay said. She may be on to something. Per the Michigan poll, the most common potty-training difficulty that parents cite is the child “not being cooperative.” Oddly enough, then, if the goal is to avoid urging a child to begin training when they’d rather not, the key may be not to delay—but to start early.

Former WA senator Mathias Cormann defends current GST system as 'working exactly as intended'
In short:
Former WA senator Mathias Cormann has defended the current GST system, saying it is "working exactly as intended".
His comments come after an interim report by the Productivity Commission recommended the WA GST deal be scrapped as it was costly and unfair.
Mr Cormann says Australia has one of the most comprehensive systems of horizontal fiscal equalisation in the world and an "appropriate balance" is needed.
One of the architects of the Morrison government GST deal that for years has seen state premiers bait each other with insults over their slice of the fiscal pie says the deal was "working exactly as intended".
Former Western Australian senator Mathias Cormann's comments were the latest in attacks launched by WA's political leaders against the Productivity Commission, which on Friday issued an interim report that described the 2018 deal as a costly mistake and recommended it be scrapped.
Premier Roger Cook has called the report's authors "east-coast clowns" and said he had assurances from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese that the current arrangements would remain.
Meanwhile, South Australian Labor premier Peter Malinauskas described it today as a "dud deal" for the rest of the country that needed to be scrapped.
Loading...
Mr Cormann, who was a WA senator between 2007 and 2020, was federal finance minister in the government of Scott Morrison that approved the deal.
He said "the unbelievable unfairness that Western Australia was on the receiving end of [was] addressed" by his government's changes.
Those changes included adding a "relativity floor" that righted a wrong that had seen WA taken advantage of for its mining industry, he told 102.5 ABC Perth.
"The national economy and the national budget benefit from Western Australia, having developed these resources,"
"That is why our federal budget is so sensitive to movements in iron ore prices, up or down. Because it has such a massive impact on the revenue of the Commonwealth."
'Appropriate balance'
The 2018 GST deal ensures WA gets a bigger slice of GST revenue every year than it would under the national formula.
That original formula was meant to give states the ability to offer a similar level of services by giving more money per person to states with higher needs or lower financial means.
It had been contentious because it resulted in GST payments falling at the same time Western Australia faced falling iron ore royalties.
The 2018 changes still courted controversy, because they delivered WA rising GST payments at the same time as its mining royalties surged as a result of high iron ore prices.
Mr Malinauskas said the interim report had found that situation a "dud deal for the rest of the country".
“Premier Cook can call other people clowns all he likes but it won’t change the independently-verified report that now says it’s a dud deal for the rest of the country,” he said.
He warned the federal government would be blamed in South Australia if it failed to intervene.
Mr Cook's government, however, has maintained that changing the GST distribution would unfairly punish WA for its success.
Mr Cormann said he believed in the GST being used to support equal service delivery across the country, but that pursuing it single-mindedly extracted too much from WA.
"There's got to be an appropriate balance,"
No state worse off
The Commission's provisional report on the 2018 reforms is part of a review required by the legislation which introduced those changes.
According to the Commission, every state and territory besides WA has 98 per cent of their expenditure met with the addition of GST returns, compared to WA's 113 per cent. For everywhere else, the "no worse-off guarantee" tops up the remaining two per cent.
Mr Cormann said other states and territories were fairly accommodated for in the GST deal via this guarantee.
"No other [state or territory] has been left worse off as a result of those reforms," he said.
The Productivity Commission is due to issue its final report in December, and Prime Minister Albanese has said he would decide on the matter then.
Mr Cormann said while the debate over the deal would help "inform the best possible final report", he still stood by the structural changes made to the GST distribution model.
"You can always make refinements to improve things at the margins, but the core architecture of the reform should remain in place."

The U.K.’s National Youth Theatre has announced a further wave of star names for “Letters to My Younger Future Self,” the one-night performance marking the organization’s 70th anniversary.
The show, supported by Netflix, is set for Sept. 20 at the Southbank Centre’s Royal Festival Hall in London.
The new names joining the lineup include chart-topper Sophie Ellis-Bextor, BAFTA Breakthrough Brit Susan Wokoma (“Enola Holmes”), leading dramatist James Graham (“Dear England”), Anita Rani (“BBC Woman’s Hour”), Daniel Ings (“The Gentleman”), Calam Lynch (“Rings of Power”), Fay Ripley (“Cold Feet”), Rhea Norwood (“Heartstopper”) and Megan Bolton (TikTok comedian). Additional letters will be penned by NYT patron Chiwetel Ejiofor, Joanna Lumley, Joan Collins, Richard E. Grant and Matt Lucas.
They join the previously announced lineup of BAFTA winner Adeel Akhtar (“Four Lions”), India Amarteifio (“Queen Charlotte: A Bridgerton Story”), Fehinti Balogun (“Down Cemetery Road”), Jessica Henwick (“Game of Thrones”), Rob Rinder (“Judge Rinder”), Takunda Muzondiwa (2026 Roundhouse Poetry Slam winner) and Jack Thorne (“Adolescence”). Further appearances and letters are set to be announced.
Popular on Variety
The evening is directed by National Youth Theatre CEO and artistic director Paul Roseby alongside director Josie Daxter, with dramaturgy from Krishna Istha and Sophie Ellerby. Will Duke handles video design, Prema Mehta lighting design, Nicola T. Chang sound design and Matthew Wells movement direction. The show will be powered on stage, behind the scenes and on screen by young talent nurtured through Netflix and National Youth Theatre’s “Ignite Your Creativity” program.
NYT patron Sophie Ellis-Bextor said: “I’m proud to be a Patron of the National Youth Theatre, which gave me a great confidence boost as a young person and continues to do the same for thousands of young performers around the country.”
Wokoma added: “NYT shaped everything for me… I learned how to be a good company member and it’s absolutely one of my strengths as an actor and writer. It’s the way you learn and grow and surprise yourself.”
Ings said: “A lot of the people I’m closest to today are friends I made at NYT, and it shaped the way I approach acting and being part of a company. That being said, I have a lot to say to my younger self, so I can’t wait to be back with the NYT this September for a night to remember.”
Lynch added: “I’m looking forward to returning to my NYT roots for a special evening celebrating seventy years of youth theatre.”
Bolton said: “NYT is where I started my performing journey and is a company that means a lot to me. I’m looking forward to joining some amazing talent on stage for an evening to remember.”
Netflix has backed National Youth Theatre since 2023 through a partnership that has generated more than 4,000 free places aimed at steering young people toward behind-the-scenes creative careers. The charity points to its alumni roster as evidence that a majority of the U.K.’s top screen talent got their start in theater. That roster includes Daniel Craig, Helen Mirren, Adeel Akhtar, Andrea Riseborough, Matt Smith, Regé-Jean Page and Susan Wokoma, along with dramatists Jack Thorne, James Graham, Miriam Battye, Lennie James and Sarah Solemani, comedians Tom Allen and Joel Dommett, and musicians Ed Sheeran and Sophie Ellis-Bextor.
Tickets for “Letters to My Younger Future Self” are on sale now, with proceeds benefiting the national charity in its 70th anniversary year. National Youth Theatre named Netflix as headline sponsor of the event, with additional backing from Arts Council England and Eon Productions.

Leading US AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic are releasing cheaper models as they fight to retain cost-conscious customers who are switching to cut-price alternatives from Chinese rivals.
The price war comes as rising AI bills push companies to curb usage and seek cheaper models, helping Chinese developers including Moonshot and DeepSeek make inroads with users from Silicon Valley to Europe.
OpenAI recently said that it was slashing prices for GPT-5.6 Luna, its “fastest and most affordable model”, by 80 percent. Anthropic has launched Claude Opus 5, touting the system’s “frontier intelligence… at half the price” of Fable 5, the company’s most capable model.
The moves have helped decrease prices that customers are paying for models from leading US labs by almost a quarter since mid-July, according to Silicon Data’s token price index. Tokens are the units of data processed by language models and are used to calculate many customers’ bills.
The cuts mark a shift for US AI groups that make proprietary “closed” models that have, until now, competed heavily on performance. Increasingly capable “open” Chinese models—which can be freely downloaded and tweaked by developers—have contributed to pressure on prices.
The moves also come as OpenAI and Anthropic plot initial public offerings at trillion-dollar valuations while investors seek evidence that the industry’s vast spending on AI can generate returns.
Corporate AI users face cost pressures as Anthropic and OpenAI shift some enterprise customers away from flat subscriptions and toward usage-based billing, under which companies pay according to the computational resources they consume.
Some businesses have responded to a rise in bills by imposing caps on AI usage or testing cheaper alternatives. Companies such as DoorDash and Airbnb have said they have started to use Chinese-made models in an effort to rein in bills.
That shift has coincided with a flurry of releases from Chinese labs that have narrowed the performance gap with leading US models, raising concerns in the US tech industry that American developers could lose customers even as they spend heavily to maintain their technological edge.

'I shot Mr Thompson'- What it was like inside court as Mangione pleaded guilty
- Published
After more than a year-and-a-half of intense spectacle and legal wrangling, Luigi Mangione appeared in a federal courtroom in New York on Friday as rumours swirled that he may plead guilty.
The 28-year-old, accused of shooting dead UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson on a Manhattan street in December 2024, arrived wearing a beige prison uniform with a white T-shirt underneath.
His feet were shackled and he held his hands behind his back, although US marshals had not handcuffed him.
A crowd of press, supporters of Mangione, observers, and a handful of court staff members who had won a lottery to attend gathered in the packed courtroom.
And in the front row seated behind the prosecution: Thompson's family members, who at times appeared visibly emotional.
As the packed room awaited the arrival of Judge Margaret Garnett, Mangione conferred with his lawyer Karen Friedman Agnifilo, reviewing papers as we waited to hear whether Mangione would admit to the killing for the first time.
The hearing had been scheduled to begin at 11:00, but started slightly later.
It began with an immediate jolt.
Friedman Agnifilo told the judge: "Mr Mangione is prepared to plead guilty at this time."
From then on it was silent, as the judge asked Mangione a series of questions to ensure he understood the decision he was about to make. She asked him about his background and use of medications. He answered the questions tersely but firmly.
Asked if he understood that he could face life in prison - he replied, "yes".
Only when began to read a statement to the court, did Mangione appear to falter. His speech was rushed, and somewhat mumbled.
After Judge Garnett politely suggested he lean into the microphone, he continued steadily until he reached his conclusion: an admission that he had killed Thompson.
There had been reports in US media leading up to the hearing that Mangione would be taking a plea deal. That is not what happened - Mangione simply changed his plea of not guilty to guilty.
"After years of enduring severe pains from a broken back" and dealing with the healthcare insurance industry, Mangione stated that he had learned UnitedHealthcare would hold an annual conference in Manhattan in December 2024.
He researched online and emailed the company posing as an investor to learn more about the event, Mangione told the court. "Unlike previous interactions with insurance" he got a quick reply, he said.
He told the court he used a 3D printer to make a gun.
And on the morning of 4 December 2024, Mangione confessed: "I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died."
It marked the first time a court had heard Mangione tell the story of how he committed a crime that prompted a media storm and worldwide attention.
"Mr Mangione, how do you now plead?" Judge Garnett asked the defendant before her.
Mangione leaned into the microphone before him and stated: "Guilty."
"I will accept your guilty plea," the judge said.
Members of Thompson's family were emotional as he issued the admission for the first time. In a statement shortly after, they said the day marked an important step toward justice.
Mangione is scheduled to be sentenced on 18 December. The maximum sentence for each of the two stalking charges is life in prison.
Prosecutors have recommended Mangione serve between 24-30 years in prison. But ultimately Judge Garnett will decide his sentence.
His trial on separate state charges stemming from the murder is still scheduled to begin in September.
