Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says the best way to win over AI skeptics is to deliver on the hype.
In a rare post on X on Saturday, Anthropic's CEO acknowledged the public's mistrust of AI and said the industry can only change that by delivering tangible scientific breakthroughs.
"At this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliché than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive," Amodei wrote. "The most accurate criticism of AI companies, including Anthropic, is that we haven't yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world."
"The thing that will work is actually curing cancer," he added.
The AI industry is facing a growing public backlash as it builds huge data centers in communities across the country, scrapes often copyrighted online data to train its models, and upends the workforce for many industries. A recent Pew Research Center study found that about half of Americans felt the increased prevalence of AI in their daily lives made them feel "more concerned than excited."
Amodei, meanwhile, has repeatedly warned on podcasts, in essays, and in Anthropic blog posts, about the dangers posed by AI's rapid development. In a June essay, Amodei wrote that the company's new Mythos models present "very real risks" to cybersecurity, the financial sector, critical infrastructure, and national security. Last year, he warned that AI would cause half of all entry-level jobs to vanish.
Some other AI leaders have criticized the kind of rhetoric for which Amodei, who left OpenAI in 2020 over concerns about the company's attention to safety, has become famous. Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis said earlier this year that his peers had been "way too certain" about their dire predictions and encouraged them to dial it back.
As OpenAI and Anthropic gear up for expected IPOs, they have followed that advice, pivoting from doomerism to boomerism. Amodei, however, said in his Saturday X post that he doesn't think his warnings are the cause of the public's distrust of AI.
"I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative," he wrote.
"I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn't feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better," he added, referring to a lengthy 2024 blog post in which he laid out how he thought AI could make the world a better place.
Instead, Amodei said that the public's distrust of AI companies reflects broader skepticism among Americans toward corporations overall. "The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it," he wrote.
Anthropic's decision not to open-source any of its frontier models, which it says is out of caution, has contributed, at least in part, to the public's wariness. Anthropic drew ire last month for being the only major AI developer not to sign a letter advocating for open-weight AI as Washington considered restrictions on some Chinese models.
Yann LeCun, the former chief AI scientist at Meta, has long argued that keeping frontier AI technology closed-source, as Anthropic does, contributes to public distrust about AI more than anything else.
In an X post responding to Amodei, LeCun wrote that the "only way forward" is for AI to be "widely available, shared, and open."
"We need diverse AIs for the same reason we need a diverse press," he wrote.
As for Amodei's argument that a major scientific breakthrough could turn the tide of public opinion, not everyone agreed with that either.
Angel Brodin, an applied AI architect at OpenAI, wrote in a response to Amodei's post that despite routinely delivering advancements in public health, the pharmaceutical industry is "still one of the least trusted industries."
"People also won't judge AI companies solely by their breakthroughs," she wrote. "They'll judge them by pricing, access, lobbying, opacity, how the economic gains are distributed, who gets to participate in its benefits, and who ultimately holds the power."
Amodei, for his part, said Anthropic is ramping up work in the biological and medical fields to test that theory.
"We hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months," he wrote. "When we've actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that."

History for Hunt and Asher-Smith as GB win relay gold
- Published
Amy Hunt and Dina Asher-Smith made history and Georgia Hunter Bell claimed a commanding 1500m gold as Great Britain maintained their bid to top the final medal table at the European Championships.
Sprint sensation Hunt held up four fingers to the camera after holding off Germany's challenge on the home straight of the mixed 4x100m relay as another sell-out crowd roared the 24-year-old on to an unprecedented fourth gold of the week.
The world silver medallist completed victory for the quartet in a European record 39.97 seconds to add to her triumphs in the 100m, 200m and women's 4x100m in Birmingham.
With her eighth gold and 11th medal overall, Asher-Smith is unparalleled as the most successful athlete in the competition's 92-year history, with a team also featuring Jeremiah Azu and Zharnel Hughes extending the hosts' domination of the sprint events.
Hunter Bell expertly controlled the women's 1500m final before bursting clear to continue her golden year by adding to world indoor and Commonwealth glory.
That represented the 32-year-old's seventh international medal in two years as she continues to build momentum on her fairytale return to the sport which she quit for five years following a promising junior career.
That was Great Britain's ninth gold medal, taking them above Italy at the top of the standings - and the team's 16th overall.
The 'GOAT' and an 'icon' combine again for GB
Less than 24 hours after combining with their respective men's and women's quartets to win 4x100m golds, Azu, Asher-Smith, Hughes and Hunt - in that order - made it six golds out of a possible seven across the sprint events.
Hunt described team-mate Asher-Smith as "the real life GOAT" [greatest of all time] after the 30-year-old won a record-equalling seventh gold on Saturday night, a decade on from capturing her first.
Despite feeling "absolutely terrified" during the event's inaugural mixed 4x100m relay, Asher-Smith, world 200m champion in 2019, leaves Birmingham a 22-time international medallist in her senior career.
Based on her performances this week, Hunt is only just getting started with her growing medal collection.
The Cambridge University graduate boldly stated her intention to take all four sprint titles this week in her bid to be "iconic".
The weight of expectation has increased with each success, but she has risen to the moment in front of her home crowd on each occasion and few expected her to falter once she took the baton and began her battle with Germany's Gina Luckenkemper.
Cheering his team-mate on after handing over to Hunt, Hughes matched Matthew Hudson-Smith, Mo Farah and Roger Black as the most successful British man with his fifth gold at the championships.
More to follow.

Myanmar’s ousted ambassador to the UK has gone on trial on trespassing charges for refusing to leave a diplomatic residence after being unceremoniously locked out of the embassy in 2021.
Shortly after Myanmar’s military seized power in 2021, triggering mass protests that spiralled into a civil war, Kyaw Zwar Minn was locked out of the embassy for declaring his loyalty to the deposed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
On Wednesday he appeared in a London court charged with trespassing at a diplomatic residence between May 2021 and November 2024. Kyaw Zwar Minn, who still lives at the ambassador’s residence in north-west London, has pleaded not guilty.
The former ambassador argues that the current president, Min Aung Hlaing, the general who plunged Myanmar into conflict and economic chaos, is illegitimate and had no power to ask him to leave the property.
Min Aung Hlaing’s pro-military party won a landslide victory in elections earlier this year that have been widely condemned as a sham. Min Aung Hlaing is wanted by the international criminal court for crimes against humanity against the Muslim Rohingya minority.
Kyaw Zwar Minn’s lawyer, David Perry, told the court: “The military authorities could not lawfully terminate his licence at the address. Nor could they legitimately use the property.”
Prosecutors said Myanmar’s authorities instructed the former ambassador to “hand over state-owned properties” in April 2021, and that the Foreign Office also told him to leave the residence, but he did not comply.
They argue that his view of the Myanmar government – which is not formally recognised by most democratic countries, including Britain – does not provide a defence.
“Having been granted permission to reside at Myanmar House as the ambassador, his refusal to vacate the diplomatic premises after he was removed from that position means that he is guilty of the offence of diplomatic trespass,” the prosecutor Louise Oakley told the court.
Kyaw Zwar Minn previously told the Guardian he spent a night in his car outside the embassy in April 2021 after his then deputy, Chit Win, and a military attache, Soe Aung, locked him out of the building on the regime’s orders.
He said at the time that he no longer felt safe at the north London residence and had contacted the police after former staff delivered a letter ordering him to move. Friends and relatives in Myanmar had been forced into hiding fearing reprisals as a result of his stance, he said.
The 68-year-old became a diplomat under Aung San Suu Kyi after a long career in the army and has called the “Rohingya issue” very important. Before his removal as ambassador, he had been told by a source in Myanmar’s foreign ministry that his staff were spying on him.
He anticipated in 2021 that the crisis would lead to civil war. “You can see the military government is not going to step back,” he said. “More people will die and the economy is going to collapse. Then anything can happen in our country.”
The court case comes as the war enters its sixth year. More than 100,000 people have been killed and more than 5 million displaced, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.
Aung San Suu Kyi, now 81, has been detained on a range charges since the military took power. She was previously held under house arrest for 15 years under a past junta, and was awarded the Nobel peace prize in 1991. After her election as state counsellor in 2015, she became a pariah for leading a regime that excused a genocide, jailed journalists and locked up critics.

Jharkhand student protests began on 25 July 2026 over alleged irregularities in the 14th JPSC Preliminary and JSSC-CGL examinations, including allegations of OMR tampering. Led by student leader Devendra Nath Mahto, protesters have demanded cancellation of the exams and an independent CBI probe. On 10 August 2026, thousands of students marched towards the Jharkhand Assembly, where police used lathi charges and water cannons. The government has since agreed to cancel three JPSC examinations, but students continue to demand a CBI probe into the alleged irregularities. As of 13 August 2026, the protests have entered their 20th day, with Mahto continuing his hunger strike and political support for the movement growing (here, here, here, and here).
Amid this, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) workers pelting stones during the Jharkhand student protest in an attempt to defame the ongoing movement. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows BJP workers pelting stones during the Jharkhand student protest in an attempt to defame the ongoing movement.
Fact: The video is unrelated to the ongoing Jharkhand student protests. It actually shows a clash between BJP and Congress workers outside the Congress office in Indore, Madhya Pradesh, on 21 February 2026, during which both sides reportedly engaged in stone-pelting. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a news report published on TheSootr’s YouTube channel on 22 February 2026 that featured the same visuals. According to the report, the video is from Indore, Madhya Pradesh, where BJP and Congress workers clashed outside the Congress office on 21 February 2026, with stone-pelting reported from both sides. This confirms that the viral video predates the Jharkhand student protests and is unrelated to the ongoing movement.
We found multiple other reports (here, and here) covering the incident. According to these reports, the BJP had announced plans to surround Congress offices in several cities in response to the controversial ‘shirtless’ protest by Youth Congress workers during the India AI Impact Summit at Bharat Mandapam in Delhi. On 21 February 2026, the situation in Indore escalated when BJP youth workers arrived to surround the Congress office and confronted Congress workers who were already present. Heated sloganeering between the two sides soon escalated into a clash, with stones, tomatoes and water bottles thrown from both sides. A sub-inspector and several media personnel were injured, and police used water cannons to disperse the protesters. Police later registered counter FIRs based on complaints from both sides at Pandharinath police station and began an investigation using CCTV footage.
We geolocated the exact place where the clash took place near the Congress party office in Indore and identified that the viral video was recorded near 2 Indore-Khandwa Road, Indore, Madhya Pradesh. A signboard for “Mica Planet” visible in the background of the video matches the location seen on Google Maps Street View. The comparison can be seen below.
To sum up, an old video of a BJP-Congress clash in Indore is shared as BJP workers pelting stones during the Jharkhand student protest.

At least seven people were killed and several others critically injured in a fire at a hotel in West Bengal’s Birbhum district early on Monday (August 17, 2026), police said.
Many of the guests were pilgrims who had come to the temple town of Tarapith to offer prayers on the last Monday of the holy month of Shravan. The famous Kali temple here has a shrine dedicated to Lord Shiva.
The fire erupted around 4.30 a.m. on the ground floor of the four-storey hotel, when most of the guests were asleep, they said.
Also read: 14 killed as fire rips through Kolkata hotel; probe ordered
Fire tenders were rushed to the spot, and they brought the blaze under control.
The injured were taken to the Rampurhat Government Medical College and Hospital.
Officials said some of them suffered burn injuries, while others fell ill due to asphyxiation.
Sources in the hospital initially said that five people had died in the blaze. However, police later revised the toll to seven.
“The death toll is seven now,” a senior official said.
Hotel officials claimed the fire was caused by a short circuit.
According to them, the fire started near the reception of the hotel after an electrical component of the power supply system caught fire. However, the exact cause of the blaze is yet to be established.
The fire spread rapidly through decorative and fibre materials inside the hotel. Smoke billowed to the upper floors and trapped several guests in their rooms.
A woman from Kolkata, who managed to escape the blaze, recalled the panic inside the hotel. “Suddenly, the entire hotel was engulfed in smoke. We could not breathe, and it was hard to find an escape route,” she said.
Another guest, Tapanjyoti Mondal, said he was trapped in his room with his wife and two children for nearly 45 minutes. “We could not come out of the door because of the blaze. Since the room had no window, they escaped through an opening near the bathroom ceiling,” he said.
Mondal’s mother was unconscious while his sister suffered injuries in the incident.

Afghan women tell the BBC their lives are unrecognisable after five years of Taliban rule
- Published
Five years on from the Taliban takeover in Afghanistan, women and girls have told the BBC their lives are unrecognisable under the rule of the regime.
The hard-line Islamist group has been eroding the rights of the 22 million women in the country since it re-gained control in 2021- two decades after being removed from power by a US-led military coalition.
The BBC is one of the few media organisations that has been able to maintain access to Afghanistan since the takeover. We spoke to women across the country, from the heart of Kabul to the vast countryside.
They have watched on as the Taliban barred access to school for girls over 12, restricted travel without a male chaperone and brought in a law implying legal approval for child marriage.
When questioned by BBC Afghan over the constraints that women face, the Taliban's foreign minister said: "Women are not totally restricted on all walks of life".
But the restrictions impact almost every part of their lives and make it difficult to tell their stories. Many of the women have not used their real names because they fear reprisals.
"People are so overwhelmed by poverty and daily hardships that many have been forced to put their education, dreams, and hopes for the future aside," Ela from Kabul said.
"Today, survival has become the priority, and many of us no longer have the time or energy to think about the future."
This story contains distressing details.
Afghanistan is currently the only country in the world where girls are officially banned from secondary and higher education.
Shakiba recounted that "15 August, when the government fell, was the worst and most painful day of my life.
"Every year when this date comes I feel as if an old wound opens again and a new feeling of defeat fills my heart.
"That day I felt that many of the dreams I had carried inside me for years were suddenly taken away."
Though Shakiba has managed to finish her secondary education online - "a very important victory" - she says her life-long goal of becoming a pilot feels impossible.
"Whenever I looked at the sky I imagined myself flying an airplane and seeing the world from above. I wanted to fly freely and experience a world without limits," she said.
The Taliban's foreign minister, Amir Khan Muttaqi, was asked by the BBC about education for girls in Afghanistan, specifically referencing a Unicef report stating that around 2.6 million girls in the country are now unable to attend school beyond Grade 6.
Amir Khan Muttaqi replied that "it is not correct to say everything is banned for women", adding that "right now, three million girls are going to schools and madrassas [religious centres focused on Islamic teachings]".
When asked how religious schools can produce doctors in the country, Muttaqi said: "Women are not totally restricted on all walks of life... Only one small part (of their affairs) is restricted until further notice."
Only 7% of women in Afghanistan are employed, after being banned from many workplaces and fields of study, the United Nations says.
News anchor Zuhal was pushed out of her job after a series of Taliban orders.
"I was very passionate about my work and did it with love. Every time I sat in front of the camera and read the news, I felt proud and happy... it was part of my identity and life.
"The days when I used to wake up to the sound of my alarm clock and get ready to watch TV have now become days when I wake up in the morning knowing that I have to spend the whole day at home."
According to the foreign minister, Afghanistan had up to 30,000 women in business in 2020 and 2021 - which has since risen to 120,000 female entrepreneurs.
"[Women] are teachers, and civil servants and entrepreneurs. There is not a total ban on women in all forms of engagement and activities," Muttaqi said.
The Taliban has resumed the public implementation of corporal punishments, with official records saying hundreds of people have been flogged since 2021 - but the true figure is likely much higher.
Shaima told the BBC she was whipped 50 times, leaving her body badly scarred and her whole family traumatised.
"They brought a paper and forced me to confess that: 'Yes, I am an apostate woman. I am collaborating with infidels and have spoken with unrelated men'.
"They hit me so hard that my head would bend toward the ground.
"Around 200 local people had gathered, including men, boys, and children. All of them were male. I was required to say out loud that I repented."
Shaima said her eldest daughter now wakes up frightened almost every night and asks her "Mother, they are beating you," or "Mother, they are killing you".
"That is what causes me the greatest pain," she added.

Manizha was publicly lashed 39 times over her friendship with a man, and then jailed.
"We wanted to get married, but unfortunately we were arrested. I do not know how the Taliban intelligence found out, or whether someone reported us.
"In prison, I experienced things that I have never even told my mother. I had no desire to continue living. I used to say that the first thing I would do after getting out of prison would be to take my own life.
"I had become a source of shame for my family and friends... I could no longer think about marriage."
If you, or someone you know, has been affected by issues mentioned in this article, BBC Action Line has put together a list of organisations which can help.
Afghanistan has one of the world's highest maternal mortality rates - rules restricting treatment by male doctors mean many women and girls are unable to access healthcare.
Midwife Marzia recounted watching a 45-year-old mother of six die in front of her after she travelled to the clinic from a remote district.
"We managed to save the baby, but now I keep thinking about the baby's future and the future of her six other children. What will happen to them without their mother? What will happen to the whole family?
"We were all heartbroken. For us, losing a patient is always the hardest part of our job. We become exhausted, both physically and emotionally."
Maryam is expecting a baby girl and said she worries about her daughter's future.
"If things continue like this, what will happen to her? She will not even have the chance to finish school like I did, let alone go to university.
"If one day she gets married, becomes pregnant and needs a female doctor during childbirth, what if there isn't one? This is a matter of life and death."
'Speak up for us'
Some of the Afghan women we spoke to said they still have hope for the future.
Noori, 24, said she had chosen to study law and political science because she wanted to give women a voice and defend their rights.
She never finished her degree because of the Taliban take over, but she's still been able to find a way to help women.
"I did not lose hope. I decided to start working and become financially independent. I found a job at a jam-making company and started working there. I have now been working for three years.
"Now, I have decided to establish my own company so that I can provide employment opportunities for other women. I want them to become independent, strong, and successful women like me and have a better future.
"Currently, 10 brave women are working there."
Asma, who is 13, wants to become a doctor and is sure someday she will be.
"One day, everything will change... but we must continue with patience, and we will not lose hope," she told the BBC.
Ela, who is a dental assistant, urged the international community not to forget Afghani women and girls.
"Speak up for Afghan women, support their right to education and work," she said.
"Keep the world's attention on their situation. We need solidarity, not silence."

The ABC is set to air the return of its Planet America program on Monday night as the US midterm elections gain steam, with a new episode featuring the leftwing commentator Hasan Piker.
Host John Barron said the episode will focus on the “rise of Democratic socialists and the populist left”, with Piker speaking about “what it’s like in the eye of a political storm”. But the appearance quickly sparked the ire of conservatives in Australia.
News Corp’s News24 host James Morrow was deeply critical of the interview on Friday, wondering if there was “something in the water at the ABC’s Ultimo HQ that makes them think they are immune to consequences”.
“If the ABC wants to have this clown on their network, that’s their business, but let them do it without our tax dollars,” he challenged last week.
Barron has urged critics to watch the appearance before casting judgment, saying he’s not surprised that “some of the usual suspects are outraged, OUTRAGED, that we would even speak to Piker”.
“Like it or not, he’s a central figure in the 2026 US election,” Barron wrote on X. “I was prepared to talk to Piker about his role in this election just as I was prepared to talk to @seanhannity about his role in the 2012 election … relevance.”
So who is Hasan Piker, and why does he have some in a tailspin?
Piker streams to millions
Piker, 35, is an extremely popular figure in left-leaning politics in the US, with more than three million followers on Twitch and millions more on YouTube and Instagram. He streams on the internet nearly every day, sometimes for eight hours at a time, and has been heralded as a modern-day kingmaker for progressive Democrats.
He has built a legion of fans – many whom are young men – with regular discourse about American foreign policy, capitalism, his support for LGBTQ+ rights and for a willingness to heap criticism on the Democratic establishment. He’s described himself as a “megaphone”, amplifying frustrations with “establishment liberalism”, not as a change maker himself.
His readiness to champion progressive challengers over established figures has angered some top Democrats. He’s also become a frequent target of the Murdoch empire in the US, with Fox News publishing running criticism of his commentary.
Piker’s opinions are unfiltered and, at times, extreme. In 2019, as part of a broader critique of American foreign policy, he said the US “deserved” the September 11 terrorist attacks (he later apologised for the remark). He’s also a frequent and vocal critic of Israel’s leadership and claimed he would “vote for Hamas over Israel every single time”. He maintains he’s not antisemitic, but strongly against Zionism and the country’s policy on the war in Gaza and Palestinians.
“I have no issues getting vilified by people on the right. I love when my enemies hate me,” he told the Guardian in December. “It is what it is: they talk shit; what are you gonna do?”
But Piker’s comments have landed him in hot water. The British government banned him from entering the country for a speaking engagement in June, saying at the time his presence “may not be conducive to the public good”.
Ombudsman’s report
Piker was last on the ABC in September to speak about the assassination of the conservative activist Charlie Kirk. The streamer spoke to Sarah Ferguson for 7.30, saying he was “horrified” at the killing, which came just weeks before the pair were set to debate each other.
The appearance prompted 68 complaints to the ABC, with viewers suggesting the national broadcaster should not have platformed Piker “as he is a far-left extremist” and had made “unsupported adverse claims about Mr Kirk’s past remarks”.
The ombudsman determined the appearance did not breach the ABC’s editorial standards.
Ferguson also interviewed Trump kingmaker Steve Bannon during the US president’s first administration, which prompted its own criticism. The ABC did not have an ombudsman at the time.
Morrow wondered if Piker’s latest appearance could lead to a similar outcome, pointing to the ABC bowing to criticism in recent weeks.
The network’s managing director, Hugh Marks, apologised to Gina Rinehart after airing a short documentary for its Race Around the World program that included crude and offensive comments about the mining billionaire. While the ABC ombudsman found it did not breach any editorial policies, Marks said it had fallen “short of community expectations” and that the ABC would change its editorial guidance.
‘It makes sense to hear from him’
Barron has defended the interview on X in recent days, saying Piker’s position in American politics is more relevant than ever due to the surge in progressive Democrats.
“He’s become a central figure in this year’s election, it makes sense to hear from him,” Barron wrote to a critic about Piker.
Barronsaid he had also interviewed Roger Stone, a longtime friend and ally of Trump who was sentenced to three years in prison in 2020 before he was granted clemency by the president.
“If you watch, I’ll be interested to know if it confirms your concerns or overcomes them,” he went on. “Either way, we choose guests of all stripes based on interest and relevance.”

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Following several turbulent months and the forthcoming end of her beverage brand, Alex Cooper is embracing change — at least when it comes to her representation.
The Call Her Daddy host is in serious talks with CAA, Deadline can confirm. Nothing is signed, sealed and delivered yet, but the expectation is Cooper will make the uberagency her new home after a sudden but not all together unexpected exit from UTA.
Cooper’s team were mum on the move, and CAA declined to comment. UTA did not respond to Deadline’s request for comment on Cooper’s departure from her now former long time business building home. Bloomberg were first to report on Cooper’s agency shift.
Along with apparent feuds with Dave Portnoy and ex-Cooper ally Alix Earle (both repped by UTA BTW), the blockbuster podcaster has seen a lot of not so great attention directed to her spouse Matt Kaplan. Specifically, Kaplan has been accused of fostering an overly aggressive and toxic workplace at Unwell. More specifically to today’s news, Kaplan apparently demanded earlier this year that UTA drop Earle, I hear.
Watch on Deadline
A demand that was obviously unmet for the Unwell co-founder.
Still, with $125 million from a new UTA negotiated deal with SiriusXM in 2024, Cooper and Kaplan’s Unwell Media aren’t exactly hurting for cash. Add to that, the company saw a big injection of cash last week from Patrick Whitesell and Jason Lublin.
With 100 million followers across various platforms, Unwell pulls the strings on a podcast network of more than a dozen shows reaches millions of listeners daily. As well as that new SiriusXM partnership, Unwell has put extra emphasis of late on growing its YouTube presence.
The WTSL investment manifested with Unwell getting a $500 million valuation.
Because, regardless of your agency, nothing says call me like cold hard cash.

TMC panchayat leader arrested over murder of Bengal Congress leader, son: Police
Anisur Rahman, the general secretary of the Nadia district Congress unit, and his son Abu Sufian, a law student, were shot dead inside their car
West Bengal’s Nadia district police arrested Fatima Bibi, a Trinamool Congress panchayat leader on Sunday as a suspect in the murder of a local Congress leader and his son on Saturday evening, police said.
Fatima Bibi, head of the Haranagar village panchayat, was arrested on Sunday along with two of her associates based on a complaint filed by the victims’ relatives, police said.
Anisur Rahman, the general secretary of the Nadia district Congress unit, and his son Abu Sufian, a law student, were shot dead inside their car by unidentified persons while travelling from Bethuadahari to their home at Nakashipara. The car was riddled with bullets, police said.
Deep Dive
Briefing the media, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari said Fatima Bibi’s husband Jabbar Sheikh, who is currently in jail in connection with a criminal case, ordered the hit.
Adhikari said, “Jabbar Sheikh got this done while sitting in jail. His wife, the TMC pradhan, has been arrested.”

(Bloomberg) -- One person has died as storm Lala continues to batter parts of Hawaii including the Big Island and Oahu, potentially bringing nearly three feet of rain and damaging winds to parts of the state Sunday after narrowly missing landfall.
The storm got closest to the South Point area on the southern tip of the Big Island where one person died in a car accident on Saturday, Hawaii Governor Josh Green said in a post on X.
Lala weakened from hurricane strength to a tropical storm, but it’s still expected to produce additional rainfall of 1 to 3 inches (2.5 to 7.6 centimeters) across the Big Island and windward Maui, while maximum storm totals could reach 30 to 35 inches over the Big Island, the US National Hurricane Center said in a statement at 8 a.m. local time on Sunday. 
The tropical storm warning was discontinued for Hawaii County, which covers the Big Island, but still remains in effect for Maui County, Oahu and Kauai County, the hurricane center said.
“This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain,” the hurricane center said. “The combination of a dangerous storm surge and the tide will cause normally dry areas near the coast to be flooded by rising waters moving inland from the shoreline.”
Almost 60,000 Hawaii customers were without power Sunday morning, according to PowerOutage.com. About 106 flights into and out of Honolulu and Hilo were canceled on Sunday as of 3:30 p.m. in New York, according to FlightAware. 
Hawaiian Electric Industries, Inc., the state’s main utility company, said in a statement Sunday that power for customers in some parts of Hawaii Island could remain out for “weeks or even months” and help from mainland electric utilities is anticipated to begin Tuesday. It is not yet clear how many transmission lines are down throughout Hawaii, a company spokesperson said.
Maximum sustained winds have decreased to near 65 miles per hour (104 kilometers per hour) with higher gusts, the hurricane center said, adding that some restrengthening is forecast by midweek.
While the Big Island has gone more than a century without a hurricane strike, Hawaii isn’t immune to tropical storms. Hurricane Iniki struck Kauai in 1992, and the state has faced weaker tropical storms and near misses since then.
In 2023, Hurricane Dora passed far to the south, but helped set up wind patterns that fanned flames across Maui, where fires raged out of control and killed more than 100 people.
No hurricanes struck the US in 2025 and so far only two tropical storms have struck the Gulf Coast in 2026. Super Typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi devastated the US Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands earlier this year.

Hawaii braces for potential first direct hit by a hurricane in 34 years
- Published
Hawaii is bracing for what could be its first direct hit from a hurricane since 1992, as category one storm Lala churns off its coast.
Packing 75mph (120km/h) winds, Lala gained hurricane strength on Saturday. In a worst-case scenario, it could dump up to 25in (63cm) of rain on Big Island and produce a 3ft storm surge.
A hurricane warning is in effect for Big Island, while Maui County, Oahu, Kauai and Niihau are under a tropical storm warnings. Officials have told residents to prepare for "life-threatening" conditions, including floods and mudslides.
The storm is expected to either make landfall or pass close to the southern tip of Big Island on Saturday, before continuing west.
The last time a hurricane made landfall on Hawaii's Big Island was 155 years ago, according to the Associated Press news agency.
Over the weekend, Lala will continue moving westwards, and may weaken into a tropical storm, with the centre passing just below Hawaii's other islands.
Hawaii Governor Josh Green warned residents to brace for "an incredible amount of water".
He said on X: "Damaging winds, heavy rain, flash flooding and dangerous surf are possible across the state through the weekend."
Dozens of flights have been cancelled.
At Ellison Onizuka Kona International - Big Island's largest airport - 40% of flights were grounded, according to flightaware.com. Some 80% of flights were called off at its other main airport, Hilo International.
The more dire forecasts from the National Weather Service (NWS) have been issued for areas within Big Island's south-east.
"Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues," the NWS said, adding that rivers and tributaries "may rapidly overflow their banks in multiple places".
Residents were repeatedly urged by officials to prepare for the storm early.
Local message boards on Facebook show residents filling bags with sand to protect their homes and inquiring whether stores remained open in the early hours on Saturday.
Hawaii County's Civil Defense Agency said public shelters were available in every county on Big Island.
"At this time, you should have completed your storm-ready preparations and focusing on your Sheltering Plan," the agency said on X.
Iniki, a powerful category four storm, was the last hurricane to strike Hawaii back in 1992.
It caused six deaths and $3bn in damage after making landfall on the southern coast of Kauai.
Hurricane season in the US has been relatively quiet the last few years - the last major storm was category three Hurricane Milton, which hit Florida in October 2024.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has said that 2026 might be another low-frequency year for hurricanes in the US, predicting , externala 55% chance of a below-normal season.
Last month, the world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, according to the EU's climate monitoring service.
The record temperatures were partly fuelled by developing El Niño conditions in the Pacific.
It was also the joint second-warmest July globally on record, with temperatures 1.47C above the estimated pre-industrial average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.

Delimitation penalises South for being good, says Opposition; BJP counters
Opposition leaders and the BJP clashed in Chennai over the proposed delimitation of Lok Sabha seats. The debate turned on whether representation should follow population alone or a broader federal balance.
Tamil Nadu leaders take part in a discussion over delimitation at India Today Tamil Nadu Roundtable in Chennai
The delimitation debate has triggered an intense political confrontation between the North and South, with Opposition parties warning that a population-based increase in Lok Sabha seats could dilute the political influence of southern states such as Tamil Nadu. The BJP, however, has rejected these concerns, arguing that the South will not be penalised and will instead see a substantial increase in representation.
At the India Today Tamil Nadu Roundtable in Chennai, leaders from the BJP, Congress, DMK and MDMK clashed over the proposed exercise, with the Opposition warning, "We would be penalised for being good," while the BJP insisted, "We won't allow the South to be penalised, but it's not going to be penalised" and accused the opposition parties of "fear-mongering".
The immediate backdrop was the government’s efforts to bring Opposition parties on board on the issue during the recently concluded Monsoon Session of Parliament, as well as a Tamil Nadu Assembly resolution calling for the Lok Sabha’s existing strength of 543 seats to be retained and the state’s share of seats to be protected. The resolution also called for 33 per cent reservation for women. The BJP and AIADMK opposed the resolution.
MDMK: SOUTH WOULD BE PENALISED FOR BEING GOOD
Marumalarchi Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (MDMK) leader and MP Durai Vaiko argued that the concern was not "mere fear-mongering" but a question of balancing two competing principles: federalism and democratic representation.
"This delimitation debate is about a consensus between federalism and democracy," Vaiko said, framing the issue as a conflict between the federal principle of fair representation for states and the democratic principle of "one person, one vote, one value".
He argued that a population-based delimitation would disproportionately affect southern states such as Tamil Nadu, which have successfully controlled population growth.
Vaiko said Tamil Nadu currently accounts for around 7.8 per cent of Lok Sabha representation and warned that this share could decline. He argued that the concern was particularly serious because Tamil Nadu had contributed significantly to the national economy while keeping its population growth under control.
"It's a very serious issue, not only for the southern states, but for progressive states," he said.
Vaiko cited figures to make the economic case, saying Tamil Nadu accounts for around 6 per cent of India’s population but contributes about 9 per cent of the country’s GDP and 13 per cent of total exports.
"If not, these states which contributed to the nation’s development we would suffer. We would be penalised for being good," he added.
CONGRESS: POWER TO OVERRIDE SOUTHERN MINORITY GOES UP
Congress MP Praveen Chakravarthy offered perhaps the sharpest numerical argument against the proposed 50 per cent increase in Lok Sabha seats. He said the issue was not simply whether Tamil Nadu would gain seats in absolute numbers, but whether its relative bargaining power would diminish.
"The strength to oppose, the power to oppose a Bill, the power to override the southern minority goes up tremendously," Chakravarthy said. "That is why we are opposed to this increase of 50 per cent," he added, referring to the government’s assurance that parliamentary representation would be increased by 50 per cent uniformly across the states.
Chakravarthy challenged the principle that population alone should determine political weight. Invoking Parliament’s role in overseeing government finances, he argued that economic contribution should also form part of the calculation.
"Babasaheb Ambedkar said Parliament's primary objective is also control of the purse. Parliament decides how much revenue the government can raise and how much it can spend."
He then cited figures that he said showed a disparity between the economic contributions of southern and some northern states.
"Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana together contribute 20 per cent to that purse, direct and indirect taxes," he said, contrasting this with "Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Madhya Pradesh", which he said contribute 5 per cent.
"If Parliament's responsibility is also the purse, not just the population, why not give a share for the purse also?" he asked.
"Why not make it population and purse?"
On women’s reservation, Chakravarthy argued that women should not have to wait for delimitation.
"Justice delayed is justice denied and that's what's happening to the women here in India," he said.
He argued that the government could have implemented the reservation using the existing 543-seat House rather than waiting for a new Census and delimitation exercise.
DMK: WE WON'T CHANGE OUR STANCE
DMK representative Salem Dharanidharan, who faced questions over whether the party had softened its earlier opposition to delimitation by now speaking about "fair delimitation", rejected suggestions of any understanding with the Narendra Modi government.
"We won't change our stance because we are in alliance with Party A or Party B," Dharanidharan said, adding, "The stance of the DMK has been consistent since 1949 on federalism or secularism on many matters."
He pointed to the Tamil Nadu Assembly resolution under Chief Minister Vijay, saying it called for the 543-seat strength to be retained and Tamil Nadu’s share to remain fixed, along with the immediate implementation of 33 per cent reservation for women.
According to Dharanidharan, the resolution was endorsed by all parties except the AIADMK, BJP and PMK.
BJP: SOUTH WILL NOT BE PENALISED
BJP leader and former Telangana governor Tamilisai Soundararajan strongly rejected the suggestion that delimitation would weaken southern India.
"First of all, we are all southern leaders, so we won't allow the South to be penalised, but it's not going to be penalised," she said.
Soundararajan cited the assurance given by Union Home Minister Amit Shah that there would be a uniform 50 per cent increase in parliamentary representation.
"Our Honourable Home Minister very clearly has said that there will be a uniform 50 per cent increase in the representation," she said.
Under that calculation, she said, Tamil Nadu’s Lok Sabha representation would rise from 39 to 59 seats, while Kerala’s would increase from 20 to 30.
"When there is uniformity in the increase of the number of members of Parliament and there is fair representation of the population and deepening of democracy why are we again and again fear-mongering?" she asked.
Soundararajan also broadened the argument, pointing to the increase in the number of districts and corporations in Tamil Nadu over the years.
"If, for administrative purposes, they increase all the numbers, why not in Parliament and why not in the Assembly?" she asked.
When Opposition leaders were asked whether their real concern was not simply population-based representation but the possibility of constituency boundaries being redrawn in ways that could benefit the BJP, they resisted the suggestion that this was their only concern.
However, Soundararajan repeatedly returned to the Centre’s promise of a uniform 50 per cent increase, arguing that southern states would gain seats in absolute terms and that the exercise would also enable greater representation for women.

Complaint filed against Sonia, Rahul Gandhi over disrespect to Vande Mataram
Earlier, today, Union home minister Amit Shah at a rally in Chittorgarh said, “The Congress forgot Vande Mataram out of greed for vote banks”
A complaint has been filed against senior Congress leaders Sonia Gandhi and Rahul Gandhi on Sunday for allegedly disrespecting the National Song during the flag hosting on Independence Day at the headquarters of the party.
The complaint filed by lawyers Kunal Vinayak and Shubh Sharma said during the rendition of the National Song, video footage circulated in the public domain, showed that “after the initial portion of the National Song had been sung and its rendition continued, Sonia Gandhi appeared to make gestures and communicate with persons present in a manner which, prima facie, appeared to an objection to the continuation of the rendition.”
The complaint further said, reports by several news organisations record the allegation that she objected to the complete rendition of “Vande Mataram”.
Deep Dive
It further said, “…therefore, the exact nature, intention and purpose of the gestures and conduct of Sonia Gandhi are matters which require investigation by the competent investigating agency….Further, in the other video footage, Rahul Gandhi can be clearly seen speaking the words, ‘We are not singing Vande Mataram.’ The said statement, viewed in the context of the ongoing rendition of the National Song and the conduct attributed to Sonia Gandhi, raises serious concerns regarding the intention behind the alleged acts and conduct of both Sonia Gandhi and Rahul Gandhi towards the National Song and its dignity.”
The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026, extend the penal protection presently available to the National Anthem to the National Song as well.
The amended section 3 provides that any person who intentionally prevents the singing of the National Anthem or the National Song, or causes disturbance to any assembly engaged in such singing, shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
Earlier, today, Union home minister Amit Shah at a rally in Chittorgarh said, “The Congress forgot Vande Mataram out of greed for vote banks,” referring to the same video from the Congress headquarters.
Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Amit Malviya also alleged that Sonia Gandhi objected to the full rendition of the National Song. However, the Congress said that her actions had nothing to do with the National Song played at the venue.

It was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.
But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.
“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.
As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.
They waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.
The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.
“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.
People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.
The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.
At least 10 people from the village of 3,000 people have died, and many remain missing. Villagers say they have seen several unidentified dead bodies floating on the Dikhou River.
Assam, in the far northeastern corner of India, is one of the most flood-prone regions in the country. About 40% of its land is vulnerable to inundation from the Brahmaputra and Barak rivers and other smaller rivers, and it sees at least two or three major floods annually.
According to official figures, about 2,690 villages in 25 districts have been flooded this year, affecting more than 1 million people. As of 11 August, 101 people have lost their lives. The death toll is likely to rise, officials fear.
In 2025, the death toll due to floods and landslides was 36. The year before, when all 35 districts of the state were affected by floods, at least 110 people died.
According to Partha Jyoti Das, a specialist in water and climate hazards with the environmental organisation Aaranyak, the current disaster was inevitable. The climate crisis has led to heavier rainfall, and changes to the landscape made flooding more likely.
“It’s a much-abused landscape, turning into a burial ground,” he says. Had it been just flood waters, the damage would have been less, but the rain brought with it debris, mud, silt and soil from the hills of Nagaland.
“These areas have seen mining and quarrying, both legal and illegal, for several years. From coal, sand or boulder mining, everything happens in these places. The whole landscape has been changed by large-scale deforestation, encroachment and excavation,” he says.
By 11 August, flood waters had receded in several villages, leaving behind heavy layers of mud and silt. However, low-lying areas of Sivasagar, Jorhat and Charaideo districts are still flooded, including the well-known Jokaichuk paddy field, a vast stretch of agricultural land shaped like a jokai, or bamboo fishing tool, near Gaurisagar.
“The floods have ruined 95% of the farmland across Sivasagar,” says Himadrijyoti Dutta, who works with farmers in the district through his non-profit organisation, Krishak Nyas, and has been visiting different villages to provide relief materials.
“The flood waters have washed away all the hard work and financial investments of the farmers. They have all been left poorer and desperate.”
Kalyan Das, a geography professor at Guwahati’s Cotton University, says the latest disaster will trigger a wave of migration. “Assam is already witnessing a serious crisis of out-migration of people from every block. There are many factors – primarily land degradation – making farming unsustainable,” he says.
Employment-driven migration from Assam rose from 16.3% in 1991 to 24.4% by 2011, according to a 2022 study. In rural areas, floods and soil erosion were the primary causes, the study said. “The latest floods have destroyed homes and agricultural fields. The villagers will be forced to migrate in search of livelihood opportunities,” Das says.
Eight years ago, Mintu Hazarika, 30, left Kosumari village in Sivasagar district for the IT hub of Bengaluru (formerly known as Bangalore). He earns 25,000 rupees (£195) a month by working double shifts as a security guard in Bengaluru’s Marathahalli suburb and sends half his earnings home.
“My father is a farmer, so is my elder brother,” says Hazarika. “They tend paddy fields, but it is not financially viable. So they also work as daily wage earners in nearby urban areas to supplement the household income.
On 22 July, Hazarika received a call from his father. He was told that the floods had destroyed their family’s two-hectare paddy field. “I don’t know how my family is going to survive. My elder brother is planning to come to Bengaluru to find work. There are already so many men from Sivasagar and other parts of Assam working in Bengaluru,” he says.
Bitupan Raidongia, district president of Sivasagar for the Bharatiya Janata party, the ruling party in Assam, says the authorities are providing support for affected communities. “Our government is doing its best to rescue marooned people. We are also reaching out to affected families by providing them with food items, clothes and other essentials.”
Sivasagar’s district commissioner, Mridul Yadav, adds that the local administration was making a coordinated effort to address the flood situation. “Various departments are working together on rescue, relief distribution, and damage assessment. Health camps, essential medicines, drinking water, livestock fodder and relief kits are being provided. Several relief camps remain operational to support affected families and restore essential services,” he adds.
But the authorities’ response has been criticised as too little, too late. In a video that went viral, the Assam-based singer Nilotpal Bora said thousands more people would have died were it not for the intervention of local charities and individuals.
“You people [the government] had a delayed response in reaching out to the affected people. If common people had not distributed relief, at least 3,000 people from flooded areas would have died because of hunger and thirst,” he said in response to a comment from Assam’s chief minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, that “the situation was under control”, and the public should not raise money to help flood victims.
Meanwhile, local groups and people are doing what they can to help. About 40 bikers from One Northeast Motorcycle Club are travelling to affected areas to distribute food, clothing, sanitary items, candles, matchboxes and other essentials. “It’s a heartbreaking sight,” says the club’s founder, Chow Sureng Rajkonwar.
“Hundreds of people across villages have become homeless. Their homes were destroyed and flattened to the ground. Those that remain are filled with polokh [alluvial silt or sediment left behind by flood waters]. All their belongings were destroyed or washed away with the water. It will take months to rebuild those houses,” he says, adding that people are living in tents made of plastic sheets and tarpaulins on roads or higher ground near their villages.
Phukon was one of the luckier ones. Although the water level was more than 1.5 metres (5ft) high in her courtyard, it did not enter her house, which is built on higher ground.
For almost a week now, she has been providing relief aid to flood victims after getting distress calls from family, friends and acquaintances. “I decided to leave my home and reach out to people who need food, clothing, and other essentials. Everyone I know has been affected by floods.”

As the CJP protests gathered momentum, a parallel campaign began online against some of the women who participated in them. Accounts targeting the protesters circulated their videos, hurled abuse at them and published screenshots containing sensitive personal information, turning online trolling into outright doxxing.
Many of those targeted had either spoken to the media during the protests or posted reels and other content on social media with abusive language against Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Several Right-wing handles subjected them to sustained trolling and abuse while putting their private information in the public domain.
The most alarming instance involved a young woman from Noida. A clip of her using expletives against Modi during the Delhi protests went viral, following which Delhi-based Supreme Court lawyer Smriti Singh Chandel filed a zero FIR against her, invoking charges of defamation and “intentional insult to provoke breach of peace”.
Chandel also posted a photo of the FIR complaint on her Instagram handle, which revealed the home address of the accused individual. She also posted a video of men outside Gautam Budh Nagar police station holding the complaint copy and claiming they had access to the personal details of the female. Police had “assured” them, they said, that she would be arrested within days.
Young Female Protester Bears The Brunt
Confusion over the female’s age — whether or not she is a minor — and her name further problematised the case. After Prime Minister Narendra Modi posted a video saying that he “forgave” everyone who had abused him during the protest, the female protester posted an apology video, admitting her mistake, apologising to him and to the country. She claimed she was “influenced” by others using abusive language against the PM.
As reports began to suggest that the protester was in fact a minor, responding to allegations of doxxing a minor, trolls claimed that the girl in the apology video was not the same as the girl in the viral video. Several Right-wing influencers took to X to claim that a minor girl was being used to cover up for the actual 25-year-old protester, so that POCSO cases could be registered. Some even claimed she was using her younger sister for sympathy while some users went to the length of comparing facial features to prove their point.
The case significantly blew up when mainstream media aired her alleged name and face on national television. Times Now amplified the claim that the protester was a 25-year-old woman named Ruchika Singh. NDTV’s Shiv Aroor made the same claim, showing her face and revealing her identity.
CNN-News18 also made the same claim, while exposing her face; the channel on July 31 reported how they have “tracked down” the girl to her society complex in Noida, from where she had reportedly absconded. Citing repeated visits from the police as well as from strangers, the single mother-daughter duo reportedly had to leave their rented accommodation and shift elsewhere.
To make matters worse, on July 31, CNN-News 18 also claimed to have gained access to “exclusive voices” from the female protesters life that “nobody else has”. In an outright case of breach of privacy, a reporter from the organisation reached the “beauty salon” where the girl had allegedly learnt nail art till the month of June.
The reporter speaks at length with the owner of the nail salon, probing over the girl’s association with the salon. The owner mentions that the her name was not Ruchika Singh, as was being claimed by the media. He also claimed that on repeated failures to furnish her identity details, specifically her Aadhaar Card, the girl was reportedly asked by the management to not come back.
In an interview with ABP News, the victim of this doxxing episode clarified that her name is not Ruchika Singh and neither is she 25 years old.
The girl, who stated her age to be 15, reportedly faced constant harassment and threats from people in the neighbourhood, including threats of “murder and rape“. The mother, who also appears in the ABP interview, urges the public to stop the relentless abuse against her daughter.
The mother stated that despite the “PM forgiving her (daughter)”, an army of anti-social elements and police were repeatedly visiting their residence, which they were eventually forced to vacate given the increasing threat to their privacy and survival. “What will you get from harassing a child?” the mother asked, while extending gradtitude to Modi for granting her daughter “jeevandaan”. She repeatedly implores Modi and the masses to “let them live in peace and return to their home”.
Notably, Chandel, by her own admission, had “learnt” about the young girl’s name and details from social media users. The police complaint as well as the FIR went on to mention her as 25-year-old while the girl and her mother maintained that she is 15. “There are people claiming that it is her younger sister who has made the apology; they are saying I have hidden my daughter. This is bizarre; why would any mother throw her child into this vicious cycle of threats?” the mother said to The Print.
‘Arrest These Women’: Online Mob Justice
This was not an isolated incident. Several Right-wing accounts on X were determined to identify and locate female protesters. Retired IAS officer Sanjay Dixit, who runs the Hindutva propaganda page Jaipur Dialogues, specifically targeted women protesters who had allegedly abused Modi. In one of his posts, he shared a collage of twelve such women, urging the Delhi Police to “arrest them”.

Jaipur Dialogues had also shared the Noida protester’s video, claiming that she was not a minor but actually 25 years old.
Popular Right-wing influencer account @KreatelyMedia shared a video of three kids who are seen using expletives against Modi in an Instagram reel. Another handle @BesuraTaansane posted a video of a seemingly young girl from the protest. NEW YORK — Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty on Friday to federal stalking charges in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, admitting matter-of-factly that he trailed the executive to an investor conference in 2024 and gunned him down on a New York City street.
Mangione, 28, said he even used a ruse to glean information about the event, contacting the health insurance company ahead of time under the guise of being an investor at a multibillion-dollar firm.
“On the morning of Dec. 4, 2024, I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan, and he died,” Mangione told the court as Thompson’s wife, Paulette, took several deep breaths and repeatedly wiped tears from her eyes. A supporter put an arm around the wife and held her tight.
Mangione is set for sentencing Dec. 18. When U.S. District Judge Margaret M. Garnett asked whether he understood that he could spend the rest of his life in prison, Mangione answered neutrally: “Yes.”
Mangione entered the plea at a hastily scheduled hearing in Manhattan federal court, resolving one of two cases against him in connection with Thompson’s death. Mangione’s lawyers could now seek to have his separate New York state murder case thrown out on double jeopardy grounds.
Surveillance video of the ambush showed a masked gunman shooting Thompson, 50, from behind. Police say “delay,” “deny” and “depose” were written on the ammunition, mimicking a phrase used to describe how insurers avoid paying claims. That detail — and revelations that Mangione’s private writings lambasted health insurers as greedy, according to authorities — made the case a fulcrum for debate about the industry and made Mangione a cause célèbre for some of its critics.
Mangione told the court Friday that he pursued Thompson “after years of enduring severe pain from a broken back and navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system.”
Mangione never was a UnitedHealthcare customer, according to police and the company. A University of Pennsylvania graduate from a wealthy Maryland family, he was arrested five days after the shooting, when he was spotted at a McDonald’s in Altoona, Pa. It’s about 230 miles west of Manhattan.
Thompson led one of the United States’ largest health insurers, but he wasn’t well known outside the industry. Trained as an accountant, he had worked at parent company UnitedHealth Group Inc. for 20 years and became CEO of its insurance arm, UnitedHealthcare, in 2021. He and his wife have two sons, who were in high school when their father was killed.
Both the federal and state cases could lead to a life prison sentence for Mangione. A federal judge earlier this year tossed out additional charges that could have exposed him to a potential death penalty.
Mangione had complained about the prospect of two trials, telling a judge in February: “It’s the same trial twice. One plus one is two. Double jeopardy by any commonsense definition.”
Under New York law, a state prosecution could potentially be barred if the federal case is resolved first.
The state’s double jeopardy protections kick in if a jury has been sworn in a prior prosecution, such as a federal case, or if that prosecution ends in a guilty plea. Mangione’s cases involve different charges arising from the same course of conduct.
In a letter last month, state prosecutors objected to the possibility of a guilty plea in the federal case wiping out the state case.
Garnett has delivered some setbacks to the defense, including ruling in January that prosecutors could use items collected from Mangione’s backpack during his arrest as evidence against him.
They included a 3D-printed pistol that investigators said matched the one used to kill Thompson and a notebook in which authorities say Mangione described his intent to kill an insurance executive.
In June, Mangione’s lawyers said they would pursue a psychiatric defense in the state case but reversed course a day later. The defense, involving claims that he was suffering from extreme emotional disturbance at the time of the killing, isn’t allowed in federal court.
—Michael R. Sisak, Larry Neumeister, and Alanna Durkin Richer

A Bleak, Violent Novel’s Unexpected Delights
For the characters in The Disappearers, seeing and being seen are matters of life and death.
This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here.
Before his latest book, Marlon James hadn’t written a novel set in Jamaica in more than a decade. In the years following his Booker Prize–winning A Brief History of Seven Killings, the author focused on his Dark Star Trilogy, set in a fantasy universe. But after that long literary detour, he returned to the land of his birth in his new novel, The Disappearers—which is set primarily in Kingston and follows a group of characters, all queer Jamaican men, who meet while rehearsing a play that will never be seen.
First, here are four new stories from The Atlantic’s Books section:
For this group, which gathers in secret in 1988, seeing and being seen are matters of life and death. The Kingston they inhabit is murderously homophobic, and accordingly, the novel can be quite bleak. But The Disappearers offers some delights too. Recently, in her article about the book for The Atlantic, Stephanie Burt noted that “the novel opens up many pleasures for literary readers,” who may recognize the numerous titles and references sprinkled throughout. I was deeply affected by how, almost universally, the characters seek out anything that proves that gay life exists on a larger scale. Lowbrow works, such as porn films and magazines, are most accessible; Playgirl and Hustler are name-checked. The songs of Boy George, Sylvester, and Prince are lifelines—the homoerotic cover of Prince’s 1988 album, Lovesexy, is an especially powerful beacon. Many of the characters are well read, and they name-drop gay novels such as Andrew Holleran’s Dancer From the Dance and E. M. Forster’s Maurice. For one of the men in particular, the type of hustling, defiant gay life that John Rechy describes in his nonfiction book The Sexual Outlaw is pivotal.
The play they put on, a 1967 drama called Fortune and Men’s Eyes, explores homosexuality among a group of prisoners. Some of its characters see sex as a means for gaining or establishing power; others, as a convenient way to access pleasure. Some are what a modern audience might recognize as gay, whereas others choose partners largely because of their proximity. The cast share the characters’ disparate attitudes toward queerness. But in the Jamaica they live in, there is no room for nuance; any man seen as homosexual is a target for violence. Brutality will soon come to the rehearsal room.
In a way, James has written a gay novel about the uses of a gay novel. When his characters invoke Oscar Wilde and Edmund White, Hadrian and Michelangelo, they’re proving, to themselves and to the reader, that queer life existed long before they came around. But James is not an unskeptical cheerleader for the healing power of visibility and representation. The Disappearers’ major theme, after all, is that being recognized can be a bad thing: Owning these books is a hazard. Buying Lovesexy as a man in 1988 Kingston invites vigilantism. Staging Fortune and Men’s Eyes puts its cast and crew in danger.
So why try to do it? The director and ringleader, Havelock Titus, asks himself this question more than a decade after those hopeful rehearsals. He knew, even at the time, that the effort was a risk. He still doesn’t know “what success would have meant,” because the unstaged play “never had the chance to become a failure.” But Havelock knows on some level that he did it because, just like those who came before him, he wanted to create some kind of evidence that gay men communed and survived in his time and place. In short, he was tired of being erased.
Marlon James Returns to Realism, and to Jamaica
By Stephanie Burt
In his new novel, gay men struggle to escape violence in Kingston.
What to Read
The Age of Reform, by Richard Hofstadter
History can’t fully explain the present or predict the future, but it can help us understand the patterns of contemporary politics and the likely paths ahead. In 1955, Hofstadter, one of the great American historians of the 20th century, published The Age of Reform—a political and social history of the years 1890 to 1940, the period of populism, progressivism, and the New Deal. Rapid technological change, monopoly power, deep inequality, endemic corruption, mass immigration, nativist demagogues, the transformation of both political parties, repeated efforts at reform, recurring spasms of reaction: Perhaps no other age so resembles our own. Hofstadter is brilliant at analyzing types that feel quite familiar to us today—the crusading urban progressive, the small-town conspiracy theorist. He was a liberal who sympathized with the passion for progress while unsentimentally diagnosing its illiberal ideas and motives. The fevered moralism of that age seems a long way from the paralyzing cynicism of ours. But reading Hofstadter will remind you that reform and reaction not only follow each other, but also often coexist in the same moment; neither ever has the last word. Americans are always dreaming of a better country, and some have actually made it so. — George Packer

Four delicious and easy noodle dishes to mix up your weeknights
Noodles are budget-friendly, filling and fun — as well as incredibly versatile.
They also have an amazing ability to get fussy eaters (if you happen to have them in your household) enthusiastic about a variety of food.
You can pick the type of noodles you use, depending on dietary requirements or what you have available, for any of these recipes.
Sticky beef with noodles, pickled celery and mint
The perfect base for slow-cooked beef isn't a bun — it's noodles.
Beef chuck is a budget-friendly cut that slow-cooks brilliantly while you get on with your day. The sticky sauce in Ismat Awan's recipe coats the noodles and contrasts with the cool crunch of the pickled celery.
You can swap out chuck for blade, shin or brisket too.
Vegetable and soba noodle salad with honey ginger cashews
Loaded with veggies and a delicious mix of textures, Heidi Sze's soba noodle salad has a tasty dressing with Asian flavours and sweet crunchy cashews.
The veggies take a little bit of chopping time, but you can reduce this by buying them pre-chopped, prepping them ahead of time or with the careful use of a mandolin (you want to cut prep time, not your fingers).
One-pot udon noodles with kimchi and cheese
Spicy, cheesy and satisfying, this dish from Hetty Lui McKinnon takes the perfect pairing of kimchi and cheese to another level by combining it with chubby udon noodles and a thick, gravy-like sauce.
It's a delicious way to use kimchi — even if you're not yet a convert — and you can mix up the cheese you use.
Green ginger and miso noodles
This little gem of a meal from Phoebe Thorburn takes just 20 minutes to have ready and is gluten-free, dairy-free and plant-based (but doesn't have to be if that's not what you need).
Sauteed garlic, ginger and miso are blended with spinach, and a few other easy and tasty additions, to make a vibrant sauce that coats the noodles.
Adding spring onion and crispy chilli to serve gives it a perfect kick and crunch.
