Manchester City has accepted FC Barcelona’s latest transfer offer for captain and star midfielder Rodri according to Fabrizio Romano, Mundo Deportivo and numerous big outlets in Spain.
Citing anonymous sources, COPE’s reliable Victor Navarro reports that the final fee is €65 million in fixed money plus a possible, additional €5 million in bonuses.
Rodri is expected to travel to Barcelona in the coming days to complete a medical then sign on the dotted line for four years until 2030 ahead of the Joan Gamper Trophy match.
The development caps off a whirlwind transfer saga, which began on Thursday morning last week.
That’s when reports spread of talks breaking down between City and Real Madrid, as per a potential switch to the Bernabeu for the Spain skipper.
Barça then gained traction in the hunt for the 30-year-old voted the Best Player at the World Cup, when leading Spain to its second victory in the FIFA flagship tournament.
A phone call from the Catalans’ head coach Hansi Flick played a big part in convincing Rodri of the sporting project at the Spotify Camp Nou. He then swiftly gave his ‘OK’, to what will be one of the club’s biggest transfers of the 21st century in terms of stature.
On Spanish radio, Rodri’s agent confirmed that his client preferred a move to Barcelona over Real Madrid, who had made the former Ballon d’Or holder a reasonable personal offer.
Barça and City then began negotiations after Rodri agreed personal terms. Barça’s initial bid of $52 million (€45 million) was knocked back, though RAC1 later claimed that a €50 million deal had been agreed.
Many sources in Catalonia and England said that wasn’t true, which it proved not be.
Barça’s second offer on Thursday this week was for €60 million plus add-ons, which took the final proposed amount to €70 million.
That too was knocked back, but after at least two known failed attempts, Barça Sporting Director Deco has finally managed to get an agreement over the line.
Rodri will take FC Barcelona’s midfield to a new dimension
Though it is an area of the pitch where Barça is traditionally stacked and never short of talent, the midfield now receives a massive boost in quality with Rodri pulling the strings.
Flick can choose a number of combinations in the center of the park, and the increased control Rodri will bring helps Barça take a step forward in the Champions League.
It’s a competition he’s already won at City in 2023, though his new club is yet to bring it home in 11 years after semifinals and quarterfinals exits in two attempts on Flick’s watch.
Rodri will also allow FC Barcelona to press higher in attack. Furthermore, his new boss’ famous defensive high line is given added protection as young prospects such as Lamine Yamal and Marc Bernal receive the perfect mentor.

Shares of edtech company Physics Wallah rallied as much as 9.5% to an intraday high of ₹128.35 apiece on the BSE today after JPMorgan and JM Financial upgraded their ratings for the stock following the company’s Q1 FY27 results. The stock later pared some gains and was trading 5.6% higher at ₹123.85 around 11:44 IST. Its market capitalisation stood at around ₹35,883.9 Cr (about $3.7 Bn). JPMorgan upgraded PhysicsWallah to ‘Overweight’ from ‘Neutral’, retaining its target price of ₹148. The target implies an upside of over 26% from the stock’s previous close of ₹117.20. The brokerage said PhysicsWallah’s Q1 performance exceeded its expectations despite disruption from the NEET exam cycle. It also highlighted the company’s decision to retain its guidance of around 30% revenue growth in FY27 and divest its NBFC arm, FinZ Finance, to sharpen its focus on the core education business. Meanwhile, JM Financial upgraded PhysicsWallah to ‘Buy’ from ‘Add’, while retaining its June 2027 target price of ₹140. The target implies an upside of nearly 20% from the previous close. JM Financial said the company delivered a decent quarter despite the NEET-related disruption and that its underlying business fundamentals remained intact. It added that the stock’s correction of more than 20% from its recent highs had made its risk-reward profile more favourable. Revenue Crosses ₹1,000 Cr PhysicsWallah’s operating revenue grew 24.4% to ₹1,054 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹847.1 Cr in the year-ago quarter. On a sequential basis, revenue increased 14.7% from ₹918.8 Cr in Q4 FY26. The edtech major’s net loss narrowed 30.5% to ₹88.3 Cr from ₹127 Cr, although it widened 27.8% QoQ. Total expenses rose 18% YoY to ₹1,247 Cr. PhysicsWallah posted an EBITDA of ₹52 Cr during the quarter, compared with an EBITDA loss of ₹21 Cr in Q1 FY26. Its EBITDA margin improved to 4.9% from a negative 2.5%. Adjusted EBITDA jumped more than fivefold to ₹135 Cr from ₹26 Cr, while the adjusted EBITDA margin expanded to 12.9% from 3.1%. Online revenue grew 33% YoY to ₹549 Cr, with online transacting users rising 2.4% to 21.5 Lakh. Average collection per user increased 9.7% to ₹4,311. Meanwhile, revenue from the K-12 and early-learning segment surged 88% YoY to ₹105 Cr, while enrolments grew 41% to 7.8 Lakh. The postponement and re-examination of NEET UG disrupted Physics Wallah’s usual admission cycle, resulting in a 28% decline in online NEET collections during Q1. However, collections rebounded after the NEET results were announced, rising 51% YoY between July 1 and August 13. Physics Wallah cofounder Prateek Maheshwari said the company expects to achieve group-level PAT profitability in Q3 FY27. “We are very confident that we will achieve net-level PAT profitability in Q3,” he said, noting that Q3 is typically the company’s strongest quarter. The company also reported an exceptional impact of around ₹42 Cr from the fair-value remeasurement of financial instruments linked to Sarrthi IAS. In July, Physics Wallah acquired an additional 11% stake in Sarrthi IAS for ₹71.81 Cr, taking its holding in the UPSC coaching institute to 51%.

7 held in Karnataka over rape, abortion of woman with mental illness: Police
According to police, Sandeep, Dr Nagaraj and Rekha gave the victim 10 abortion pills and carried out the termination of her three-month pregnancy
Seven people, including a doctor and a nurse, were arrested on Friday in connection with the alleged repeated rape of a 26-year-old woman with mental illness by four men and the subsequent abortion in Karnataka’s Gadag district, police said.
Police registered a case on July 26 at the Gadag Women Police Station. The accused were identified as Sikandar, Shabirahmad Junasab, Pradeep, Bharat, Sandeep, Dr Nagaraj and nurse Rekha.
Gadag district superintendent of police (SP) Rohan Jagadeesh said, “According to the initial complaint, two men had sexually assaulted her on separate occasions and got her pregnant. Three others were accused of carrying out the abortion to cover up the crime. But as the investigation progressed, more facts came out. Police found that two more accused had also raped the woman on different days and at different places. In total, four men were involved in the sexual assault.”
Police said that when the woman became three months pregnant, her parents came to know about the ordeal. The victim’s parents alleged that during this time, the accused tried to suppress the case by luring the family with money and also threatening them with dire consequences if they filed a complaint.
The SP further said, “This is a very serious case. We have formed special teams and arrested seven people so far. We will not spare anyone.”
He added, “The victim’s parents have also named three more individuals in their statement. The parents have alleged that these three were involved in trying to cover up the illegal abortion. An FIR has been registered at Gadag Women’s Police Station under Sections 64 (rape) and 88 (voluntarily causing a miscarriage) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) against them, and their role is currently under investigation.”
According to police, Sandeep, Dr Nagaraj and Rekha gave the victim 10 abortion pills and carried out the termination of her three-month pregnancy, while the other four were allegedly involved in the sexual assault.
“Police have also launched a separate probe to trace the owner of a medical shop who allegedly sold abortion pills to the accused without a doctor’s official prescription. Authorities are checking if this was part of a larger illegal abortion racket. Additionally, police are investigating whether arrested staff nurse Rekha was involved in similar illegal activities in the past,” the SP said.
The 26-year-old victim is currently undergoing medical treatment and receiving psychological counselling and support from the Women and Child Welfare Department, the SP said, adding that the investigation is still underway and more arrests are likely.

Don’t Expect Russians to Protest the War
Ukraine may have hoped that deeper drone attacks would cause Russians to rise up, but mass demonstrations don’t look likely.
This summer, Ukraine began one of the most ambitious campaigns of its war with Russia. It launched drones deep into Russian territory, hitting some of the country’s biggest oil refineries and causing a nationwide fuel shortage. In some areas, Russians have waited for gas for as long as 69 hours, in lines stretching miles. Impatient drivers have beaten and stabbed one another. Even state-controlled media have acknowledged the problem.
Ukraine and its allies seemed to hope that frustrated Russians would rise up in protest. After more than four years, the war had finally “come home.” Now that more citizens were feeling its effects, one might assume, they would demand its end and apply pressure to President Vladimir Putin ahead of parliamentary elections in the fall. But so far, no mass uprising appears likely, now or anytime soon.
Russians are used to inconveniences. Under Soviet rule, they lived with shortages of just about everything. Lines were so ubiquitous that academics theorized about Russian identity being shaped by waiting. Books were published with chapter titles such as “The Queue as a Form of Soviet Life.” The newspaper Socialist Industry estimated that Soviet citizens spent 30 billion working hours a year waiting in line for essential goods.
In the late 1980s, at the peak of Soviet scarcity, my family lived on the outskirts of Gorky, a city east of Moscow. Sometimes my mother would send me shopping. I hated it. At a small, gray store called Vegetables, I would wait in line to pick through boxes of rotting produce, hoping to find an acceptable carrot or beetroot for borscht. Then I went to Bread, where I waited some more. Shelves were half empty. The only item that never seemed to run out was margarine; enterprising salespeople tried to make it more appealing by sculpting it into hedgehogs, which they put in display cases. Lines got even longer on the rare days when cheese or butter were delivered. Meat hardly ever came.
Still, nobody protested. We waved away the deprivation and delays. Everyone lives this way, we told ourselves. After all, Soviets knew the cost of complaining. In 1962, thousands of demonstrators gathered to protest wage cuts and government-imposed price increases. In response, Premier Nikita Khrushchev’s government deployed thousands of troops, who killed roughly two dozen demonstrators in what became known as the Novocherkassk massacre.
Russians continue to fear their government. I recently called my former neighbor in St. Petersburg, an art teacher and activist whom I’ll call Svetlana. When I asked whether she had witnessed any street protests, she laughed. “Are you guys living on the moon out there?” she asked me. “Don’t you get how dangerous it is here?”
“It’s even worse than in the Soviet days,” Svetlana continued. “One guy bragged to me the other day that he’d reported his neighbor to the FSB”—the successor of the KGB—simply for listening to anti-war music. She also told me about an acquaintance who had spent two years in prison for leaving a poem and flowers at a monument to a Ukrainian poet. In most households, gripes about the regime don’t leave the kitchen.
At the start of the war, demonstrations were more common. In 2022, police arrested nearly 19,000 anti-war activists, according to OVD-Info, an independent human-rights group. Since then, protests have all but disappeared. This year, one of the most notable critics of the regime was a veteran named Alexander Lunin. In June, Lunin put on his military uniform and recorded a speech denouncing Putin and the war. He posted it on social media, where it received more than 12 million views in 24 hours. The police jailed him, and Lunin publicly apologized for “giving in to emotions due to fatigue.”
Earlier this week, the only anti-war party was banned from parliamentary elections. Far-right politicians had sued the party, named Yabloko, alleging that it had received foreign funding, violated copyright law, and promoted “extremism.” The supreme court ruled in the far right’s favor, removing Yabloko from the ballot. Only a few hundred Russians protested outside the court.
Most Russians seem to have inherited the long-suffering mentality of the generations who grew up under Soviet rule. Rather than tiring of the war, “Russians realize that they are under attack, and that it’s time to stand together and tighten their belts,” Irina Borogan, a journalist who has studied Russian dissidents, told me. When the BBC asked a middle-aged man living in Crimea about the fuel shortages, he shrugged them off: “We are humans. We’ll adapt.”
Last month, I called Konstantin Sonin, an economist and a professor at the University of Chicago who left Russia in 2015. He told me that his friends in Moscow have made only the barest wartime accommodations—such as sending their kids to summer camp in Gelendzhik, a town on the Black Sea coast, instead of one in the heavily shelled Crimea, even though both areas are well within range of Ukrainian drones. He sounded astonished by his friends’ comfort with risk. “We’ve seen what Ukrainians have been capable of coping with,” Sonin told me. “Russians can endlessly adapt to this crisis too.”
I heard a similar message from Vladislav Inozemtsev, a Russian economist and political scientist who lives in the United States. Inozemtsev told me that his friends in Moscow have used their contacts to circumvent the fuel shortage and get gas delivered to their door. “It’s twice the normal price, but they can afford it; the middle class quickly adapts to difficulties,” he said, while acknowledging that Russians in rural areas will likely have a harder time.
By some accounts, Moscow hardly looks like the capital of a country fighting a war of attrition. Denis Volkov, the director of the Levada Center, an independent polling organization, described his walk to work to me. The city center, he told me, is filled with decorations that the government has put up: an oversized samovar, an inflatable elephant, sprawling flower beds. Volkov said that he sees no sign of a public revolt. “I would say that the expectations of a revolution in Russia are not based on any real facts,” he said. “All our data proves the opposite.”
A few months before the war, Levada found that Putin’s approval rating was 63 percent. In June, it was 74 percent, although it has been dropping since the start of the year. A majority of Russians—52 percent—said that their country was moving in the right direction. “People blame mainly the West and Washington for all their troubles” instead of Putin, Volkov said. These findings undoubtedly reflect the reluctance of citizens in an authoritarian country to complain to pollsters about their government. Nonetheless, according to Volkov, Levada found that 16 percent of Russians said that they would participate in street protests, up from 11 percent in 2024. Last year, 16 percent of respondents said they felt fear or sadness. This summer, that figure was 29 percent.
Even though there have been no signs of mass protest, Putin is preparing. This year, the Kremlin increased the budget for the national guard and other law-enforcement agencies to a record high of more than $47 billion. Just like Russians who fear the reprise of Soviet-era government violence, Putin also has a precedent to worry about. In 1991, after years of keeping Russians off the streets, the Soviet regime was unable to stop a rally of hundreds of thousands in Moscow, which accelerated its end. Putin may not have much reason to fear such a protest in the near future, but he can’t be too careful.

After Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi and Congress leader Sandeep Dikshit took a jibe at Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s customary hugs with foreign leaders and his public camaraderie with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Thursday, August 13, a statement purportedly issued by the Italian Embassy in New Delhi began circulating on social media.
Speaking at the Rachnatmak Congress national convention, Gandhi gave Dikshit a big hug. Dikshit quipped, “You weren’t hugging me thinking I was Meloni?” Gandhi replied, “I haven’t reached that stage yet,” drawing laughter from the gathering. The exchange triggered outrage among Bharatiya Janata Party leaders and its supporters.
The purported statement was posted on X by an account named ‘Italy in India’ (@AINga5f). It claimed that the embassy had expressed “deep concern and strong disapproval” over the “derogatory remarks” attributed to Gandhi.
“We respect India’s democratic institutions and political discourse, and we expect the same respect for Italy and its democratically elected leadership,” the purported statement read.
Media outlets Republic and Gujarat Samachar published reports based on the purported letter.
Several other influential and verified X handles, including Right-wing influencer Ajeet Bharti, K S Radhakrishnan, International Business Times, CNN News 18 journalist Vaibhav Singh, Saravanaprasad Balasubramanian (Modi ka Pariwar) and Damodar Singh amplified the purported letter on X.
The purported statement is also viral on Facebook and Instagram.
Fact Check
It is pertinent to note that the X handle that released the letter, @AINga5f, is a troll account and not the official handle of the Italian Embassy in India. The account has since been taken down from X.
The bio of the handle clearly stated that it was a satire account. Here is an archive.
The real handle of the Italian embassy in India is called @ItalyinIndia which also has a grey verification badge which is given to government or multilateral organization accounts.
We checked the website of the embassy and found no such statement. We also discovered that the last update on their website was on July 24, about a ministry of foreign affairs and international cooperation (MAECI) scholarship.
Thus, it can be conclusively stated that the letter circulating online is fake and was not released by the official handle of the Italian Embassy in India. The letter was first shared by a troll account that has since been taken down.

Who are the Chawinga sisters leading Malawi's bid for Wafcon glory?
- Published
Malawi have been the surprise package of the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon), but the source of the goals which have fired the tournament debutants into Sunday's final against Cameroon (19:00 GMT) has been less of a shock.
Sisters Tabitha and Temwa Chawinga are the undoubted stars of the show, scoring nine of Malawi's 12 goals - with Temwa leading the golden boot race with fives strikes alongside Zambia's Barbra Banda.
And while the Scorchers are the lowest-ranked side at the finals in Morocco, at 153rd in the world, the siblings have already won silverware for some of football's biggest clubs.
Who is Tabitha Chawinga?
Born on 22 May 1996 in the northern district of Rumphi, Tabitha is the older sister.
The 30-year-old began playing football as a child with boys in her village, with a ball made out of plastic or paper.
"Growing up, I never saw myself as different from boys," she told the BBC. "Whatever they did I believed I could."
However, her mother did not approve.
"My mum beat me because she was embarrassed," Chawinga told Africa Daily in 2023.
"People would provoke my mum: 'Look at your daughter - maybe she will not be married in the future. Your daughter, she doesn't want to go to school.'
"Even my friends said: 'No women can play football in this world'."
Tabitha persisted and her journey to international stardom began when she moved to join DD Sunshine in the capital Lilongwe.
Tabitha draws strongly on her Christian faith, paying tribute to God during many of her media engagements.
Where has Tabitha Chawinga played?
A switch to Europe came in 2014 after an American working for a non-governmental organisation had a spell at DD Sunshine before relocating to Sweden.
The NGO worker joined third-tier side Krokom Dvarsatts, and DD Sunshine owner David Dube then suggested the Swedes try out Tabitha as well.
"When Krokom Dvarsatts hesitated, Mr Dube offered to pay visa and flight costs for me to travel to Sweden for trials," said Tabitha.
"I joined the team and they were immediately impressed with my strength, dribbling, shooting from far and scoring skills."
She had to wait until after her 18th birthday to make her debut, then became the first Malawian woman to play in Europe and scored 39 times in 14 games.
Tabitha continued her exploits at second-tier Kvarnsveden, netting 43 goals to help them win promotion, and was then leading scorer in the Swedish top flight in 2017.
A six-year spell in China followed, which saw her win three league titles, three golden boots and two player of the season awards.
A successful loan with Inter Milan in 2022-23 also saw her win the Serie A golden boot.
"My goal is to achieve for African people," she said after that feat.
"I need to play for the girls in Africa. They need to see there are women in this world that can play football like men."
It was Paris St-Germain next for the striker, and another landmark as the first woman from Malawi to play and score in the Uefa Champions League in 2023.
France's most decorated female side, Lyon, came calling and Tabitha has helped them to back-to-back domestic titles.
She played in last season's Champions League final defeat by Barcelona.
Who is Temwa Chawinga?
Born on 20 September 1998, Temwa - whose name means 'love' in her native Tumbuka language - followed the path trodden by her elder sister.
She acknowledges that Tabitha has been "instrumental" in her career, with the two playing together for both DD Sunshine and Kvarnsveden after Tabitha recommended that the Swedes sign her younger sister.
"She made connections for me to leave Malawi to play abroad, but most importantly has always advised me to fight hard, to know what I want and to pursue it without listening to distracting people," Temwa told BBC Sport Africa.
The 27-year-old impressed in Sweden, scoring 35 league goals in 2019.
With agents in China asking Tabitha how to find a well-rounded player like her, the response was once again to recommend Temwa.
Wuhan Jianghan pounced and the forward helped the club win four consecutive league titles - including the 2021 edition alongside her sister.
Temwa Chawinga – world record goalscorer
In 2023 she was the world's top goalscorer of the calendar year, outscoring the likes of Erling Haaland, Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi with 51 strikes for her Chinese club and 12 for Malawi.
"When I found out I was so happy. I didn't believe it, but it was so amazing," she said.
Kansas City Current of America's National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) swooped and Temwa was the division's top scorer in her debut season in 2024 with 20 goals.
She bagged another 15 last year as the Current ended the regular campaign with the best record in the NWSL before being beaten in the play-offs.
She was named league MVP in both campaigns.
Despite their roll of achievements, neither sister has yet been named as African Women's Footballer of the Year.
A stunning impact for Malawi
Both have been prolific at international level since making their Malawi debuts in 2011 and 2016 respectively.
Tabitha usually captains the Scorchers, but it was Temwa who skippered the side to their first piece of silverware, the regional Council of Southern Africa Football Associations Women's Championship title in 2023.
"I was waiting to qualify for the [Women's] Africa Cup of Nations [for] a long time," Tabitha said before this tournament began.
"I've been playing big games in Europe, but I tell the girls 'Don't be shy, don't be scared'."
Those words proved invaluable as Malawi upset 10-time champions Nigeria in their Wafcon opener and also finished above 2022 semi-finalists Zambia in Group C.
The Scorchers came from behind to beat Ghana 2-1 in the quarter-finals - sealing qualification for next year's Fifa Women's World Cup - before both sisters scored in the semi-final win over Algeria.
"I'm so happy because a lot of people didn't give us a chance at this level, but we showed the world that we have a good team," Temwa said.
Malawi FA boss Fleetwood Haiya says funds received from world governing body Fifa have helped stoke the success of the women's side, but both sisters have called for more investment.
"If we can put money in Malawi to support girls' football I think there can be so many like me and Tabitha," Temwa said.
Should Malawi become just the fourth side to win the Wafcon title, after Nigeria, Equatorial Guinea and South Africa, they will be indebted to two sisters from humble beginnings.

Parul has fallen behind England’s Elise Thorner and Kenya’s Celestine Jepkosgei Biwot who are fighting for the third position.
Parul is still in fourth position. Bronze medal is a possibility for the Indian as Peruth Chemutai of Uganda and Kenya’s Faith Cherotich have moved away from the pack to battle it out for the gold.
After the first 250m, India’s Parul Chaudhary is in the fourth spot in the women’s 3000m steeplechase final.
All eyes on the track where India’s Parul Chaudhary will be in action.
No Indian woman has ever won a CWG medal in this event. Can she create history tonight?
India’s Sagar Thayat (51.79m) and Devender Kumar (46.40m) are placed sixth and seventh, respectively after four throws.
India’s Nayanmoni Saikia wins the first set 11-2 against Isle of Man’s Caroline Whitehead in women’s singles sectional play.
Wow!!! India’s Dilip Mahadu Gavit takes the gold with a Games Record of 10.71s while the silver goes to his compatriot Mohammed Basil Morssinganakath who clocks 10.83s.
A historic double podium for India!
England’s Kevin Santos bags bronze in 10.85s.
India’s Mohammed Basil Morssinganakath and Dilip Mahadu Gavit are in action.
The Indian swimmer records a timing of 15:36.25s. Australia’s Sam Short takes the gold, Northern Ireland’s Daniel Wiffen claims the silver while the bronze goes to Australia’s Benjamin Goedemans.
Jamaica’s Lloydricia Cameron moves into the bronze medal position with a last throw of 17.87m and will stay there as India’s Manpreet Kaur (17.49m) commits a foul in his final attempt.
Nigeria’s Jessica Oji takes silver. She also had a best of 17.87m, same as Cameron but Oji’s second-best throw of 17.70m was better than Cameron’s second-best throw of 17.40m.
Canada’s Sarah Mitton bags the gold medal with a best of 19.88m.
A brilliant throw of 17.49m in the penultimate round takes Manpreet Kaur into the bronze medal position!
She is behind Nigeria’s Jessica Oji (17.87m) and Canada’s Sarah Mitton (19.88m)
Jamaica’s Tajay Gayle’s final jump is 7.87m but it doesn’t matter. His fourth-round jump of 8.15m is enough for him to take the gold medal.
He has to at least match Gayle’s best jump of 8.15m to have a shot at gold. Can he do it?
No, he can’t! He finishes with a jump of 7.97m which means he will, for the second edition in a row, take the silver medal.
Mitrevski goes for his final jump. It is well below his expectations - 6.75m. He takes the fourth spot.
Now, time for the home favourite to jump one last time - Mackenzie is ready for his sixth attempt. A medal is confirmed for him anyway. It’s 8.06m!!!
Top stuff from the Scot as he takes the bronze.
It is a 7.62m jump, which is not better than his opening effort of 7.97m. He finishes fifth on his CWG debut.
Manpreet Kaur continues to occupy the fourth spot but keeps improving as well. A 17m throw in her third attempt.
Adcock finishes his competition with a foul and takes the eighth spot. His best of 7.74m came in the first round.
Daniel has decided to skip the last round as well. Therefore, he finishes in seventh place with a best of 7.90m
Ryan signs off with a jump of 7.48m. His best of 7.93m came in the second round. He finishes in sixth position.
Mackenzie commits a foul by the barest of margins and stays in the third spot. Tajay Gayle records an 8m jump in the penultimate round. His best effort of 8.15m came in the fourth round.
Now, here is Sreeshankar. He has had two fouls in the last two rounds. It’s not a foul this time but it is only a 7.94m jump which keeps him in second place going into the final round.
He needs a big jump to enter the Top 3. Unfortunately, he does not manage to do it in this round. In fact, it is his worst jump of the day - 7.32m and he stays in fifth place.
Mitrevski has moved up to fourth with his fifth-round jump of 8.02m. Massive effort from the Australian which pushes Lokesh to fifth spot.
India’s Manpreet Kaur has improved to 16.66m in the second round but she stays fourth.
India’s Suyash Jadhav (31.63s) and Chaitanya Kulkarni (33.17s) finish fourth and fifth respectively in the final.
Sreeshankar goes for a huge jump but ends up committing his second foul of the day. He is now second.
Jamaica’s Gayle reclaims the top spot with a massive leap of 8.15m. And he didn’t even use the board completely!
Mackenzie’s fourth jump is measured at 7.96m.
Lokesh records a jump of 7.65m in the fourth round. He will hope to do much better in the remaining two rounds.
Australia’s Adcock records a 7.71m jump, not his best today.
Daniel of Trinidad and Tobago has skipped his fourth attempt, just like his third one.
Mitrevski improves as he registers a jump of 7.90m.
Ryan only manages 7.70m. No improvement but he stays in fifth spot.
India’s Manpreet Kaur is fourth at the end of the first round with an opening effort of 15.92m.
Jamaica’s Jordan Turner, Isle of Man’s Regan Corrin, Namibia’s Chenoult Lionel Coetzee and Kenya’s Isaac Kirwa Yego are out of the competition.

Mitrevski goes next and registers a third jump of 7.74m.
Mackenzie has decided to skip his third-round jump as he probably thinks his opening jump of 8.08m should be enough to stay in Top 8 for the next three rounds.
Both Indians have made it to the 400m hurdles final as the two fastest losers.

Gayle (6.08m), Mitrevski (7.70m), Mackenzie (7.92m) and Turner (7.40m) could not better their first-round attempts.
Santhosh also finishes third in his 400m hurdles heat but he clocks 49.51s, which is better than Yashas’ time of 49.65s.

Jamaica’s Tajay Gayle and Scotland’s Stephen Mackenzie are tied for the top spot at 8.08m.

Scotland’s Stephen Mackenzie matches Gayle’s first attempt! Another 8.08m jump.

Final round underway. After two rounds, Jaismine has a slight advantage as according to two judges, she leads 20-18 while one judge has score 20-18 in Glynn’s favour. The remaining two judges feel there is nothing to separate the two pugilists.

Navneet has been absolutely terrific so far. And he continues to do an amazing job! India, at the moment, is currently winning two points after both Navneet and Steenkamp finish their three attempts.
Wentzel tries his best to bring his team back in the contest. He does change things with his first two bowls as Namibia has the advantage but it is not big enough to save the match.
Namibia does win the final end 2-0. But India takes the set 6-3 and the match 2-0!
Two wins in as many games for Navneet Singh and Dinesh Kumar.
Navneet hits the jack with his second bowl. Top stuff from India’s lead. Once again, he has given a great start - the team is currently winning two points.
Wentzel’s first two bowls fail to make any impact. Meanwhile, Dinesh has sent one more red ball closer to the jack.
The Namibian skip’s final attempt was aimed at the jack but he misses the target.
India wins the end 3-0 and leads 6-1 in the second set with one end to go.
Navneet puts India in front. One point at the moment but still, anyone’s end.
Over to Dinesh and Wentzel.
Wentzel hits the red ball closest to the jack but doesn’t manage to displace it.
One attempt to go. India still in front but only just.
Wentzel’s bowl does not affect the situation. Dinesh could have made it 2-0 for India but he wasted his final attempt.
India leads 3-1 with two ends to go.
Yet again, Navneet provides the ideal start. At least two red balls seem to be closer to the jack than the closest blue ball. Dinesh continues from where Navneet finished.
And Wentzel, my word! A brilliant bowl in his second attempt and now, Namibia is getting one point.
Yes, Namibia takes the end 1-0. India leads 2-1 with three ends to go.
India in front in the first end after Navneet and Steenkamp get done with their attempts.
Wentzel has done it again. With his very first bowl, he has turned a 1-0 lead for India into a 2-0 lead for Namibia.
With his final bowl, Dinesh hits the closest blue ball and with that, India has the advantage again. Would you believe it? India has won a topsy-turvy first end with a 2-0 scoreline!
Navneet continues doing a decent job. After his three attempts, India is winning the end 3-0. But it is far from over.
Wentzel starts off well but still, India has the advantage. Dinesh Kumar keeps the pressure on the Namibians.
Wentzel responds in style as he hits the jack with his penultimate attempt and now, it is a pretty close call.
Dinesh’s last attempt ends up closer to the ditch. Can Wentzel turn this end in Namibia’s favour? No, he can’t!
India wins the end 1-0 and takes the first set 5-3!
Navneet’s three attempts are done. With his final one, he hits the jack and puts India in an advantageous position.
After Dinesh’s opening attempt, India is winning as many as three points from this end.
Make it four unless Wentzel can do what he did in the first end. He manages to do a little bit of damage limitation but still, India wins the fourth end 2-0 and takes a 4-3 lead with one end to go in this set.
Superb start from Navneet in this end. With his first roll, the red ball is almost touching the jack. But that happiness does not last long as Steenkamp displaces that ball with his third and final attempt.
Wentzel’s penultimate attempt hits the jack and may have given India a chance.
Dinesh takes it and sends his second-last attempt really close to the jack for a potential point for India.
Wentzel’s last roll goes way past the jack. Chance for India to get one more point if Dinesh gets this right. He does!
India wins the third end 2-0. Overall, Namibia leads 3-2 with two ends to go in the first set!
Namibia poised to bag the second end as well unless Dinesh can come up with something. Nope, he can’t.
Namibia wins the second end 2-0 and takes a 3-0 lead in the opening set.
Great start from Navneet in the first end as after his three attempts, India is currently winning two points. Brilliant work from Dinesh as well as India seems to have four points in the bag.
However, with his last ball, Wentzel turns things around as he displaces the four red balls around the jack and wins the end for Namibia.
What a start to this contest!
India’s Navneet Singh and Dinesh Kumar, who began their campaign with a win, take on Namibia’s Christo Steenkamp and Waylon Wentzel in a Section B game in the men’s pairs section play.

The 31-year-old pugilist will take on Samoan Michael Seko in the men’s 90+kg quarters.
Seko lands two light punches, but the Indian looks for the perfect opening before landing a left hook squarely on the former’s face. That would have caused some heavy damage. A perfect combination has left the Samoan shellshocked at the edge of the ring. A split decision sees only the Mexican judge hand the first round to Seko.
The second round begins with Narender’s coach screaming from the sidelines, insisting the Indian not throw futile jabs about. Narender gets warned about his head position for the third time, and points will now be deducted. Seko gets a standing count after Narender gets another point deducted for landing a punch after the referee asks for a break. Bizarre! Narender, now seemingly pushing forward seamlessly, is at advantage here.
The Samoan is leading on two cards here after the deductions. It’s all come down to the wire and fitness. Another standing count for the Samoan as Narender celebrates. The victory may not have come his way yet, though.
Oh, he’s done enough, it seems. A split decision hands Narender the 3-2 victory. Five out of five for India.
The last round of what’s been a heavily one-sided contest in favour of the Indian. Micock comes out of the blocks aggressively, trying to catch Ankush off guard, but the Indian remains unfazed. The boxer from Seychelles needs a knockout to win from here.
The bout is briefly paused as Micock has a wardrobe malfunction. Once again, Ankush’s quickness is too hot to handle for Micock, and he’s getting beaten quite comprehensively here.
Micock finally successfully lands a punch, but he gets a heavy counterblow from Ankush almost immediately after. And that’s that. Ankush is through to the semis! He has assured himself of at least a bronze medal!
The Indian will face Joshua Ofori for a place in the final after the Canadian got a walkover in the quarterfinal.
Round two is underway. Ankush once again steps forward early and teases Micock with a couple of half-punches to trick his opponent. Ankush, incredibly sharp with his left-right combination, moves out of the way once again just before Micock can connect with his counterpunches.
Quick reflexes from Ankush, and now he’s cornered Micock to land a few more blows. The boxer from Seychelles is clearly on the backfoot. Can he conjure some magic? Cheeky from Ankush, he smiles at his opponent almost mockingly, and does it again as he continues to successfully steer clear of Micock’s punches.
We’re just moments away from the start of the bout, and there he is! Ankush makes his entrance clad in the red gear. Flexes his shoulders confidently as he enters the ring.
His opponent joins him in the ring and camps at the right corner. The referee rings the bell, and we are underway.
Ankush is immediately onto his front foot, pushing forward and cornering Micock near the ropes. Ankush unleashes a quick left-right combination to unsettle Micock, and he continues to be on the front foot. Micock tries to fight back with a backhand, but Ankush reacts just in time to block his offence.
Oh, nice sequence of punches. Micock punches with his left, but Ankush ducks and gets under with a jab on the ribs, and that’s time. As expected, it’s Ankush that takes a perfect ten from all five judges going into round two.
Mauritius’ heavily tattooed Merven Clair pierces a few hefty blows on Ghana’s Precious Nettey to book his place in the semis of the men’s 70 kg event.
We continue with boxing, as Ankush Panghal will be in action in the 80 kg quarterfinal against Seychelles’ Jade Micock at 7:00 PM.
A win will make Ankush the fourth Indian boxer today to confirm at least a bronze medal.
Okay, that was short but definitely not sweet. Wales’ Holley Sotomi flattens Lesotho’s Refiloe Thai with a vicious punch.
He’s not moving as he continues to lie down after the blow; concerning visuals. The medics are out to check if he is okay.
Good news, Thai is back on his feet but the contest is over. The referee awards the win to the Welshman by KO and he advances to the semis of the 70 kg event.
Sachin, in blue, looks pumped ahead of the clash. He charges into the middle of the ring after mouthing a very audible “ C’mon”. Moremi’s dressing site will be an easy target for the Indian. The gash above his right eye shall most likely open should a punch land cleanly on the spot. And as I type, the ever-so-slight permissible taping has started to come off. Both try to outfeint each other in the first round. The doctor has been called on even as Moremi’s forehead has started to bleed. The dressing has been removed. All the judges have ruled in favour of the Indian.
Sachin, World No. 5, is a favourite to win the gold in this category. Moremi is having trouble trying to push into Sachin, who’s quick to evade the hits. A couple of hooks unsettle the Botswana boxer. A nice chop from Treasure there, but that has been bested as well by a strong left hook from his opponent. As expected, the Indian has been unanimously voted for in this round as well.
Sachin hangs back and puts his guard down, almost taunting Moremi to lean into him for a hook. The boxer in the red corner does try taking advantage but fails. Moremi does manage to push Sachin into a corner, and perhaps that has been his best move in this contest. And it’s over, Sachin takes all five cards. He is now the third Indian boxer to make the semifinal from this first session.
Sachin Siwach to take on Treasure Moremi, who’s wearing battle scars on his face from his two previous contests at CWG 2026.
It’s an RSC (Referee Stops Contest) in favour of Rosie Eccles of Wales as the fight halts midway into the second round. She will face Arundhati Choudhary in the semis next.
The Indian takes a 3-2 win in the first round over the Kiwi.
The second round is underway. Henderson is going at it, Arundhati mostly left tracking back and taking the shots. She even falls down once. Henderson has taken the bout to the Indian. Arundhati gets some punches in at the end as the bell rings the end of the bout. Those last few punches must have worked in India’s favour as she gets the judges on her with a 4-1 win, and she leads 2-0 in the bout.
Arundhati can be seen using her left hand to attack Henderson’s face, but the Kiwi pugilist herself is able to land a few punches after missing a few at the start of the third round.
Arundhati takes the win 3-1 via split decision and confirms another medal for the Indian boxing contingent! She’s bagged at least a bronze. She’ll face either Rosie Eccles of Wales or Samukelisiwe Ncube of South Africa in the semifinal.
Clad in blue, Arundhati Choudhary goes up against New Zealand’s Morgan Henderson in the women’s 70kg quarterfinal. A win here would take Arundhati into the semis, and confirm at least a bronze medal.
Arundhati Choudhary to take on New Zealand’s Morgan Henderson in the women’s 70kg quarterfinal shortly.
Sakshi Chaudhary on her way to the blue corner. Caitlyn chooses the aggressive approach, going for the powerful punches since the get-go. The referee has already had to separate them on a number of occasions within the first 30 seconds. Caitlyn leans in to keep the Indian from using her stronger left arm. A powerful punch to the head from Sakshi draws a few oohs and aahs from the crowd. All five judges have ruled in favour of Sakshi at the end of the first round.
Sakshi uses her backfoot to effectively evade Caitlyn’s probing left hooks. A minute into the second round and the boxers are seen going for full-blooded body blows. A timed one-two from Sakshi. The Indian is eager to finish this off in style. Caitlyn and Sakshi both take the tumble. But they are up on their feet quickly enough. The same result with a point deducted from Sakshi’s kitty after the warning.
Sakshi, looking to channel her inner Nikhat Zareen, the champion from the same weight division four years ago, keeps bouncing about inside the ring, avoiding taking any damage using nimble footwork. And Sakshi emerges on the right side of this one-sided affair. A comprehensive win, this. She heads into the semifinal, where she will face Amber-Jane Wall of Canada.
We will be here for a while. Sakshi Chaudhary will get things rolling in the women’s 51kg quarterfinal in 10 minutes from now, taking to the ring against Caitlyn Fryers of Northern Ireland.
The 23-year-old sprinter, with a Personal Best mark of 20.32, will be hoping to go as close to the mark, if not better it, in minutes from now.
Kujur is off the blocks. The aggressive start holds him in good stead until the finish. Emmanuel Eseme of Cameroon strangely shutting down in the final stretch further helps the Indian’s cause. At one point it did seem that the race was headed towards a photo finish.
Kujur finishes in 20.46s. This is his seasonal best.
Kujur to run 200m heats in the fifth lane shortly at the Scotstoun Stadium. 10 Heats are scheduled with the top 16 set to advance to the semifinals.
After almost clearing the mark in the first attempt itself, Toor returns to register a 20.14m throw. That is well clear of the 20.00m direct qualification mark.
Samardeep, also done with his throws, will qualify despite not bettering the 19.95m mark, having finished fifth on the leaderboard.
Swimmers Suyash Narayan Jadhav and Chaitanya Vishwas Kulkarni are done with the men’s 50m freestyle S7 Heats. Kulkarni is fourth with 32.77. Jadhav has a 35.35.
Interestingly, eight top athletes from the Heats are supposed to make the final. There were seven participants.
Tom Walsh, one of the favourites to win the men’s shot put event, registers a 21.03m throw. That only means that he is done for the day, having secured direct qualification for the final.
Reigning Asian Games champion Tajinderpal struts in for his very first attempt. There is a loud cheer from the stands that suggests there is quite the following which he has built. A powerful release – is it good enough to seal his qualification? No, 19.93m it is.
Samardeep Singh Gill, in the meantime, has notched up 19.95m in his first attempt in the other group.
Sajan finishes fifth in his heat in 1:51.99s. Aneesh is seventh with 1:51.64. The results aren’t good enough to take them into the finals.
Swimmers Sajan Prakash and Aneesh Gowda will participate in the Heats of men’s 200m freestyle.
The former will participate in Heat 2, while Gowda will try and qualify for the final from Heat 5. The eight fastest swimmers are set to advance.
Mia Scerri’s first 6.29m attempt still holds good in the women’s long jump of heptathlon. The Australian leads with 940 points after two jumps.
Sanjana enters at 94kg. A pull not high enough and the 19-year-old has dropped the bar. She will go again shortly. She does make a slight adjustment in the second attempt, the catch is good, but she has let go again.
Herbert is up to attempt her last lift. She fails to clear 94kg.
Sanjana is back to right the wrong. Can she evade a looming elimination? NO! She has dropped the weight behind. India’s challenge in the said category of weightlifting is over.
A good lift! Rachel Achieng Enock of Kenya executes the perfect lift at 90kg with her outstretched arms perfectly in line with the barbell.
A super wide grip and Herbert gets three greens on the 91. Putting up a show here is the home favourite.
Enock, the 2024 African junior champion, fails to get a successful second lift. Can she undo the damage on the last attempt? An extra minute of cooldown, and then we will know. Nope, her elbows give up while on the rise.
Agata Herbert of Scotland on her home turf... can she get off to a good start? An easy lift this, for her, at 87kg.
Isabella Andueza is up next. And it goes horribly wrong. First her entire body gives in to the momentum of the rising bar, and her torso awkwardly twitches towards the left. However, it would have still counted had her knees not made contact with the floor. Her second attempt at 89kg also drops behind her head. Unfortunately, she crashes out of the competition after letting go of her last attempt as well.
Northern Ireland’s Kaitlin Saunders gets the 77kg weightlifting competition started with an opening attempt of 82kg. It’s a good lift.
It will be Saunders going for the second lift (84kg) as well after a cooldown period. The Northern Ireland contingent has decided to revise the weight and hike it by a kilo. And she’s dropped the bar.
She’s failed the last attempt as well, completing her snatch with a best mark of 82kg.
Sanjana’s entry weights are set at 94kg in snatch and 122kg in clean and jerk. That’s the second highest after Stowers at 435kg combined.
Sanjana takes the stage. A bronze medallist at the Asian Championships earlier this year and also a bronze medal winner at the 2024 World Youth Championships, Sanjana will face a hefty challenge from the likes of Samoa’s Seine Stowers, Canada’s Rosalie Dumas, and England’s Isabella Brown.
Plenty to keep track of today. Here’s hoping you keep up.

On a pitch where the ball did not quite hurry, T. Natarajan had decided that perhaps the best way to hurry the batter was not to hurry the ball.
There was the slower bouncer, worked on for two years. There was the yorker, the old companion. There was the new ball, which was not quite new in behaviour, holding in the surface and denying the batter the easy pleasure of playing on the rise. And there was, above all, the need to adjust.
Natarajan did that rather well against Vida Kovai Kings, producing his best figures of this TNPL season so far. The iDream Tiruppur Tamizhans left-arm pacer finished with two for 24 in four overs, both wickets coming from slower bouncers at the death. R.S. Ambrish pulled one to hole out at deep midwicket, while skipper Shahrukh Khan couldn’t put it past short third man.
The spell helped Tiruppur Tamizhans restrict Kovai Kings to a moderate 166 for eight. The target was chased down with four wickets to spare, but Natarajan’s satisfaction was less about the figures than about seeing a plan come to life.
“When we first bowled, the wicket was holding up and stopping a bit. With the new ball, it was holding up, so it wasn’t that easy. The speed wasn’t there to hit on the rise from a good length. The wicket became slow for batting.
“So, we adapted to the wicket. Whether it was the spinners or the fast bowlers, whatever plan we had, we executed that. Especially, whatever I thought, whether with the new ball or at the death, I tried to execute that,” he said after the match at the NPR College Ground.
The slower bouncer was particularly satisfying. It had been two years in the making, and on that pitch it found a natural home.
The work behind that ball has been less visible. For the last three years, Natarajan has been working with former India and Karnataka left-arm pacer Sreenath Aravind.
“I worked with him even before going to the IPL this year. In modern cricket, batters easily start hitting whatever you bowl at the death. It’s very difficult for us to survive with just one type of ball.
“So, I felt that having a slower bouncer would be useful. I have worked on it for two years, and it is better now,” he said.
ALSO READ: Kovai Kings routs Trichy Grand Cholas for timely win
Their association goes back around seven years to Natarajan’s first Ranji Trophy match on this very ground.
Aravind was then a bowler Natarajan admired and sought advice from. He told Natarajan he could call him anytime.
“From then on, we communicated a lot. That’s how we got acquainted,” Natarajan said.
Their work together is rooted in the small details of fast bowling: creating angles for right-hand and left-hand batters, correcting technical errors, and spotting things a bowler cannot always see in himself.
“Even if I’m coming back from an injury, there may be some small technical mistake that I don’t notice, but he does. That can make a big difference.
“I had a shoulder injury (collarbone fracture) last year, so I worked with him during that time. I’ll tell him what I feel is wrong, and he’ll make a lot of small corrections. He even came to my ground (in Chinnappampatti, Salem) last year and worked with me for around four days. It is very convenient and easy for me to work with him since there is good communication between us,” Natarajan said.
The same practicality that informs his thinking at the death overs also shapes Natarajan’s thoughts about his larger ambitions. An India comeback is the obvious question for a bowler who has played for the country. Natarajan, though, is looking no further than the tournament in front of him.
“This is my identity - this TNPL. It is through this that everyone came to know me as Natarajan. Many youngsters like me are coming up, and it is a big opportunity for everyone.
“I don’t have any big goals as such. I have to play for the team, and the team has to win. My contribution is for the team. If we think of something big, we will miss out on what is here now,” he said.
Natarajan has become a source of information for young players around him, much as Aravind continues to be for him.
“There are a lot of young players coming into our team. I share my experiences with them and they learn a lot of things. It’s nice. Our team bonding is also good,” he said.
He helps even when the question comes from outside his own dressing room. “Even if someone from another team asks me, I do it. That makes me very happy.”
Perhaps, then, there is a certain symmetry to the journey. A young Natarajan once turned to an accomplished bowler for advice on this ground. Years later, he is the experienced bowler answering questions from younger players.
The larger ambitions can wait. The Indian team can wait. Even the next tournament can wait. For now, there is only the next ball.

Cape Verde coach Bubista resigns as Ivory Coast reappoint Renard
- Published
Bubista has resigned from his post as Cape Verde head coach to join Moroccan club RS Berkane while Ivory Coast have hired Herve Renard for a second spell in charge.
Bubista guided the island nation to the last 32 of the World Cup last month, where the Blue Sharks were beaten 3-2 by eventual runners-up Argentina after extra time.
The 56-year-old also reached the quarter-finals of the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations with Cape Verde, having taken charge in January 2020.
He has signed a two-year deal with RS Berkane, who finished second in the Moroccan top flight last season, and replaces Moin Chaabani, who has been appointed as Tunisia's new head coach.
Renard has won the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) twice as a coach including with Ivory Coast in 2015. He previously led Zambia to a fairy tale title in 2012.
The Ivorians lost 2-1 to Norway in the last 32 at the World Cup and decided not to renew Emerse Fae's deal when it expired at the end of last month.
The former Nantes and Reading midfielder took over the reins midway through the 2023 Afcon - after the Elephants had failed in a bid to reappoint Renard - and the tournament hosts were crowned champions following a remarkable run through the knockout stage.
Renard has had stints with Morocco, Saudi Arabia (twice) and France's women since leaving Ivory Coast in May 2015, and was in the dugout for Tunisia for two games at this year's World Cup.
The length of the 57-year-old's contract has not been disclosed and the Frenchman is expected in Abidjan "in the coming days" to take up his official duties.
Bubista hailed for 'dedication'
Bubista's sustained success with Cape Verde has raised his profile across the continent.
And while RS Berkane, from the north-east of Morocco, are not traditionally seen as one of the kingdom's big clubs they have enjoyed success in recent years.
They claimed their first domestic league title in 2024-25 and are three-time winners of the Caf Confederation Cup, Africa's second tier continental club competition.
Berkane caused controversy in 2024 by wearing a shirt in the Confederation Cup which featured a map of Morocco including the disputed territory of Western Sahara.
Cape Verde qualified for the World Cup for the first time ahead of Cameroon and the debutants proved to be the underdog story of this year's finals.
Cape Verde's football federation thanked Bubista for his "dedication, professionalism, and contribution to the development of the national team's sporting project" before wishing him "much success" in his future endeavours.
Another African World Cup manager departs
Bubista becomes the latest coach to leave one of the 10 African sides which appeared at the World Cup.
Vladimir Petkovic parted company with Algeria, who exited against Switzerland in the last 32, by mutual consent on Monday.
The 62-year-old Bosnian, who was appointed in February 2024, had extended his contract with the Desert Foxes until 2028 earlier this year.
Meanwhile, Hugo Broos stepped down as South Africa boss when his contract expired at the end of July, with the 74-year-old deciding to retire from management.
Senegal sacked Pape Thiaw in the wake of their dramatic last-32 exit against Belgium, with the country's football federation saying it had made the decision "in the best interests of Senegalese football".
The Teranga Lions have been linked with former France and Arsenal midfielder Patrick Vieira as a possible replacement.
Elsewhere, Tunisia appointed Chaabani on a four-year deal last month.
The 45-year-old replaced Renard, who himself took over the Carthage Eagles one game into their Group F campaign when Sabri Lamouchi was removed after a 5-1 defeat by Sweden.
Internal discussions are continuing at the Ghana Football Association after Carlos Queiroz led the Black Stars to the last 32, where the West Africans lost 1-0 to Colombia.
Queiroz appeared to announce his own departure on social media shortly after that defeat.

When I lived in Los Angeles, I considered Palm Springs a sunny respite about a few hours away from the hustle and bustle of the city. I made a point of visiting the desert city a few weekends a year to enjoy perfect winter weather and laid-back, poolside hangs.
I never imagined living there, though, until the COVID-19 pandemic hit. Suddenly, Los Angeles felt claustrophobic.
Like many others in the city during this time, I wanted to find a place with more breathing room. Since most of my work was already remote, I was not tethered to a location and decided to make a move.
Palm Springs offered a lower population density, plenty of wide-open vistas, and a slower pace of living, all of which appealed to me.
I planned to just "wait out" the pandemic in Palm Springs and return to LA when it was over. So, I negotiated my lease down to a six-month stay.
Pandemic-related restrictions lasted well beyond that initial period, but I didn't want to leave. I'd started truly falling in love with the desert, so I kept renewing my lease on a month-to-month basis.
I quickly fell in love with the city's nature and arts scene
One of the biggest immediate perks of living in Palm Springs was the easy access to nature and hiking. Even within the city limits, there were great, secluded trails to explore, not to mention spots like Joshua Tree National Park just over an hour away.
In those early days of social distancing, I took full advantage of these hikes — as well as neighborhood walks, which offered so much Modernist architecture and gorgeous desert landscaping.
Once physical-distancing restrictions were lifted and we could start sharing more spaces again, I began working for the Palm Springs International Film Festival, which remains one of my favorite local events.
I developed friendships within the community of coworkers and volunteers, and built several meaningful intergenerational relationships that continue to this day.
As things continued to open up, I frequently attended live music events throughout the region, including shows at Pappy and Harriet's and the Coachella festival.
As someone who has always worked in arts, music, and culture, these places provided great opportunities to meet like-minded people in town and get a cultural pulse on the city.
Community, friendships, and work helped me decide to stay in Palm Springs
By the time the peak of the pandemic had passed, LA had changed — many of my friends had also moved elsewhere.
Plus, I'd become deeply ingrained in Palm Springs' community through work and new friendships, and fallen into routines here. I didn't want to leave.
So, I didn't. And six years later, I'm still in the city.
There have been benefits I didn't necessarily expect. Compared to living in Los Angeles, drives are short, traffic is light, and parking just about anywhere downtown is easier (and free!).
You also simply cannot beat the winter weather here, with mainly sunny days and temperatures in the mid-70s.
Though I miss many things about Los Angeles — like the amazing, varied food scene and late-night culture — Palm Springs has a lot to offer for everyday life.
And it doesn't hurt that I'm only a two-hour drive away from my old home, so I can head back as often as I need to for work opportunities or visits with friends who still live there.
I'm not ruling out a return to Los Angeles eventually, and I always like to stay flexible and open to new opportunities. For the foreseeable future, though, Palm Springs is home.

Kushner meets with Hamas on the Gaza road map ahead of talks with Netanyahu
CAIRO — U.S. negotiator and President Donald Trump 's son-in-law Jared Kushner held a rare meeting with the Hamas chief on Sunday in a new diplomatic effort to make progress in the stalled Gaza ceasefire. Kushner will meet with Israel's prime minister on Monday.
The talks aim to salvage the new 15-point, U.S.-backed road map for Hamas to disarm in Gaza and Israel to withdraw from the Palestinian territory shattered by war.
At stake are the lives of some 2 million people in Gaza and the reconstruction of the crowded enclave now largely controlled by Israeli forces, more than 10 months since the ceasefire ended major military operations. A meeting between Kushner, fellow envoy Steve Witkoff and Hamas leaders in Egypt last year helped clinch the ceasefire, whose progress until now had been stalled over the key issue of Hamas' disarmament.
The rare meeting in Egypt with Hamas' Khalil al-Hayya was confirmed by a regional official and a Hamas official, both speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to reporters. Kushner was one of a trio of envoys meeting with al-Hayya, with officials from mediating countries Egypt, Qatar and Turkey also there.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last week rejected the 15-point plan in a rare public show of defiance against the Trump administration, Israel's closest ally.
Now Kushner, former British prime minister Tony Blair and the director of the U.S.-created Board of Peace overseeing the ceasefire, Nickolay Mladenov, are set to meet with Netanyahu on Monday, according to a source familiar with the plans and a diplomatic source. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a closed-door meeting.
Regional powers accuse Israel of obstructing peace effortsAhead of Monday's meeting, several regional powers including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates issued a statement condemning Israel's rejection of the road map, saying that "Israel now bears responsibility for obstructing the efforts to bring peace in Gaza." Other signers included Jordan, Pakistan, Indonesia and the ceasefire mediators.
The statement by foreign ministers also called on the Board of Peace and the U.S. to take "immediate and concrete measures" to keep any party from obstructing the plan's implementation.
Kushner's meeting with the Hamas leader aimed at ensuring the militant group's commitment to the road map, particularly disarmament, before his meeting with Netanyahu, the regional official said.
The Hamas official said the group is committed and waiting for mediators to start the 14-day negotiation period to work out a timetable for implementation. That period requires all parties' approval of the road map to begin.
The Hamas official also said the Hamas leader demanded that Israel halt its attacks on Gaza and withdraw to the so-called "yellow line" dividing the territory before beginning implementation. The yellow line was never precisely defined. Israeli forces have moved beyond it and now control about 60% of Gaza.
In May, Netanyahu said the next step was to move to 70% control, with Israel "tightening the grip" on Hamas "from every direction."
The White House had no comment on the talksThe White House referred questions about Kushner's meetings to the Board of Peace, which did not immediately comment. The Tony Blair Institute did not comment.
Under the road map, Hamas would hand over weapons to the Palestinian technocratic committee meant to oversee daily operations in the territory. The committee has not yet entered Gaza. But Hamas has linked the surrender of its heaviest weapons to the creation of a Palestinian state, something Israel's current government rejects.
The road map involves Hamas gradually giving up its weapons while Israeli forces halt attacks and begin withdrawing from Gaza. But Netanyahu says Israel will not retreat from any position in Gaza until Hamas has been completely disarmed.
That stance leaves other elements of the ceasefire, including reconstruction and the deployment of international forces to separate Israeli forces from committee-controlled areas, on hold.
Netanyahu faces a challenging election on Oct. 27 as he tries to hold on to power with a coalition that includes ministers taking a harsh line on Gaza, and it's not clear whether he will take decisive steps on the ceasefire before then. Also coming up is the anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on southern Israel that sparked the war.
Netanyahu's Likud party on Sunday responded to the statement by regional powers by claiming that "Arab states want to topple" Netanyahu so that centrist challenger Gadi Eisenkot and center-left party leader Yair Golan "will give them everything they want. That will not happen."

Artificial intelligence (AI) could help India identify people at risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) earlier and enable more personalised prevention, but the technology is not yet ready to guide routine clinical decisions, according to a recent systematic review by researchers from the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), M.S. Ramaiah University of Applied Sciences, and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.
Published in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making, an open-access journal, the review assessed 30 studies published since 2017 on AI-based models developed to predict future cardiovascular disease among adults without established heart disease.
The researchers identified the studies through a systematic search of more than 6,700 records across major scientific databases. Most of the models were developed using datasets from the U.S., the U.K., and South Korea, and relied on routinely collected clinical information and machine learning algorithms such as Random Forests, Support Vector Machines, and neural networks.
Relevance for India
The findings are particularly relevant for India, where cardiovascular disease accounts for nearly one-third of all deaths and often affects people at younger ages than in many other countries.
Denny John, faculty of life and allied health sciences, M.S. Ramaiah University of Applied Sciences, and one of the authors of the review, said AI could potentially make cardiovascular risk assessment more precise, but the evidence was not yet adequate for widespread clinical use.
“AI offers an opportunity to make cardiovascular risk prediction more precise and more personalised. But our review shows that the evidence is still incomplete,” he said.
Several Indian institutions have already developed AI-based cardiovascular risk prediction models incorporating locally relevant factors such as smokeless tobacco use, psychosocial stress, and physical inactivity. However, Dr. John said such tools needed rigorous independent validation before they were used in primary care or public health programmes.
“Many models demonstrate good discrimination, but very few studies examine whether the predicted risks correspond to what actually happens in different populations,” he said.
He said that robust external validation, calibration, and assessment of clinical usefulness were necessary before AI tools could guide long-term treatment decisions, such as starting blood pressure- or cholesterol-lowering therapies.
Comparable with conventional risk scores
Twelve of the studies reviewed directly compared AI models with established cardiovascular risk calculators, including the Framingham Risk Score, which estimates a person’s 10-year risk of cardiovascular events such as a heart attack or stroke.
The review found that AI models generally performed as well as, and in some cases slightly better than, conventional tools in distinguishing people at higher risk of cardiovascular events from those at lower risk over five to 10 years.
However, the researchers cautioned that better statistical performance by itself did not establish that an AI model would improve patient care.
Major validation gaps
A key concern identified in the review was the lack of evidence showing whether the predicted risk accurately reflected what happened in real-world populations.
Almost all the studies assessed discrimination — the ability of a model to distinguish high-risk individuals from low-risk individuals. None assessed calibration — which determines whether the predicted probability of disease corresponds to the actual number of cardiovascular events observed.
Only seven studies validated their models using independent patient populations. Sensitivity — the ability to correctly identify people who subsequently develop cardiovascular disease — was reported in only four studies. None conducted decision-curve analyses to establish whether using the AI models would lead to better clinical decisions than existing approaches.
For India, this gap is particularly important because a model developed using populations in the U.S., U.K., or South Korea may not perform similarly in Indian populations with different risk factors and patterns of disease, Dr. John said.
Need for independent testing
The researchers have called for prospective validation of AI-based cardiovascular risk models across diverse populations, including Indian populations, before their integration into routine healthcare.
They have also recommended that future studies follow international reporting and assessment frameworks such as TRIPOD+AI and PROBAST+AI to improve transparency, reduce bias, and enable independent evaluation.

Trump orders Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea
After South Korea declined to help denuclearise Iran, Trump said the exercises are costly and send a ‘hostile’ signal to North Korea
US President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon on Sunday to scale back planned joint military exercises with South Korea after the Republican president said South Korea declined to help denuclearise Iran.
Trump said in a social media post that the exercises scheduled to begin this week are costly and “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea, which he said “has been unthreatening and respectful” while Trump has been in the White House.
“Therefore, and based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!” Trump wrote.
The 11 days of exercises involving 18,000 South Korean soldiers were designed to strengthen readiness against North Korean threats.
US and South Korean forces were expected to practice joint operations in complex situations, including a live-fire exercise to test joint precision targeting and manoeuvre, a wet gap crossing, and distribution of pre-positioned military equipment, according to the US military.
A day earlier, Trump posted a photo of himself standing next to North Korea’s Kim Jong-un, writing that the two leaders get along great “despite the unfriendly look on this particular picture”.
