Malaysia to scrap 55-year-old university law, but will campus reform follow?
Student activists have blamed the law for giving university authorities the power to curb protests, political organising and campus dissent
Anwar announced on Friday that his government would repeal the 55-year-old law, a significant reversal from the administration’s position only months earlier that AUKU should be retained and improved rather than abolished.
The law has been the backbone of Malaysia’s public university system since 1971, governing the establishment and administration of universities, their finances, appointments and academic affairs.
For student activists, however, its most contentious feature has been the disciplinary powers it gives university authorities – powers they say have been used to curb protests, political organising and campus dissent.
Anwar was himself a prominent student activist in the 1970s and was detained after the 1974 Baling protests, which stemmed from anger over rural poverty and the plight of rubber tappers and farmers.

The former governor of Guerrero state in Mexico has been formally charged over his alleged involvement in the disappearance of 43 students in 2014, a case that has become a symbol of the country’s brutal cartel violence and government impunity.
Ángel Aguirre, who was arrested last week, is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice for ordering the destruction of surveillance tapes that may have shed light on what happened to the students from the Ayotzinapa teacher training college on the night of 26 September 2014.
On Wednesday, a judge ruled Mexico’s attorney general had presented enough evidence to formally charge Aguirre with forced disappearance and ordered that he remain in a maximum security prison awaiting trial.
A lawyer for Aguirre denied his client’s wrongdoing. Guillermo Baradas told reporters: “We presented evidence demonstrating a high-level meeting attended by Mr Ángel Aguirre at the time the videos were allegedly handed over to him.”
Aguirre’s indictment is the biggest breakthrough in the Ayotzinapa case since the 2022 arrest of Jesús Murillo Karam, who served as Mexico’s attorney general at the time of the students’ abduction.
The brutality of the case rocked Mexico and continues to haunt the country more than a decade on. With the remains of only three students identified, it is not known what happened to the 40 others.
On the night that they were abducted, the students from the Raúl Isidros Burgos teacher training college in the village of Ayotzinapa had commandeered several buses in the city of Iguala to get to a protest in Mexico City.
But before they could leave Iguala, in Guerrero state, the students were attacked by a local criminal gang working with municipal police. A years-long international investigation determined that federal forces, both police and military, were also involved either by participating directly or failing to intervene as the students were taken away and presumably killed.
The government at the time orchestrated an elaborate coverup, attempting to place blame for the attack solely on the criminal gang and local police. Suspects were tortured into giving false confessions and crime scene evidence was manipulated.
Meltión Ortega, a spokesperson for the 43 students, said: “We want no more deception; we want to be told the truth and for those responsible to be punished. The victims from Guerrero deserve to have the actual perpetrators and the masterminds punished, rather than just seeing a charade, as has happened in serious cases of human rights violations.”
Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has vowed to get to the bottom of what happened to the students and formed an investigative unit to dig into the case last year. “I’m going to put all my effort, all my energy, all my willpower [towards obtaining truth and justice],” she told reporters at a news conference last week.

Trump says US to scale back military drills with South Korea after it stayed out of Iran war
- Published
President Donald Trump has said the US will "substantially reduce" joint military exercises with South Korea, citing his "very good relationship" with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.
"These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday.
He also noted that South Korea had recently declined to join the US in the "denuclearisation" of Iran.
The decision comes after Pyongyang this month conducted ballistic missile tests that are banned by the United Nations.
Trump said in his social media post that it was "too late to cancel", as the US and South Korea were due to start their annual military exercises on Monday.
He added: "While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, 'No thanks!'"
Last week, US and South Korean military leaders held a joint press conference announcing Ulchi Freedom Shield.
They said the 11-day event would be similar in scale to previous years, with about 18,000 South Korean soldiers participating.
During the news conference, military leaders also mentioned North Korea's deployment of troops to aid Russia's war against Ukraine.
US military spokesperson Ryan Donald said "our training accounts for that threat", referring to North Korean soldiers returning from the battlefield.
North Korea's foreign ministry commented on the joint drills on Friday, reiterating its rejection of any threat or challenge by exercising its right to self-defence.
The joint exercises come days after South Korea, the US and Japan detected the second North Korean missile test in days.
Pyongyang has accelerated efforts to expand its nuclear and missile programmes since the collapse in 2019 of Kim's high-profile diplomacy with Trump during his first term in the White House.
He became the first ever sitting US president to set foot in North Korea when he visited seven years ago.

Trump’s Latest Vaccine Order Is Making Things More Confusing
Americans have been stuck in a state of vaccine whiplash.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
In January, the Trump administration attempted to fundamentally change the way the United States handles childhood immunizations. Following a memo from the Department of Health and Human Services, the CDC updated its vaccine schedule to recommend that some shots no longer be given to all children. A federal court undid the effort in March. In an executive order in May, Donald Trump called on states to adopt the narrower schedule anyway. On Monday, Trump issued a new executive order on the same subject, focused on lowering the number of vaccines that the government recommends for all children. As I wrote earlier this week, this White House has a habit of doubling down when it doesn’t get its way. But only states have the power to put these proposals into practice—and many state policy makers, concerned that the White House is contradicting existing research, aren’t keen to follow its guidance.
According to the new executive order, preventive shots for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, dengue, and other diseases should be recommended for “high-risk” groups only. The order also calls to split up vaccinations for measles, mumps, and rubella—the two-dose MMR shot that has been a standard recommendation for U.S. children for decades—into three separate stages, and directs the attorney general to pursue legal action against states that don’t respect “parental authority, religious freedom, disability accommodations, and equal protection under the law.” (The order says it will align U.S. policy with the best practices of other countries, such as Denmark, but the experts I spoke with highlighted that what works in one country won’t necessarily work in another.)
The mandate may not have any legal authority to compel states to change their guidelines in the near term, although the invocation of the attorney general suggests that litigation may be on the horizon. And the single-disease vaccines that the executive order encourages aren’t yet available in the U.S. But this week’s order risks creating even more uncertainty about vaccines than already exists. “If you set out to write a policy that confuses people, it would look a lot like this one,” Jake Scott, an infectious-disease specialist at Stanford, told me.
Between the policy priorities of the Trump administration and the guidance of public-health experts, Americans have been stuck in a state of vaccine whiplash. When the American Academy of Pediatrics broke with the government earlier this year over its proposed vaccine schedule, the chair of the organization’s committee on infectious diseases told reporters that the recommendations are a “strong departure from the medical evidence and no longer offer the optimal way to prevent illness in children.” Some state lawmakers have been fighting over how best to adapt to the CDC’s changing guidelines; Kansas’s GOP-dominated legislature tried to bring the state’s vaccine rules into alignment with the CDC’s, only for its Democratic governor to veto the effort in April. And many other states have publicly said that they will reject the guidelines.
Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has questioned vaccines’ safety in the past, has been driving the discussions of the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee, as my colleagues Tom Bartlett and Katherine J. Wu reported. And although the secretary has moved away from explicit anti-vax rhetoric in recent months (following a reported White House push for health officials to stick to messages with broad public support), vaccine skepticism clearly lingers within the administration. During the press conference for Monday’s executive order, Trump suggested that the MMR vaccine could be “quite lethal.” There is no evidence for this. Measles, though, can kill: Last year, the U.S. saw its first deaths from measles in a decade.
Rethinking MMR at this moment poses extreme logistical challenges. Even if pharmaceutical companies opted to invest the time and money to introduce these shots to the American market, splitting up the doses would create new problems for caregivers. “We are essentially tripling the operational labor required of the parent or guardian (who must now schedule three separate appointments for their child),” Maimuna Majumder, a Harvard epidemiologist, told me in an email, which is “all but guaranteed to result in missed vaccines.”
In the meantime, the executive order risks misinforming Americans who are already unsure of how they feel about vaccination. The Kaiser Family Foundation released a study in June suggesting that about a third of American adults fall into a “mixed middle group” of vaccine skepticism—they believe some myths and reject others. My colleague Nick Florko, who covers public health, told me that these are the people most likely to be swayed by the administration’s latest push: “Those are the folks that might see this and think, Okay, maybe my belief that I want to delay this vaccine is well founded because the federal guidance now says that we should do that.” Under the White House’s rubric, the Americans who most need clear guidance are those who stand to lose.

The Kerala State Drugs Control department has begun acting against medical shops displaying boards that offer arbitrary discounts on drugs.
According to sources, drug inspectors and assistant drug controllers have been authorised to check if the shops are putting up misleading advertisements that can influence the purchasing decisions of consumers. Based on a complaint from the All-Kerala Chemists and Druggists Association (AKCDA), a drug inspector in Alappuzha has reportedly begun an inquiry against a newly opened shop in the district.
This follows a recent circular issued by K. Sujith Kumar, State Drugs Controller, based on the orders of the Kerala High Court. In the circular dated July 17, Mr. Sujith Kumar says that the court had on June 19 upheld the State Drugs Controller’s authority to seek an affidavit from medical shop licencees while applying for or renewing a drug licence, undertaking that they will not display discount boards with misleading or vague claims about drug prices.
The court had also clarified, however, that there is no ban on selling drugs below the maximum retail price, and that it is not illegal to give an actual discount to customers. Exhibiting boards with misleading or vague advertisements offering discounts alone is restricted. Medical shops should not display or install discount boards, banners, posters, hoardings, or digital display systems with misleading or vague claims on the prices or discounted prices of drugs. All announcements related to drug prices should be transparent, honest, clear, and examinable. The existing licensees and those applying for new licences should give the required affidavits in the prescribed manner, the circular says.
The departmental action also comes against the backdrop of a legal dispute between traditional pharmacy shops and new-generation outlets offering discounts between 20% and 80%. A section of such new pharmacies, too, had approached the High Court. Official sources say that concerns have been raised about the quality of drugs coming to Kerala via dealers not directly authorised by pharmaceutical companies.
A.N. Mohan, president, AKCDA, says that the manufacture and sale of drugs are regulated under the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules. He points out that the prices of medicines are directly controlled by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority, under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, wherein the margins fixed are between 8% and 16% for controlled category medicines like insulin drugs and between 10% and 20% for de-controlled products for wholesalers and retailers, respectively. “When retail chemists gets 16% margin on products like insulin, how can new-generation shops offer 25% to 80%? Either it is their calculated attempt to finish off small retail chemists, who have been in this business for years, and monopolise the medicine trade with their money power, or to procure medicines from unauthorised sources with doubtful quality. Also, objectionable advertisements are banned under the Drugs and Magic Remedies [Objectionable Advertisements] Act,” Mr. Mohan says.

Friedreich’s ataxia, or FRDA, is a genetic disorder that progressively damages the nerves and the heart.
The affected individuals typically begin to show symptoms between the ages of 5 and 15. They become unsteady and their coordination is impaired. Their speech slows down and slurs. Swallowing becomes difficult. Hearing and vision deteriorates. They feel fatigued, lose sensation, first in the arms and legs, then in the trunk and other parts of the body, and the spine curves to one side. Eventually, most patients die relatively young, of heart disease. There is no cure.
According to Ashwin Dalal, a medical geneticist at the Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences in Hyderabad, the institute diagnoses one case of FRDA every month on average — and almost all of these individuals come from consanguineous marriages. That is, marriages between relatives, such as uncles and nieces, or between cousins. Many Indian communities practice consanguinity — and it greatly increases the risk of genetic diseases that are otherwise rare. Friedreich’s ataxia is one such disease.
Curiously, so far, FRDA has not been reported in people from sub-Saharan Africa, North America, and China, Japan, and Southeast Asia. For a long time, scientists have only found it in individuals of European, North African, West Asian, and South Asian descent.
A new study from researchers at the University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center in the U.S. has finally cracked the puzzle. Their findings were reported in June 9 in the journal Human Molecular Genetics.
Inefficient powerhouses
FRDA is caused when a gene called FXN becomes mutated.
The FXN gene codes for a protein called frataxin. Frataxin is essential for mitochondria, which are our cells’ powerhouses. The chemical ATP, which is the cell’s energy currency, is made mostly in the mitochondria. Nerve, spinal cord, brain, and heart muscle cells use a lot of energy. When their frataxin levels become abnormally low, the mitochondria produce ATP less effectively and also accumulate toxic by-products. This renders the cell dysfunctional, leading to the symptoms of FRDA.
The most common disease-causing mutations occur in a part of the FXN gene called the intron. A mutation takes the form of modifying the number of times a particular sequence of bases is repeated in the intron. Normal variants of the FXN gene contain 5-11 or 12-33 repeats. They’re called the short normal and long normal variants. The short-normal variant is common in Europe and South Asia (85-90% of the population), sub-Saharan Africa (90%), and East Asia (over 99%). The long-normal variants are absent in East Asia and make up most of the rest in sub-Saharan Africa and in Europe and South Asia.
However, the DNA sequences of people with Friedreich’s ataxia revealed their FXN alleles variants had 100-1,500 repeats. The researchers called them expanded variants.
The short-normal and long-normal variants have an open structure in the chromosome that allows cells to make frataxin as needed. However, the expanded variants forced the chromosome to assume a closed shape that reduced frataxin expression.
Individuals who develop Friedreich’s ataxia carry two copies of the expanded variant, one from each parent. A person with only one copy is called a carrier. Even though they themselves won’t have the disease, carriers can pass their defective introns to their children.
Fortunately, genetic tests can find out if a person is a carrier and whether they passed their extended variant to their children.
From mutation to disease
The researchers also found that 95% of the expanded variants of the intron originally came from just two long-normal variants. Specifically, they reported that at two times in history, a long-normal variant mutated to an extended variant, both times in Eurasia. We don’t know why these events happened nor why only long-normal variants mutated this way. We also don’t know why this never happened in sub-Saharan Africa. On the other hand, the absence of long-normal variants in East Asian populations could explain why these problematic mutations didn’t arise there.
These originator mutations, which the researchers called protomutations, didn’t straightaway lead to Friedreich’s ataxia. Instead, they slowly but steadily changed into pre-mutations — where the number of repeats was abnormally high but not enough to significantly impair frataxin expression.
The non-disease-causing but still abnormal pre-mutations turned into an extended variant in a sudden burst of repeat expansion in a single or few parent-to-child transmissions.
Recall that people with Friedreich’s ataxia die earlier. So over time, the extended variants disappear from the population. People with protomutations and pre-mutations on the other hand did not present that risk. As a result, they acted as ‘reservoirs’ in the population that steadily replenished the depleting extended variants over time.
Taken together, the patchy distribution of protomutations can explain why Friedreich’s ataxia occurs only in some populations. The protomutations arose only a few times and only in populations with a sufficient number of the long-normal variants.
Ancient DNA
Finally, by analysing DNA from the skeletal remains of individuals who lived in ancient times, the researchers also found both the two protomutations were present in Europe and Western Asia at least 9,000 years ago. However, they were not seen in the Neanderthals and Denisovans.
In a statement, research team leader Sanjay Bidichandani credited “the longstanding tradition in the human genetics community of freely sharing DNA sequence data” to be “crucial to accurately track the presence of susceptibility to Friedreich’s ataxia from prehistoric humans to a wide variety of extant populations”.
These findings will help scientists understand what makes the two protomutations different from other long-normal variants that don’t turn into pre-mutations. This answer in turn will help find ways to prevent or at least slow down the genetic changes.
D.P. Kasbekar is a retired scientist.

Maharashtra FDA suspends Parle Agro's licence after expired Frooti, Appy found in Chembur godown
The action comes as a part of FDA's wider statewide campaign against restaurants, hotels, dhabas, bakeries, online food platforms and other food businesses.
The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) suspended the licence of M/s Parle Agro after finding expired stocks of Frooti, Appy and Apple Fizz at its Chembur godown. Stocks worth ₹99,970 were seized from the Velocity Express Warehouse near Chembur Naka.
The action comes as a part of the agency's wider statewide campaign against restaurants, hotels, dhabas, bakeries, online food platforms and other food businesses under its commissioner Tukaram Mundhe. Mundhe took over as the Maharashtra FDA chief in May, 2025.
The FDA, as of August 13, had inspected 109 hotels, restaurants and dhabas, issuing 49 improvement notices and suspended four food-business licences. It had, a few days ago, also found dirty cooking utensils, significant fly infestation, wastewater and food residue in the kitchen at Bollywood Cafe in Film City, Goregaon East.
FDA crackdown on quick-commerce outlets: Cockroaches, rats and expired chicken found
The FDA, during its special inspection drive targeting quick-commerce food delivery outlets across Mumbai, found several hygiene lapses. These included cockroaches crawling through food storage areas, expired chicken lying in refrigerators, rotten vegetables, rodent droppings and food packets kept directly on dirty floors.
Earlier this week on Friday, the agency suspended the licences of 10 food delivery chains, including Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart. The action followed inspections of 86 outlets on Thursday. Of these, 60 were served improvement notices, 14 had their licences suspended, while one outlet was ordered to stop business operations immediately.
The officials found cockroaches moving through the storage area, along with rodent and pest droppings near food packets, at an Instamart facility on the first floor of Gitaneel Arcade on Hill Road, Bandra. Dust, cobwebs and food waste were also found across the warehouse, with the facility also lacking adequate pest-proofing. It had an ant infestation, rusted racks, chipped flooring and poor housekeeping.
Another Instamart facility in Andheri West, near Azad Nagar Metro station, was found storing curry-cut chicken that had expired on August 12.
SRK, Ajay Devgn, Tiger Shroff get FDA notices over Vimal ad
The Maharashtra FDA also recently issued show-cause notices to Bollywood stars Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn and Tiger Shroff for their participation as brand endorsers in an advertisement for Vimal Elaichi, allegedly a tobacco product.
The show-cause notice gives them a period of 15 days from the date of receipt to submit a written explanation. The agency says the campaign could be a surrogate or indirect promotion of prohibited pan masala/tobacco-related products. The agency has warned that if no explanation is received, or if it is found to be unsatisfactory, further action may be initiated under applicable law.

‘I’m a little sad over my KFC’: Bear bursts into Kentucky woman’s home and steals her dinner
A Kentucky woman is warning neighbors to secure their doors after a large bear shattered her glass table and snatched her dinner while she slept
A Kentucky woman woke up to a broken table and a missing dinner early Thursday morning after a bear broke into her home, likely lured by her leftover fast food.
Kendra North was asleep when the animal entered her house, but her sister, who lives next door, witnessed the bear leaving the premises around 5 a.m., as reported by FOX 56 News.
“My sister started calling me, like, five in the morning, and I declined her at least twice, and she just kept calling,” North told the local news station.
Upon answering, North learned what had occurred.
“I answered the call, and she was like, ‘Bro, there’s a bear, and it just walked out of your house, and it came down your steps,” North said. “It came and looked at me, dead in the eyes, on my side of the yard.’”
The force of the bear's entry broke a heavy piece of furniture inside the home.
“My table is really thick glass, and it completely shattered it. She said she actually heard the table shatter from inside her house, and she thought that it was a car wreck outside,” North said, adding that she believed the animal was large.
North said she suspected the bear was drawn inside by food left out in the open.
“I’m a little sad over my KFC,” North said.
Wildlife officials advise residents to take precautions to prevent wild animals from approaching homes in search of food. John Hast, Kentucky Fish and Wildlife Bear Program Coordinator, noted that outdoor food sources are a primary driver of these interactions.
“If you store pet food or if you feed your dogs outside, just think about that,” Hast told FOX 56. “Make sure you’re not leaving any out on the porch, and that’ll keep the bear from just coming right in and getting an easy meal.”
Hast added that residents should evaluate other potential attractants if bears are reported in the area.
“If you’ve got reports right there close to the house, just think about where your garbage is,” he said.
North said the incident prompted her to change her routine moving forward.
“Definitely don’t leave your leftover KFC on the kitchen table and make sure the door is shut very well,” she said.

Taking a safe bet here that most of you who have heard of Louise Joy Brown have not heard at all of Jean Purdy, or her role in the birth of Baby Brown. Louise Brown was the first baby born of an IVF procedure on July 25, 1978. But this might not have been a joyful story, but for Jean Purdy.
Like all the heroines in this column, Jean Marian Purdy, a clinical embryologist and a critical part of the development of in vitro fertilisation, remained uncredited for a long while. Born in Cambridge, U.K., she went to work with physiologist Robert Edwards and gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe at the Physiological Laboratory in Cambridge. They were working on a high-risk experiment and taking medical science where it had never been before – who would have thought babies could be created in test tubes before the trio managed to show that it is possible.
Purdy trained as a nurse in Addenbrooke Hopsital in Cambridge, and joined Edwards in 1968 as a research nurse and quickly became indispensable to the team. Going back to study the records later, scientists established that it was Purdy who managed the laboratory, prepared and tested culture media, and recorded and organised the data of the early IVF work in the lab. Besides this, the records also put her at the centre of patient care, in this case, supporting women who volunteered their eggs and wombs at a time when public sentiment was entirely against it.
Purdy was the first to recognise and describe the formation of the early human blastocyst – the cluster of cells that forms five or six days after a sperm fertilises an egg, in the culture, a key milestone in pre-implantation development. It represents the early stage of embryonic development, where the embryo implants itself into the wall of the uterus to establish a pregnancy. Purdy was the first to see the embryonic cells successfully dividing in the lab, soon these cells would go on to become on 25 July 1978, she was the first to see the embryonic cells that would become Louise Brown. This moment is significant, because it was the first indication that their pioneering technique had worked.
That was not all; between 1970 and 1985, until her death, she co-authored 26 academic papers with Edwards and others in leading journals, including Nature, documenting methods, outcomes and sophistication that made IVF safe and more reliable.
After NHS funding for IVF was withdrawn following early successes, Purdy helped establish the world’s first dedicated IVF clinic, Bourn Hall Clinic near Cambridge in 1980, and served as its technical director. Again, she helped standardise medical protocols for IVF and scale up treatment, overseeing the birth of more than 500 IVF babies before her death from cancer at just 39 years, in 1985.
In their article The Oldham Notebooks: an analysis of the development of IVF 1969–1978. V. The role of Jean Purdy reassessed, archived in PubMed, Martin H. Johnson and Kay Elder, look at her body of work in early fertility care. The authors pored over the Oldham Notebooks - 21 handwritten laboratory notebooks and loose records kept primarily by Purdy between 1969 and 1978. They concluded that: “Purdy’s interests were clearly focused on the research and development aspects, especially those exploring viable embryo development and improved transfer procedures. For example, in a film made in 1980 (Williams, 1980), she talks about a modification to the transfer cannula that she was trying. Thus, whilst Edwards provided the ideas and the intellectual stimulation and Steptoe the authoritative clinical skills, it is arguable that without Purdy’s systematic approach and dedicated contributions, the project at Oldham may have faltered.”
Despite all this, centuries of sexism weighing in on the scientific community, a classic example of the Matilda Effect, her role was minimised in public memory for decades. Even though Edwards and other colleagues objected to it, Purdy’s name was omitted from a commemorative plaque installed at Oldham Hopsitals, associated with IVF’s breakthrough. Correspondence from Edwards archived at Cambridge later described Purdy as “crucial” to their work, underscoring how her erasure contradicted the team’s own view of her importance. In fact, Edwards’ own records state his growing confidence in her and her essentiality in the team: Purdy was “being ‘particularly good with the patients’, and her ‘cooperation had become crucial. It was no longer just Patrick and me. We had become a threesome’.
However, only Edwards was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for IVF. While recognition for the work that Purdy did, has grown only recently, thanks in good measure to the research of Johnson and Elder, some things cannot be corrected any more. Now, some museums and clinics cite Purdy as the first clinical embryologist, and other institutions have begun naming awards and exhibitions after her. Sidelined again, this time, though her collaborators acknowledged her work, Purdy’s contributions were callously and credit consistently denied.
Though belated, it’s now time to undo the wrongs. It is time to say her name! Say Jean Purdy, shout it out from the rooftops!

Dirty Monkeys’ war comedy-drama “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” took command of the mainland China box office during the Aug. 14–16 weekend, grossing RMB477.9 million ($70.3 million) over the three-day frame, according to data from Artisan Gateway.
Following its Tuesday, Aug. 11 rollout and earlier previews, the production has amassed a cumulative total of $134.1 million. Directed by Wen Muye (“Dying to Survive”) from a screenplay co-written with Lang Qunli and Wei Zhong, the film stars Shen Teng as a Chinese chef who moves to the Middle East to open an eatery to pay off family debts. Alongside his floor manager, played by Jiang Qiming, their business turns into an unexpected sanctuary for local civilians and children when armed conflict erupts. The cast also features Aarif Rahman and Omar Sherif. From the Imax screens left over from the saturation “The Odyssey” release, “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” collected $2.1 million.
Universal’s Christopher Nolan epic “The Odyssey” debuted in second place, pulling in $28.4 million across its official three-day opening weekend. Bolstered by early previews, the tentpole has reached a cumulative $35.9 million in the territory. The 20,000 screen Middle Kingdom release followed a high-profile Beijing promotional tour and secured an extensive Imax footprint across the country. Including previews, the Imax cume is $19.3 million in China and the company said that this marks the biggest opening weekend ever for a Christopher Nolan film in China, both in Imax box office and Imax indexing.
Popular on Variety
Pearl Studio’s animated fantasy feature “All Wishes Come True!” moved to third position in its fifth weekend, taking in $13.1 million. Directed by Mu Zhengyang, the mythological comedy has accumulated $235.9 million since its July 18 debut, tracking eight ordinary mortals who combine their wit to outsmart celestial deities and earn the mantle of the Eight Immortals.
Sony’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” placed fourth in its third full weekend, collecting $9.9 million. The film has reached a cumulative total of $209 million since launching on July 29, continuing its run as the top-grossing Hollywood import in China this year.
Enlight Pictures’ animated fantasy romance “To Your Island” held onto fifth place, taking $2.6 million in its sophomore frame for a cumulative total of $15 million. Directed by Zhou Haoran and adapted from Fan Dawang’s popular web novel, the story follows a young woman led by a paper crane to a mysterious island, where she reconnects with her former boyfriend, who has lost his memories and been transformed into a rabbit.
Mainland China’s overall weekend grosses reached $132.9 million, while the 2026 year-to-date revenue stands at $3.79 billion, down 30.4% from the same period in 2025.

I Tested the Best Cat Water Fountains—These Are Worth Buying
Featured in this article
As seen with the rise of automatic litter boxes, automatic feeders, pet trackers, and now cat water fountains, technology has made it so that we can take care of our pets without having to do as much of the manual labor.
These fancy fountains don't just make our lives easier. They can also help cats stay hydrated and live healthier. Ever wonder why your cat can't resist a dripping faucet but ignores its water bowl? In the wild, cats are drawn to moving water, since stagnant puddles can house bacteria. A water fountain plays into this natural instinct, encouraging cats to drink more. These techy fountains are also often connected to an app, which sends reminders and tracks drinking habits.
After prolonged testing, I now look for these three things when shopping for an automatic cat water fountain: a wireless pump for easier cleaning, stainless steel (or glass) construction so it's more hygienic, and a window to monitor water levels (especially if it's not connected to an app). I think the Petkit EverSweet Ultra with AI Camera Pet Water Fountain ($250) is the overall best cat water fountain, and the cheaper Oneisall 3.5L Cord-Free Pet Water Fountain ($40) is the best choice for most people who are on a budget.

Fountains We Don't Recommend
Petcube Ceramic Pet Water Fountain for $65: I really wanted to love this fountain; although its basin is plastic, it has a ceramic top, which is more hygienic than plastic (plus, I had never tested a ceramic model before), and the brand makes some of my favorite pet cameras. However, setup was a bit confusing; it took a long time to get the base charged to power the fountain's water flow, and the sensor to start the water flow can only be triggered from one side, making placement awkward. After a few days, it would only run while plugged in. Soon, its stream was barely strong enough to reach the top, and after just over a week, it stopped working altogether. Also, it's overly expensive for what it is.
Cat Mate 3-Level Pet Fountain for $28: This tall automatic Cat Mate fountain sets itself apart with three tiers for cats who like to drink at every level. Cleaning the motor requires disassembly using tools and extended soaking. Because of the long distance the water has to travel, it evaporates quickly and needs to be refilled about every other day. Plastic also harbors bacteria, and previous plastic models I’ve owned have had mold issues. The basin is quite large and sits flat. Because of this, some debris lingers in the front rather than flowing to the filter system behind. The plastic material and lack of ergonomic gravity design caused this fountain to be dirtier than others.
Whisker City Free Fall Cat Fountain for $30: This huge fountain is better suited for dogs, with its 150-fluid-ounce bowl and waterfall design. Although the basin has a small splash pad to help offset the waterfall noise, this was one of the loudest fountains I tested. The evaporation from the waterfall-like system also caused me to refill it every other day. Because of the structure of the fountain, my cats had to bend their head at an awkward angle. They tended to avoid drinking from the basin because of that, and their heads got slightly wet from the splatter of the waterfall. The basin is also not angled, so crumbs and debris sit at the bottom of the bowl.
Petkit EverSweet Solo SE for $25: This very simple, straightforward fountain has a square-shaped body, is translucent to easily see water levels from the outside, and has a nearly silent 25-decibel cordless pump to circulate water from the basin to the top level, where 2 ounces of water are always available for drinking, even in case of power failure. The basin sits on a base and all parts easily detach, making it easier to clean. This fountain doesn’t have multiple modes or an associated app—you’ll have to check water levels manually. I noticed this fountain didn't keep water as cold as some of the others, and because of the design of the top, debris often pooled in the dipped areas, which required more frequent cleaning.
How We Tested
I used each fountain for a week as my cats’ main source of water. As mentioned, I noted the ease of setup, evaluated parts and filters, and generally compared the various types of water fountains—spigot, bubbling, or waterfall. Some flows were continuous and some were intermittent (my cats didn’t prefer intermittent). Cats may also be intrigued and want to play with the machine rather than drink, so be sure to give them time and keep another water source around until they are fully adjusted to the new gadget.
Why a Fountain?
Cats sometimes struggle to consume enough water, which can lead to potentially lethal UTIs and blockages, especially in male cats. This is one of the reasons vets are moving toward encouraging owners to give their cat at least a partially wet-food diet, as this helps them consume more moisture, especially since cats don’t naturally drink as much as dogs. Also unlike dogs, cats are generally quite particular in their likes and dislikes, and cats can see stagnant water as potentially harmful. (If the cat was in the wild, stagnant water has more potential for harmful bacteria). Cats are more drawn to moving water in nature, and these fountains help encourage them to drink more by emulating what they’re naturally drawn to.
While automatic water fountains are better for cats' overall water consumption, they do require a bit more work and money. Rather than refilling a bowl, these take a little elbow grease—but it’s worth it for your cat’s health. Along with routine refilling and cleaning, you’ll need to disassemble the fountain to clean all parts, including using a brush for the bowl and tubes. You may also have to disassemble the motor to deep-clean mineral buildup. There are different types of filtration cartridges in specific shapes for the brand’s fountains, which require you to buy and change out filters, usually monthly but sometimes more often.
What to Look for in a Fountain
Let’s be honest, a lot of these fountains are pretty much the same. I looked especially for the overall design—I am a fiend for stainless steel because of the potential of porous plastic harboring harmful bacteria. I also favor a wide reservoir without high sides to help reduce the chance of whisker fatigue. I prefer fountains that have a small basin reservoir of water available at all times, in case of low water levels or power failure. I took into account ease of setting up, refilling, and cleaning, as well as overall design. And of course, there were some that my cats took to straight away, and some they didn’t seem to favor as much.
After prolonged testing, I now look for these three things and encourage you to as well: a cordless pump for easier (and safer) cleaning, hygienic stainless-steel construction, and a window to monitor water levels (especially if it's not connected to an app).

‘They’re anti-school’: CJP's Saurav Das claims ‘BJP goons’ beat Bengal school volunteer's father
The father of 25-year-old CJP volunteer Shaik Abdul Hafeez was allegedly assaulted on Thursday after his son raised concerns about a school at Karisunda.
A day after the Cockroach Janta Party alleged the death of the father of one of its volunteers from West Bengal after assault, its chief spokesperson Saurav Das claimed that “BJP goons” were responsible for the incident.
The father of 25-year-old CJP volunteer Shaik Abdul Hafeez was allegedly assaulted on Thursday after his son raised concerns about a primary school at Karisunda in the Indus community development block. The volunteer had conducted an audit as part of the CJP’s nationwide ‘School Thik Karo’ campaign that aimed at improving government schools.
Speaking about the incident, Das said that the volunteer's father was beaten “brutally”, while saying it was “absolutely condemnable.”
Deep Dive
“We launched a campaign called 'Fix the Schools'... Abdul, a 26-year-old CJP member who had participated in our protests at Jantar Mantar, visited his local government school in Bengal on the 13th and informed the teachers that he would return the next day to conduct an audit,” Das told reporters, according to a video posted by ANI news agency.
“That very night, BJP goons arrived at Abdul's home and beat him brutally. When his father tried to save him, they beat him as well, so severely that he lost his life,” Das added. He said the volunteer's father was rushed to a hospital but his condition deteriorated, following which he passed away in the evening.
‘They’re anti-school…anti-intellectual’
Das claimed that the incident had taken place because the aggressors were “anti-school and anti-intellectual”, while referring to the alleged assault as “hooliganism.”
“This is absolutely condemnable... It is happening because they are anti-school and anti-intellectual... but people do not believe in such hooliganism...” ANI cited the CJP spokesperson as saying.
Das said that strict action would be taken against those responsible “when the time comes”, adding that “such tactics won't work in the post-Jantar Mantar India.” The CJP co-convenor was referring to the student protests at Jantar Mantar over the alleged NEET irregularities. He said a delegation led by CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka would meet the family of the victim and “urge the strictest possible punishment” for those responsible.
“An awakening is taking place at the grassroots level... From Gen Alpha to Gen X and Gen Z coming together on their own to fix their schools. Instead of helping, they are effectively killing people,” Das said, according to ANI.
CJP demands immediate arrest, CM Adhikari says three held
The CJP said the deceased, Sk Muhammad Mafik, and his son Shaik Abdul Hafeez were allegedly assaulted on Thursday. In a post on X, CJP founder and national convener Abhijeet Dipke demanded the arrest of the accused persons on Sunday afternoon.
“Abdul went to inspect the govt school in Bengal where he once studied. He lost his father after they were attacked by goons (allegedly from BJP) for speaking up about the poor condition of govt schools. It makes my blood boil that people are being murdered simply for demanding better schools,” Dipke said. He asserted that CJP “stands firmly” with the deceased's family, saying the organisation would “only fight harder.”
Meanwhile, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari reacted within hours and said that police arrested three of the five persons named in the first information report (FIR). He said a hunt was underway for the remaining two accused.
“I am also the home minister. It is our duty to maintain law and order. Three of the five accused persons have been arrested. But the complaint did not refer to these people as BJP workers. The complaint said they were unknown individuals,” the chief minister said at a press conference, adding that five more people had been detained for interrogation.

Nigeria's mass wedding - and how telling lovers from fraudsters is proving tricky
- Published
Celebrations have turned the northern Nigerian city of Kano into a riot of colour and excitement over the last week as 1,500 couples married at a mass wedding.
For days the city's streets have been buzzing with bridal parties and their families preparing outfits and attending other organised events.
On Friday, brides in red hijabs with grooms in matching red hats and white robes went to the palace of the Emir, the city's traditional Muslim leader, for the main ceremony where they officially became husband and wife.
The nuptials culminated on Saturday with a wedding breakfast hosted by Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf, who offered his blessing to the newlyweds.
The Kano state government sponsored this initiative, spending 1.5bn naira ($1m; £815,000) to support those tying the knot - providing the bride's dowry and furniture for the couple's first home.
The scheme targets low-income individuals who cannot afford the significant financial costs associated with marriage.
The annual event was initiated in 2012 by the then-governor when 100 couples - primarily widows and divorcees - wed at the palace.
The mass weddings have continued under subsequent governors, with numbers expanding each year as demand has grown and included those in polygamous Muslim marriages.
Such is the popularity of the scheme that 5,000 couples applied this year.
The event is always overseen by the Hisbah - the city's Islamic police force - and one of their main tasks is to vet the couples wanting to wed.
Kano has a majority Muslim population and Sharia operates in the state alongside the secular legal system.
Mujahid Aminudeen, deputy commander-general of the Hisbah, admits it is not an easy task.
"Whenever we find out that there's something dubious or fishy about a couple, we disqualify them," he tells the BBC.
He says some couples will go to great lengths to convince the authorities that they are a genuine love match when their eye is more on the benefits on offer.
The state government has spent approximately 1m naira ($735; £544) on each participating couple.
According to the Hisbah, the support package a couple receives includes essential household items needed to establish a new home: beds, mattresses, bedsheets, pillows, furniture and food supplies.
Each bride receives a dowry of 100,000 naira, while a further 100,000 naira is provided as start-up capital to encourage small-scale entrepreneurship and help the couple achieve financial self-reliance after marriage.
All intending couples must undergo comprehensive medical examinations - including tests for HIV, hepatitis, pregnancy and genotype compatibility - before being cleared for the programme.
Aminudeen revealed that some couples had been disqualified after being discovered to have altered their medical test results.
In one case, an intending bride was found to have presented her brother as the groom in an attempt to benefit from the scheme.
Local journalist Yusuf Ali Abdallah, who has covered the mass weddings for years, said Nigeria's struggling economy had been fuelling desperation among the applicants this year.
"As we all know, marriage involves spending money and the country's economy is not bright at the moment," he told the BBC.
"This makes some people desperate to get on this list."
One couple who were already married had even attempted to present themselves as an intending pair before being detected and removed from the programme, he said.
Other charlatans have tried to take advantage of those desperate to get on the sponsored list, which was made public two weeks ago.
One Kano resident, who asked to be anonymous, said he had been asked to pay a bribe to get on the list.
"But to be fair to the organisers, I later found out those who asked me for money were not Hisbah staff," he said.
He and his fiancée failed to be chosen for this August's wedding but he said he would try again next year.
Aminudeen admitted that the Islamic police were aware of such allegations: "We have found that there are some people asking others to pay certain money so they can make the list."
But the Hisbah officer wanted to assure all those wishing to wed in future that the entire process should not cost them a single naira.
"We want to announce to the people of Kano that the whole process is free: from the selection to the medicals and the goods set aside for couples - all are covered by the government."
One of successful grooms, 43-year-old clothes trader Rabiu Yusuf, agreed the process of applying to be married had gone smoothly for him.
"Personally, no-one asked me for anything. I was told the government would sponsor it all," he told the BBC.
His new wife is Aisha Auwal - the couple met as she regularly visited his shop to buy clothes.
Yusuf, who already has five children with his first wife, said he was "very happy and can't wait to start a new life" with his customer-turned-bride.
24 year-old Amina Alhassan echoed his sentiments, adding that she had not encountered any problems when applying to marry 40-year-old Nura Abdullahi.
Their union was first arranged by their families in Dambatta village before they presented themselves to the Hisbah.
"Everything has been free and I want to commend the Kano government for this scheme because without it, many couldn't have afforded to marry due to the high cost of living."
After Saturday's wedding feast, the presentation of the household goods began.
But it will take several more days for the excitement to die down in Kano and as the newlyweds busy themselves with setting up home together.

The Taliban in Afghanistan have launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regional and international powers show a readiness to engage more closely with the repressive regime despite its systematic human rights abuses.
Five years after the Taliban took power, an increasing number of countries are renewing ties or scaling up diplomatic contacts with the hardline Islamists, who seized power in Kabul in 2021 after 20 years of brutal insurgent warfare.
Campaigners fear that the individual contacts by different countries risk undermining “coherent, consistent” demands for an improvement in human rights in return for any diplomatic concessions.
The United Nations described a recent “cascade of [Taliban] edicts and laws” that have banned women from universities and most employment, denied teenage girls education and imposed strict dress codes. Minorities have been persecuted, while activists and journalists face repression. Afghanistan has become a “graveyard for human rights,” the UN said in March.
India, Qatar, China, Iran and several central Asian states all recently welcomed Taliban officials or opened new channels of communication. Russia, which recognised the Taliban government in Kabul just over a year ago, signed a military cooperation agreement last month. In June, the European Union held talks with Taliban officials in Brussels about returning failed asylum-seekers to Afghanistan. Individual European countries have also deepened their own contacts with Kabul.
“There is no doubt there has been an evolution. The Islamic emirate is now in a confident position. They have realised they are indispensable for regional countries right now and even with Europe and the US they have identified how to engage,” said Shivam Shekhawat, at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.
“The Taliban see any kind of contact as a diplomatic win and they have been able to capitalise on that as a sign granting legitimacy to the regime.”
A strict policy of isolation imposed after the Taliban seized power in 2021 towards informal or “de facto” recognition is now fragmenting. Some western commentators have suggested more countries recognise the regime. Others want intensified “back channel” engagement.
“We are not against any engagement … There is a need for engagement even if just for aid agencies to mitigate the ongoing humanitarian crisis but we are worried about the end goal of these contacts and the discussions that are taking place,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“There should be a consistent and coherent message from the international community to the Taliban that they will not have any friends if they do not show real progress in terms of the women’s rights and human rights situation … and that is not happening.”
The new contacts stem from a combination of regional security concerns, pressure in the west to reduce illegal immigration and a general recognition that the Taliban are unlikely to be forced from power in the foreseeable future.
The European Commission downplayed its discussions in Brussels with a Taliban delegation, the first such formal encounter since 2021, as merely “technical” and focused on returns, but a Taliban spokesperson claimed it was a historic visit that was a step towards regularising consular relations with EU countries.
The meeting prompted outrage.
“You cannot condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and then announce talks on immigration in the next … The Taliban are telling their constituency back home that they are now accepted by the international community,” said Abbasi.
This year officials from Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have all visited Kabul or other Afghan cities, seeking trade routes and pipeline deals that would allow their landlocked countries access to seaports or third countries beyond.
India too has moved to reinforce relationships that were frosty after the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, in part to exploit new tensions between the movement and the Islamist movement’s historic sponsors, Pakistan.
New Delhi secured a sanctions waiver last year so that Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban foreign minister and a veteran official who has spent decades at the heart of the movement, could travel there.
In June, India’s UN envoy suggested a rethink was necessary on sanctions, such as travel bans, asset freezes and arms embargoes, that target dozens of Taliban members.
“The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current UN sanctions regime must take that into account,” said Harish Parvathaneni.
Afghan authorities’ diplomatic strategy has involved hosting envoys in Kabul, including those from China, Japan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Last year, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, made the first visit by an Iranian foreign minister to Kabul for almost a decade.
The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan “seeks relations with all countries”, Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said, though “the countries of the region and our neighbouring states have particular importance, because our economic ties and interests are closely linked”.
Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute focusing on Russia’s policy towards the Middle East, said Moscow had multiple reasons for recognising the Taliban regime and seeking closer relations.
“One likely objective is simply having allies … Afghanistan is also very significant for Russia geographically and Russia just wants influence in that part of the world. There was an opening and they were able to take it,” Borshchevskaya said.
“It’s a very cold, cynical calculation. It’s part of a very simple zero-sum view that for Russia to win the US has to lose. From the Kremlin perspective, this is a global battle and whether you are looking at Europe or Afghanistan or wherever, it’s one geopolitical chessboard.”
Britain has said it pursues a policy of “limited and pragmatic” engagement with Taliban officials, largely through the UK Mission to Afghanistan based at the British embassy in Qatar. Discreet meetings with the Taliban have also repeatedly been held by other western countries in Qatar. In Germany and at least four other western European capitals, key consulates are now controlled by the Taliban, not representatives of the former Afghan government.
Taliban officials have also sought cross-border infrastructure projects to boost the country’s fragile economy and diplomacy. Natural resources are another lure for overseas powers. Kabul has expanded the mining sector, attracting firms from neighbouring China and elsewhere.
China, which is worried about Islamic militancy on and around its south-western borders, has welcomed Taliban officials in recent years, and hosted talks when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war earlier this year.
The Taliban are split, with deep disagreements on the ban on women’s education among other issues, but remain dominated by the most conservative factions. Recent laws have further reinforced repression, designating many religious minorities, including Shia Muslims, as heretics and imposing strict punishments to silence dissent.
Other new laws recognise only “excessive” beating as domestic violence against women and facilitate the marriage of girls without their consent. 
Analysts do not believe the Taliban are likely to moderate their position in the near future and point to the continuing authority of Hibatullah Akhundzada, the reclusive and authoritarian cleric leader.
Ramin Mansoori, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Endowment who studies Afghan politics, said the Taliban’s priority was its domestic agenda.
“They are not going to make any significant concessions. Most of them don’t have an international perspective,” Mansoori said.

Stating that mushrooming instances of hotels and eateries stocking and supplying expired food cannot be treated as stray violations of regulatory norms, the High Court of Karnataka has said that such instances “reveal a disturbing malaise creeping into the hospitality industry, where the hunger for profit has, in some cases, overshadowed the basic obligation to safeguard consumers’ health.”
Justice M. Nagaprasanna made these observations while refusing to quash a criminal case against an expired food recycling firm for allegedly selling expired item by relabelling them.
The court’s observations assumes importance amid recent raids by authorities on hotels and other establishments.
Taking note of recent enforcement actions that have disclosed alleged rackets employing methods to push expired products back into the stream of commerce, the court said increasing recurrence of such discoveries must awaken the regulatory machinery.
“Surprise inspections cannot remain occasional exercises undertaken only after public outrage erupts. Food safety requires constant vigilance, rigorous traceability of expired stock, prompt destruction of articles unfit for consumption and consequences sufficiently stringent to ensure that treating the consumer’s health as expendable never becomes a profitable business model,” the court observed.
Pointing out that a customer who eats in hotels with an implicit faith that what reaches his plate is wholesome, hygienic and fit for human consumption, the court said that the customer cannot be expected to enter the kitchen and scrutinise every packet for its expiry date or examine the origin of every ingredient before taking a morsel. “Customers’ trust is the very foundation for food industry,” the court said.

Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
- Published
Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way.
But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life.
Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving.
Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges.
There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted.
The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.
The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate.
We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond.
Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks".
We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death.
It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder.
In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting.
One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers - the case that Mathipa had been investigating.
After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police.

The case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive.
It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017.
Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks.
Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government.
We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond.
Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia.
Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia.
The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction.
We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment.
When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence.
He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police.
He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg.
The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do.
The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible.
The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover.
At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment.
Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military.
So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court.
Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise.
They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them.
Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency.
We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment.
When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved.
When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer.
"When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC.
On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time.
Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria.
When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway.
He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police.
And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi.
This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga's disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add.
New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa's death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police's Criminal Intelligence division.
Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, "we will kill all of them".
Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa's special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo - both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case.
The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction.
All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody.
Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa's murder, and Abotese's abduction and murder.
The military has refused to hand them over.
In July, their lawyers cited mental health treatment for their absence. Three years after Mathipa's killing, no trial date has been set.
Meanwhile, Abadigga's body has never been found.
"[Mathipa] was barking up the right tree. He was taking on the right lion," Vreugdenburg says of the late detective.
Mathipa's daughter Basetsana puts it starkly: "We need justice. I'm never going to see my dad anymore... Why my dad? Because he was doing his job."

For 28 days, Keshav had a new item on his daily to-do list: masturbate for research purposes.
Both before and after self-pleasuring, he logged his mood, energy levels, cravings for various vices, and whether he was procrastinating.
Keshav was taking part in AI companion company Joi AI’s experiment assessing what happens if erotic self-stimulation becomes “an AI-guided wellness ritual.” Throughout July, 10 “masturbation consultants” were instructed to masturbate every day except Sundays, enlisting Joi AI’s sultry digital companions twice a week and using their own preferred methods the rest of the time. “It's almost like you are chatting with a real person,” says Keshav, a single, 38-year-old Indonesian trader, who did not want to use his surname for professional reasons.
Joi AI invites users, for a fee, to chat and play with premade characters or to create their own companions, including with X-rated kinks such as blackmail fantasy, gangbangs, and emotional dependency, and capabilities and functions like squirting and roleplay.
During five-minute video calls with the digitized characters, Keshav explains, his female companions opened and closed their nude legs to reveal their genitals and would “do blowjobs and handjobs” while talking dirty. He often rendered the scenes in airplane bathrooms because he has a mile-high-club kink.
Some of the companions were “quite pushy and extroverted,” whereas others were more reserved and required a degree of courtship before the relationship became sexual—even soliciting gifts like handbags and lipstick, which cost up to $5 in the platform’s internal currency.
After ejaculating, Keshav’s “energy levels [were] a little bit down, but focus was a little bit up,” he says.
Keshav and his nine fellow masturbation consultants will receive $2,000 each for the qualitative, in-house research project run by Joi AI, which is promoting a daily guided “jerk off with purpose” masturbation tool combining “sound [and] ritual” as part of its professed goal to “solve male loneliness.” Of the 10, six completed the study. The website costs a minimum of $3.99 a month to access, but users are likely to spend far more on the platform, with 10,000 “Joi neuron” coins costing $99.99 and private videos from companions costing 1,000 neurons.
Joi AI surveyed 2,500 adults before launching the study, finding that 75 percent masturbate to reduce stress and anxiety and that 43 percent self-pleasure before “a big event,” like a date, exam, or difficult conversation. The company sought to discover how masturbation affects sleep, stress, craving intensity, focus, and ease of arousal—and how masturbating with AI held up versus other methods.
“You get this boost of dopamine when you ejaculate,” says Julie Levin, head of brand and communications at Joi AI. “We wanted our consultants to track whether their cravings [for vices] are worse or better and how it affects their self-discipline.”
Preliminary analysis of 134 masturbation session reports, seen by WIRED, suggests that participants' stress levels reduced by 25 percent and focus increased by 17 percent. The pre-research survey suggested that 37 percent of respondents are open to AI-guided masturbation or are already practicing it. In the masturbation experiment, AI-guided self-pleasure produced comparable satisfaction scores to the established methods. “The study found no significant differences between the methods; so there is no one best way to masturbate,” the company said in the report.
It also indicated that the study group’s self-reported cravings for nicotine, alcohol, junk food, and doomscrolling reduced by 44 percent after they had masturbated. “Masturbation may be the most accessible tool people have for managing addictions,” the report said—a claim that is not based in science.
“The fact that their unhealthy cravings decreased feels like a genuine breakthrough to me: What if this is an unexpected way to tackle addictions?” Levin says. “Masturbation is obviously way healthier than alcohol or nicotine.”
But Nicole Prause, a neuroscientist studying human sexuality and addiction, says “this is a gross overstatement from the evidence they claim to have.” Prause is not aware of any scientific evidence that masturbation reduces vulnerability to substance abuse, and she was critical of the research methodology.
“Since masturbation can never be placebo—people always know if they masturbated—it is important to use markers that are less subject to bias than self-report,” she says. “They use none. Someone saying ‘I feel focused’ is just that. There are dozens of cognitive tests that could be used to support a self-report. I do not see any.”
However, Prause, who is working on a large laboratory study of male orgasms, says masturbation to orgasm is a potent method of mood management. She adds that the most “dramatic shifts” among her study cohort come from people who report decreased anxiety and increased relaxation after climaxing.
Keshav, having recently completed the 28 days, looks back fondly on the experience. He says he was more clear-minded after masturbating and believes he is now better equipped to approach women. “Because I'm an introvert, it's difficult for me just to open myself to people,” he says. “This kind of helps me ... [with] what to expect, how to speak [to], or how to get a partner.”
He defied extraordinary odds to get the gig. More than 150,000 people applied for the 10 places in the monthlong experiment, with five handpicked by the company and another five chosen through public competitions, including one judged by porn stars—“may the best hands win,” the company posted on X—and another in which Joi AI made a call out for the “most unhinged” fetish. The winner had a balloon fetish.
Chloé Locatelli, a sex-tech researcher at King’s College London, was one of those invited to participate in the study because she is undertaking a collaborative project with Joi AI to see how different demographics build intimate and erotic relationships with the platform’s characters. “When they asked me to be a masturbation consultant, it was a bit of a no-brainer,” because of her research interests, says Locatelli, who recently split from her long-term partner.
“Masturbation is definitely something that I do to release stress,” says Locatelli, who was already a “daily girlie” with regards to her masturbation frequency. “I think there's a lot of physical and well-being benefits from self-pleasure.” She was less enamored with the AI companions than Keshav was: “I would engage with it and then be like, ‘OK, this has done it a little bit for me in terms of arousal, but there's more to be had.’”
She is acutely aware of the potential downsides of having a highly sexual AI companion. “I don't want to yuck anyone's yum as long as things are safe and consensual,” she says. But as AI companions become increasingly sophisticated, Locatelli is concerned about “the level of interactivity and personalization” they can give you: “If it becomes a bit of a crutch [and] your only form of sexual exploration, then that's not something that I would necessarily encourage.”
Despite the ubiquity of masturbating, surprisingly little research has tested what happens when healthy men and women do it every day. A 2024 review of 22 studies found masturbation tended to be negatively associated with sexual satisfaction among men, though the findings for women were mixed.
One interpretation is reverse causation: particularly among men, people dissatisfied with their sex lives may masturbate more, possibly increasing their discontent. A 2017 study published in Archives of Sexual Behavior found evidence that masturbation is often compensatory for men—a substitute for when partnered sex is not available—whereas for women it is more complementary, accompanying rather than replacing partnered sex.
Yet masturbation has documented benefits, too, such as stress relief through endorphin and oxytocin release and improved sleep, as well as providing the opportunity for connection with oneself. Public discussions about self-pleasuring, however, remain decidedly uncommon.
“We wanted to fight the taboo and stigma around masturbation and highlight that it's a normal part of a wellness routine, especially if you're single,” says Levin. “It's not some kind of a shameful habit.”
Locatelli says she is going to take her best friend on holiday to Spain, while Keshav says he will use the money from his gig to help fund purchases of stocks. But for Joi AI, which claims to offer men respite from isolation, the more consequential question is whether users will become so accustomed to its artificial companions that they retreat further from real-world connection.
