Kenya bids to host 2029 World Athletics Championships
- Published
Kenya has submitted an official bid to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships as it seeks to become the first African nation to stage the sport's flagship event.
Nairobi faces rival bids from London, Rome and Munich, with a decision by World Athletics expected next month.
Athletics Kenya said its "robust" bid is backed by the country's government and presents a "compelling case" to bring the championships to the continent.
"The government has committed its full support to the bid, ensuring the necessary organisational framework, security measures and modern infrastructure required to host a world-class global showpiece," a statement added.
BBC Sport Africa understands that Kasarani Stadium, which has a capacity of 48,000, would be the intended venue.
Kenya has a long and decorated history in athletics, especially middle- and long-distance running, and boasts 72 World Championship and 38 Olympic gold medals.
Seventeen current world records are held by Kenyans across track and road events, including both men's and women's marathons.
The Kenyan team finished second in the overall medal table at last year's World Championships in Tokyo, with seven golds among their 11 podium finishes.
Kenya has previously hosted the 2007 World Cross Country Championships in Mombasa, the World Under-18 Championships in Nairobi in 2017 and the World U20 Championships in the capital in 2021.
Nairobi also staged the 2010 African Athletics Championships at Nyayo National Stadium.
Kenya failed with a bid for the 2025 World Championships, but winning the rights to stage the 2029 edition would be another big step for the East African country on the international sporting scene.
It is set to co-host next year's Africa Cup of Nations football tournament alongside neighbours Tanzania and Uganda.
In May, Botswana became the first African nation to host the World Athletics Relays when they took place in Gaborone.

Advocating for secession from Pakistan, Baloch separatist groups and leaders declared August 11 as ‘Balochistan Independence Day’. They have appealed to the United Nations and the international community to recognise them as a sovereign nation rather than a province of Pakistan. However, to date, neither the UN nor any individual country, including India, has officially recognised Balochistan as an independent state.
Against this backdrop, a video (here) has gone viral on social media, claiming to be Balochistan’s newly released national anthem praising the Hindu deities. Let’s verify the authenticity of this claim.
Claim: Viral video shows the new national anthem of independent Balochistan, which praises Hindu gods.
Fact: The song in the viral video was never declared the national anthem of Balochistan. It is an AI-generated track uploaded by a YouTube channel named “Beyond Conscious”. Furthermore, Balochistan has not been officially recognised as a sovereign nation by the UN or any other country including India. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
An internet search regarding this claim yielded no credible results. There is no evidence or official statement from any Baloch separatist groups or leaders declaring this song as their national anthem. Additionally, no credible national or international media outlets have reported on such a development.
A reverse image search of the keyframes from the viral video led us to the original clip, which was uploaded (archived) by a YouTube channel called “Beyond Conscious” on 18 July 2026. The creator explicitly stated that the video’s visuals, music, and vocals were entirely generated using Artificial Intelligence (AI). To corroborate this, we ran the video through AI detection tools like SynthID and Hive, which confirmed that the content is 100% AI-generated. A deeper look into the channel revealed that it regularly creates and uploads similar AI-generated devotional songs (here & here) dedicated to various Hindu deities.
Geographically the largest province in Pakistan, Balochistan remains its most severely underdeveloped region. Accusing the Pakistani government of exploiting their vast natural resources while resorting to unlawful arrests and systemic oppression, separatist outfits like the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) have waged an armed insurgency for decades. Moreover, Baloch separatists strongly oppose the multi-billion-dollar China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) infrastructure projects, accusing China of plundering their resources. Consequently, between 2024 and 2026, the region witnessed a surge in massive attacks targeting both the Pakistani military and Chinese nationals. This prompted fierce retaliatory military operations by Pakistan.
The primary catalyst for the recent social media rumours claiming “Balochistan has declared independence” is the historical significance of August 11. On 11 August 1947, following the end of British rule, the princely state of Kalat (present-day Balochistan) emerged as an independent state, only to be annexed into Pakistan in 1948. In defiance of this annexation, Baloch separatist organisations symbolically observe August 11 every year as their ‘Independence Day’ and issue declarations. However, despite these symbolic gestures, the region remains under Pakistani state control, and no international body recognises it as an independent country.
To sum it up, the viral video circulating as the new national anthem of Balochistan praising Hindu gods is AI-generated.

Trump’s 2028 hat and ‘We are going to win’ message sparks fury among left about third-term ambitions
Some social media users compared the font President Donald Trump used in his latest image to typeface used by the Nazi regime
President Donald Trump drew ire from the left and other critics over the weekend after sharing an image of himself wearing a “Trump 2028” hat along with the troublesome message: “We are going to win.”
The 80-year-old has long suggested that he would run again for president in 2028, even though the 22nd Amendment to the U.S. Constitution places a clear limit on the number of terms one can serve as president.
While Trump has previously tried to pass off his third-term ambitions as a joke, many online seemed to think that the black-and-white image — which dramatically cast shadows over Trump’s face alongside the campaign message — was a clear indicator that he would be running again.
“Call it what it is: Trump just announced his intention to run for a 3rd term in 2028,” one X user commented.
“He’s old, sick and demented,” another user wrote.
Another chimed in, writing: “Trump is out of his mind.”
“Oh please this is not ok! Take them all to jail !!!” another wrote.
“Completely effed up behavior,” one person commented on X.
Other social media users catastrophized about what the post might mean for the future.
“Anyone who still thinks he’ll go quietly at the end of this term is either not paying attention or too gullible for words,” one X user wrote.
“No one listens when he says this. Why? Because he’s a liar they assume he’s a liar. But he’s actually telling the truth that he plans to not leave the WH. Election or not. He will try not to leave. Jan 6 was a trial run,” another commentator theorized.
“I already told everybody he’s not leaving office. We are in America’s first dictatorship, and have been since he retook office,” one user added.
Other social media users slammed the font Trump used, comparing the style used for his “We are going to win” message to Fraktur, a traditional German typeface used in Nazi Germany to promote the regime.
“The gothic style lettering makes the message even more chilling…Whiffs of 1930s Germany,” one user wrote.
“And tell me why they put a Nazi font on the bottom left?” another person questioned.
Another X user simply noted: “‘We are going to win.’ …in an INTERESTING font.”
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment regarding the post.
The bizarre message comes days after Trump seemed to have given up on his pipe dream of serving an illegal third term as president. The president has donned “Trump 2028” baseball hats and repeatedly brought up the idea — all while ignoring the fact that the Constitution would not allow for him to seek a third term.
In comments made Tuesday at Joint Base Andrews, Trump was asked if he was “serious” about seeking a third term, an illegal notion he has long flirted with the possibility of, and seemed to waver from his previous stance.
“Everybody asks me that question,” he said. “And you know that the law is very strong on that. I’d love to run, but the law is very strong.”
He continued: “I get asked by everyone. Even tonight, they’re screaming at the event, ‘2028!’ No, everybody wants me to do it, but the law is very strong.”
However, the president ignored the reporter who tried to press for further clarification, moving on to the next question.
Trump has floated the idea of another term countless times, including during his State of the Union address earlier this year, telling the nation: “First year of the second term…it should be my third term,” he said, bringing up his long-held, debunked belief that the 2020 election was “stolen” from him when he lost to former President Joe Biden.

Thomas's phone alarm buzzes at 9:30 pm -- it's time for the aspiring bodybuilder to start injecting himself in the stomach with several banned peptides.
He takes vials from his refrigerator of GHK-Cu, which he tells AFP will give him "beautiful skin", and Retatrutide, which will help him "feel less hungry".
After adding a liquid to reconstitute the synthetic peptides, he disinfects the syringes and shoots both into his lower abdomen.
Thomas, whose name has been changed, takes GHK-Cu daily and Retatrutide three times a week.
"It takes a little organisation, but it's become a routine," said Thomas, who goes to the gym almost every day.
He is one of a growing number of people attempting to "optimise" themselves by using peptides, a class of substances being widely promoted online by influencers, celebrities and the wellness industry.
Viral social media posts claim peptides can offer a range of seemingly miraculous benefits including glowing skin, stronger muscles, deeper sleep, a more alert mind -- and even provide an avenue to prevent ageing.
However experts warn there is little evidence to support these claims, and that because these peptides have not been studied properly, they can pose serious health risks.
That is why these peptides remain banned in many countries, including in France where Thomas lives.
In the United States, however, a panel recommended loosening restrictions on a range of peptides last month.
The decision outraged many medical experts, who accused Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. -- an avowed fan and user of peptides -- of packing the panel with people who have strong ties to the peptide industry.
Very real health risks
Peptides are short chains of amino acids that assemble to form proteins, which are the body's building blocks.
They occur naturally in the body, helping dictate processes such as repairing tissue.
Peptides reproduced in a lab are the active ingredients in many common medications including insulin and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs.
However unauthorised forms of synthetic peptides sold online have increasingly been promoted by influencers and gyms promising a more effective workout.
Thomas was already using steroids when he was introduced to peptides six months ago.
Along with GHK-Cu and Retatrutide, he sometimes injects himself with Selank for help with anxiety and BPC-157, which promises to more quickly repair soft tissue such as ligaments.
Because these peptides are not authorised for sale in France, there are no official guidelines for how to use them.
In online discussion forums such as Reddit and Discord, communities of mostly men exchange advice on how much and how often they should inject themselves.
"You read the studies, you look at the lab tests, and you see all the positive effects," said Thomas, who believes that the risks are "rare and not serious".
Self-experimentation 'worthless'
However neuroscientist Armelle Rancillac at French research institute INSERM warned that knowledge on how to use these peptides remains limited because they "have often not been tested on humans".
Earlier this year, INSERM said that "no large-scale, randomised controlled clinical trial has confirmed" the promised benefits of peptides, warning that some pose "very real health risks".
"We are not giving research enough time to prove its worth," Rancillac emphasised, adding that" scientifically worthless" accounts of self-experimentation were being given too much credence.
Numerous nations have reported people being hospitalised after using peptides. In June, Australia's government reported six cases of acute liver injury linked to products labelled Retatrutide.
It is difficult to determine how many people are using peptides, but the recent increase to exposure is enough to "raise alarm", Fabien Ohl, a sports sociologist at the University of Lausanne in Switzerland, told AFP.
Ohl criticised the "biological view" being pushed online that the human body is "capital" to be exploited by taking chemical substances to improve one's physical appearance.
For example, one website selling peptides promised to provide "the chemical architecture for those seeking absolute biological optimisation".
Self-proclaimed experts online also sell advice vowing to help men "optimise" their physique.
Ohl criticised this view of masculinity as problematic, warning it normalised an idea of "the biological male who is potentially more violent and aggressive".

The display is gorgeous. Excellent touchpad and backlit keyboard. Decent battery life and performance. Charges from both sides. 16-GB model available, unlike MacBook Neo.
TIRED
8 GB of RAM in base model is just not enough. No headphone jack.
It’s hard to talk about the new Dell XPS 13 without mentioning the MacBook Neo. To say it takes inspiration from the choices of its rival would be an understatement—whether that’s the type of processor, the quality of the display, or the amount of memory.
But don’t think that’s a bad thing. The Dell XPS 13 feels different from other Windows laptops you can buy for $700 (or $900 for the better configuration), and a lot of that is for the better. I have some beef with this laptop's starting configuration, but I also can’t deny what makes it so compelling and unique, even among the very best laptops you can buy.
Incredible Value
The MacBook Neo did one thing very well: translate what people love about MacBooks into a $700 package (or $600 at the time it was announced). In terms of the things you can touch and feel, the MacBook Neo is every bit as premium-feeling as a MacBook Air. The materials used in the chassis, the quality of the keyboard and trackpad, and the caliber of the display—none of it has the “budget device” stink. There's more to the story of the MacBook Neo than that, but you can tell it’s how Apple made decisions on which features to cut or compromise on.
Unlike nearly every Windows laptop selling for under $1,000, the Dell XPS 13 takes that same approach. Even the base configuration comes with a 2560 x 1600-resolution touch display with a 120-Hz refresh rate, up to 427 nits, and excellent color reproduction. The touchpad is glass and feels excellent to use. In terms of build quality, it’s top-tier. It’s made out of aluminum, and there’s no flexing to be heard of in the chassis. It opens with one finger, and the hinge doesn’t wobble. The bezels around the display are tiny, giving it a very modern look. It’s also incredibly thin at just half an inch thick, matching the MacBook Neo. That’s all very attractive stuff that makes a strong first impression when handling the device for the first time.
Here are some things the new Dell XPS 13 has that the Neo doesn’t:
A touchscreen display
A 120-Hz refresh rate
A backlit keyboard
Two up-to-date, 10-Gbps USB ports (one on each side!)
Support for two 4K monitors (or three if the lid is closed)
Fast storage speed
The one thing it’s missing is a headphone jack. The MacBook Neo includes one, and I do think that’s an unfortunate miss. But I really appreciate that Dell didn’t skimp on port quality. There’s one USB-C port on each side of the device, both of which can support a 4K display simultaneously at 60 Hz, charge the device, or transfer files at 10 Gbps.
While the speakers aren’t what I’d call good, Dell did throw in two tweeters for 8 watts of output. They’re at least on par with the Neo. It's the same story with the 1080p webcam. The addition of an IR camera for Windows Hello login is appreciated.
So, with all that, you might be wondering how Dell is getting away with selling the XPS 13 for a starting price of $700. There's a catch, as always.
More Memory Please
Dell made two significant compromises to reduce the price of the XPS 13. First, it uses a lower-powered Intel processor, the Core 5 320. Dell is surely saving money on this six-core chip, but to my surprise, I was impressed by this modest little piece of silicon. The XPS 13 is one of the first laptops to use this chip, which is part of the new Intel Wildcat Lake line. There are some other laptops coming out with this chip, meant to compete with the Apple A18 Pro used in the MacBook Neo and the Qualcomm Snapdragon X. The Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i is one such option, which uses the Intel Core 7 350, but as a 16-inch laptop, it's hardly a competitor to the highly compact XPS 13.
But really, there’s plenty of performance here for what the device is intended to be used for. The Core 5 320's raw single-core performance and graphics aren’t as strong as the A18 Pro, but in terms of multicore performance, it’s much more powerful. Then, there's the battery life. You're not getting quite as much as the MacBook Neo, but I was satisfied being able to stay away from the outlet all day and still last 15 hours in local video playback.
Memory is the other major area of compromise, and it’s where my concerns lie. The $700 model starts with only 8 GB of RAM, which is what I tested. This is rare these days. You’d have to be shopping in the sub-$500 category to find an 8-GB Windows laptop, which puts the $700 Dell XPS 13 in perspective. It’s a more premium laptop than you could ever find at that price in terms of build quality, display, trackpad, and keyboard. But it’s actually quite expensive for the amount of memory you get. Fortunately, Dell includes 512 GB of storage in all the models, which is also an important consideration when evaluating the price. While it was originally stated that the device would be configurable up to 1 TB of storage, right now you're maxed out at 512 GB.
But maybe you’re wondering whether you really need 16 GB of RAM. After all, five years ago, it was the default on laptops at this price. I was curious how well an 8-GB model could handle multitasking. Outside of the MacBook Neo, I haven’t used an 8-GB laptop in a long time, as even budget-level Windows machines have come with 16 GB of RAM over the past few years.
The RAM limitation was much worse than I even expected. Performance generally starts to slow when you’re using 80 percent of the available memory. At idle, with no open applications, Windows 11 was using well over 80 percent of memory due to background processes. Ending the background tasks that Microsoft Edge is always running brought that down to 70 to 75 percent, but Search alone was taking somewhere between 150 and 190 megabytes of memory at all times. That’s not Dell’s fault, but there’s a reason Microsoft has been pushing for broader acceptance of 16 GB of RAM as a base. More AI functionality means more background tasks running at all times, which drastically eats up your available memory.
Ten tabs in Chrome put this dangerously close to maxing out the memory. You get spikes up to over 95 percent at times. As you can imagine, getting the Dell XPS 13 to use up nearly 100 percent of the available memory took almost no effort at all. Just play one YouTube video in the background while keeping a handful of browser tabs open. A laptop that feels sluggish with just a few browser tabs open is acceptable for a laptop that costs $300. But it’s questionable, given that Dell is selling this device for $700. Regardless of how pretty and portable the design is, I would only recommend this version of the laptop for those with fairly minor computing needs. You don't want this if you're using it for most of your day.
That wasn’t quite my verdict, however, about the MacBook Neo. And I promise: That’s not because I’m biased against Windows. Apple has taken a lot of flak over the years for suggesting that 8 GB of RAM on a Mac is equivalent to 16 GB on Windows. That’s an exaggeration, but it is true that it takes a bit more to slow down the MacBook Neo. I pulled up the same exact series of tabs in Google Chrome, and the Neo experienced less lag and choppiness. Neither is meant for professionals, but it's worth mentioning since Dell is trying to position the XPS 13 directly against the MacBook Neo.
There's Good News
Here’s the upside: Unlike Apple, Dell does sell a 16-GB model. It’s a $200 increase, but it takes the XPS 13 from being disappointing to something incredibly solid. I can’t, in good faith, recommend that most people buy the $699 model that comes with only 8 GB of RAM. But as a $900 laptop with 16 GB of RAM, the Dell XPS 13 is excellent. In fact, it just might be the best laptop you can buy under $1,000. It’s $100 more than the MacBook Neo with 512 GB of storage, but it’s the superior laptop in nearly every aspect you can measure.
None of my favorite Windows laptops under $1,000 can really compete. That includes the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x, HP OmniBook 5 14, Asus Zenbook A14, and the Dell 14 Plus. Some of those are cheaper or more powerful than the base Dell XPS 13, but none are more compelling than the 16-GB variant. So, yes, the XPS 13 is fantastic, and you should absolutely buy it—just not the 8-GB version.

There is a lot of excitement and some trepidation among The X-Files fans about Ryan Coogler’s reboot for Hulu, currently in production. While we’re waiting, Hulu just released Chris Carter’s revamped (and R-rated) director’s cut of the 2008 standalone spinoff film The X-Files: I Want to Believe, distinguishable from its predecessor with a slightly different title: The X-Files: I Want to Believe–Vrach Frankenshteyn.
(Minor spoilers below but no major reveals.)
I Want to Believe received mixed reviews at its release and didn’t exactly light up the box office, but it still grossed $68 million against its $30 million budget. By 2015, the project led to the return of The X-Files as a limited-run TV series, with the six-episode season 10 debuting in 2016. Mulder and Scully were reunited 14 years after the events of season 9 as the FBI reopened the X-Files under Assistant Director Walter Skinner (Mitch Pileggi). The response was strong enough to warrant a follow-up ten-episode season in 2018, focusing on Mulder and Scully’s search for their missing son, William.
So one could hardly call I Want to Believe a failure. I quite enjoyed the film, but I always had a niggling sense that something was missing. That suspicion was confirmed when Carter made an appearance on David Duchovny’s podcast last summer and revealed that the studio had insisted he cut numerous scenes to get the desired PG-13 rating. Carter also hinted that a director’s cut was in the offing. “I made it too scary,” Carter told Duchovny of his original vision. “Now I have a chance to go back and make the scary movie that I always intended.”
Originally slated for a June release on Disney+, I Want to Believe–Vrach Frankenshteyn eventually moved to Hulu with an August 14 release. It’s largely the same film as in 2008, just rejiggered to emphasize the stronger horror aspects that Carter originally envisioned. Per the official premise:
When a group of women is mysteriously abducted, it becomes a case right out of The X-Files. Years after walking away from the FBI, Fox Mulder and Dana Scully are pulled back from the shadows when a federal agent vanishes without a trace. In a case you’d never see on TV, their only lead is a disgraced, defrocked priest claiming to have horrific psychic visions of the crime. Forced to confront the ghosts of their past, the partners must navigate a chilling winter landscape and an even darker human monstrosity. The truth of these crimes is out there somewhere… and it will take Mulder and Scully to find it.
Ars Technica caught up with Carter to learn more.

Ars Technica: The original series always had some elements of horror. I’m curious about why you wanted to make a feature film that was more overtly horror with I Want to Believe.
Chris Carter: We certainly mined the horror genre over and over. The show always works at the intersection of science and science fiction. The original inspiration for this movie was that I read about a doctor who had done a head transplant from one monkey to another monkey’s body, and he’d done it successfully. Immediately I said, “That’s an X-File. I’ve got to tell that story.”
Of course, I wanted to tell it with human beings. So I flew to Cleveland, Ohio, where this doctor was, and he told me how he did it. It was successful, but ultimately the monkey died. But then I started thinking, “Well, maybe this is a way to live forever.” If you could transplant your head onto a younger person’s body, you could possibly keep doing that until something went wrong.
There’s this tech-bro fascination with living forever right now. So this story is as relevant now as it was back then. It’s a great time to tell this story. And I got to go back and revisit something that I was unable to make the way I wanted to make it, due to studio executives who really didn’t know the show. I had promised them I’d make a PG-13 movie because I thought, “That’s what I make on TV every week.” But it turns out that both the executives and the MPA, the people who do the ratings, are less permissive with a PG-13 movie than network television was with horror.
Ars Technica: There’s more to your director’s cut than just restoring a few deleted scenes. You’ve done a full re-edit.
Chris Carter: I worked with two different editors, people I respect and I’ve worked with before who weren’t involved with it all originally. I asked them to watch the movie and help me to refine the cut and make it the scary movie that I originally intended to make. It was heroic on their part. The movie was originally edited by an Academy Award winner, and so coming in and basically re-editing his vision took some courage.
That said, I think the editors alone, just in the way they re-approached the movie, really helped it. I gave them the reins early on, and then when they gave those cuts back to me, that’s when I started to work on it. They added material, they took out material, they restructured material. I wanted to make a good, scary movie. The [2008] movie was a relationship movie for Mulder and Scully that happened to have an X-Files case. The weighting was wrong, and I wanted to remaster that.

Ars Technica: Vrach Frankenshteyn is Russian for Victor Frankenstein. You dabbled with that theme in the series occasionally as well. What keeps drawing you back to that particular well?
Chris Carter: Creating life anew, breathing life into something that is inert, is fascinating to me. That story just fascinates me. The Mary Shelley story is much different than the original Frankenstein movie. They didn’t use lightning bolts to bring the creature to life. It was much more like an X-Files story. I’ve always drawn on my love of that story. Even if it’s not as pointedly like The Postmodern Prometheus, that science lives and breathes in several places in The X-Files.
Ars Technica: For many fans, Mulder and Scully will always be the beating heart of The X-Files. What makes them such an enduring couple, even if they are not always technically “together”?
Chris Carter: Scully being a scientist and Mulder being a believer in the paranormal, and that they agree to disagree wonderfully—it’s part of the nature of their relationship. I think it’s their mutual respect for one another. That, for me, is the ideal man-woman relationship. It feels inevitable. It feels destined. I have that relationship with my wife. I believe in those connections, and I believe that everyone has a path. It’s just figuring out what path to take. Sometimes the path presents itself and you can’t see it. But with Mulder and Scully, they found their paths, and they’re traveling them together for better or worse.
Ars Technica: Back in 2008, you said that if I Want to Believe did well, there was a third X-Files film you were eager to make. Is that still ticking away in the back of your mind?
Chris Carter: It is ticking away in the back of my mind. If you watch the two reboots, there are four episodes [collectively] called “My Struggle.” They are the bookends for each of those series. They ended up in a place where people either loved me or hated me—when Scully revealed that she was pregnant. That is part of a bigger story, and I want to tell that story sometime. Right now, I think everyone’s focus is more on the Ryan Coogler reboot, and I don’t want to do anything to get in the way of that. I respect him, admire him, and want to see his vision. The story that I want to tell, if it is told—and I sure hope it will be—will be apart from that, but we certainly can’t ignore it.
Ars Technica: Did you envision when you created The X-Files that the series would become such a cultural touchstone for so many people?
Chris Carter: No, I didn’t. I was sitting alone in my mid-30s. I’m working in Hollywood. I’ve been hired to create TV shows. I love movies like the Sherlock Holmes movie Murder by Decree. I love Kolchak: The Night Stalker. I have all these things that are inspiring me. I put them all together into a—call it a kiln. And I fired the kiln, and I opened it up and it’s The X-Files. I had never in my wildest dreams believed that I’d be sitting here talking to you today about The X-Files, that there’d be a Lego set coming out, that it would’ve changed people’s lives.
At the 30th reunion anniversary in Minneapolis, I had 12-year-old, 10-year-old kids come up and say they love the show. And I have to think to myself, “Your parents probably didn’t even know each other when the show first aired.”
I’ll tell you another story that is near and dear to me. My wife and I were running on the beach not long ago; we run for 10 minutes, and we walk for a minute. When we started walking in that minute, I look up and I see an image that I recognize immediately. I start walking toward this young woman in her early 20s who’s wearing a graduation gown and holding her mortarboard in her hand. On the top of the cap, it’s got an image of Mulder and Scully. And it says, “The future is out there.” I say, “I know that image.” She said, “Oh yeah, it’s Mulder and Scully from The X-Files.” And I said, “I know, I know. I wrote that show.”
It was a wonderful moment. She didn’t grow up with the show, she found the show. That’s the mind-blowing thing to me: it inspired her enough to put it on her graduation gown and cap. That kind of thing you can never imagine when you sit down to create something.
The X-Files: I Want to Believe–Vrach Frankenshteyn is now streaming on Disney+ and Hulu.

US Attorney General Blanche defends colleague after Trump’s reflecting pool slam
Judging the US Attorney on a single case ‘is not fair’, Blanche said after Trump criticised the way she handled a vandalism allegation
US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Sunday that he backs top Washington prosecutor Jeanine Pirro, who was criticised by US President Donald Trump for the way she handled a case of alleged vandalism at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
“I absolutely support US Attorney Pirro, as does President Trump,” Blanche said on NBC’s Meet the Press programme.
The Trump administration fast-tracked a renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool ahead of the nation’s Fourth of July celebrations, at a cost of about US$14.7 million.
Within weeks an algae bloom developed and material at the bottom of the pool started peeling off. Federal authorities subsequently charged former US Olympian David Hearn and others with vandalism.
In a court filing asking for the case against Hearn to be dismissed, Pirro blamed the Reflecting Pool’s peeling issues on “flawed” work by a contractor and accused the Interior Department of providing incomplete information at first.
Trump subsequently posted that Pirro should revisit her “hastily made decision” to drop the case.
Blanche said he does not fault Trump for being frustrated over the matter, adding that a witness said they observed vandalism.

It’s been a wild first half of the year in the US power sector, with announcements of gigantic natural gas power plants and some long-awaited renewable energy projects coming online.
At times of rapid change, forecasting is difficult. So I feel a measure of comfort focusing on something concrete like the list of 368 utility-scale plants that began operation from January to June, according to data from the US Energy Information Administration. The group is dominated by utility-scale solar.
This is a top-heavy list, led by SunZia Wind South and SunZia Wind North in New Mexico, which went online this spring and are the largest wind farms in the country, with a combined generating capacity of 3,650 megawatts. SunZia has been in the works for about a decade and arrives at a time when US onshore wind power development has dwindled for a host of reasons related to regulations and public opinion.
In other words, the SunZia is not indicative of an onshore wind-energy boom. It is more like an echo from a past boom.
Next is Trumbull Energy Center in Ohio, a 900-megawatt combined-cycle natural gas plant that is part of an expansion of natural gas power in the PJM Interconnection grid region, which covers parts of the Mid-Atlantic, Midwest and South.
The fourth-largest new power plant—if we’re counting SunZia as two—is Vineyard Wind, the offshore wind project near Massachusetts, which, much like SunZia, has been in development for a long time and whose completion doesn’t reveal much about future trends.
It isn’t until the fifth-largest new plant that we see one that is connected to the broader trend in the data: Green River Energy Center in Utah, with 800 megawatts that includes 400 megawatts of solar and 400 megawatts of batteries.
Indeed, the story of power plant completions in the first half of 2026 was mainly about utility-scale solar and batteries.
Utility-scale solar led in the number of projects coming online, with 207, followed by batteries, with 95.

After its cloud storage provider went defunct, a PBS affiliate decided to sue a data center provider to regain access to 50TB of TV shows, videos, and other data dating back 70 years.
As reported this week by Current, a trade newspaper covering public broadcasting, St. Louis affiliate Nine PBS filed a lawsuit against Iron Mountain Data Centers on July 28, seeking access to the data. In the litigation filed in Denver District Court, Nine PBS says that its cloud storage provider, Open Source Storage (OSS), used one of Iron Mountain’s Denver data centers to store the channel’s data. However, OSS is being unresponsive, and Nine PBS says Iron Mountain has refused to release its data.
The data in question includes the station’s coverage of the COVID-19 pandemic, East St. Louis’ history, The Great Flood of 1993, and over 11,000 files, The Denver Post reported in July. The lawsuit claims that “most” of the data is “unique and irreplaceable,” according to the Post.
Last month, a judge blocked Iron Mountain from deleting or modifying the data.
In a hearing on Wednesday, a judge ruled that Iron Mountain must hand over any physical devices holding the data, Current reported today. The judge also said that Nine PBS must find a third party, such as a former OSS worker, who can help retrieve the data within 30 days and without sharing or corrupting data belonging to other OSS clients.
Nine PBS is already communicating with a former OSS employee “who is willing to help,” the report said. If complications arise, such as from the data being encrypted, another hearing will be scheduled. Nine PBS and Iron Mountain must provide updates by September 14.

Bus crash in Hungary kills 12 people, injures at least 10 others
Police say a passenger bus traveling on a highway in Hungary early Sunday went off the road and into a ditch where it overturned, killing 12 and injuring others
BUDAPEST, Hungary -- A passenger bus traveling on a highway in Hungary early Sunday went off the road and into a ditch where it overturned, killing 12 and injuring others, police said.
The bus, which was carrying a group of Polish tourists, was traveling on eastbound lanes near the town of Mezokeresztes when it overturned on the M3 motorway around 140 kilometers (87 miles) east of Hungary’s capital, Budapest, at around 1 a.m. on Sunday.
In a statement, police said it was likely that the driver fell asleep, causing the accident, and that the driver had been taken into custody.
Hungary's National Directorate for Disaster Management said in a statement that 57 passengers and two drivers were traveling on the bus at the time of the accident, and that several of the passengers had been trapped under the vehicle when it overturned.
Polish Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maciej Wewiór told Polish news agency PAP on Sunday that all of the people on the bus were Polish citizens.
The bus was carrying people from Poland’s southeastern Podkarpackie region who were returning from a pilgrimage in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the regional government in Rzeszow, Poland, said in a Facebook post.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar wrote in a statement on Facebook that at least 10 people were seriously injured in the crash. He offered his condolences to the families of the victims and thanked rescue workers who were dispatched to the scene.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki expressed his “deep sorrow” over the accident, writing in a post on X: “I join the families and loved ones of the victims in prayer and deep sympathy.”

A decade ago, SpaceX began to land the first stages of the Falcon 9 rocket with some regularity, but it’s only within the last five years that the company has begun flying the rocket dozens and then hundreds of times a year.
As a result, SpaceX has very rapidly become responsible for more than three-quarters of all mass launched into orbit. Much of this is the company’s Starlink satellites, but due to cost and the lack of alternatives, SpaceX has also stepped up to launch payloads from all comers, including direct competitors such as Amazon, Northrop Grumman, AST Space Mobile, OneWeb, and more.
New research is beginning to quantify just how much the introduction of the Falcon 9 rocket, the adoption of reuse, and the vehicle’s high cadence have upended the global launch market.
Cumulative payload to orbit
Public policy researchers based in the United Kingdom and Italy have published new research in Economics Letters that showcases the marked changes wrought by the Falcon 9 by mining a dataset of more than 6,700 launches from 1960 to 2025.
One of the more striking findings comes in the cumulative payload to orbit by nation. From 1990 to the early 2000s, the United States and the Soviet Union tracked fairly closely to one another. Then, in the wake of the Space Shuttle Columbia accident in 2003, Russia began to pull ahead. This trend slowly reversed course in the mid-2010s and then, amid the Falcon 9 ramp up in the early 2020s, the United States pulled ahead dramatically.
Just a handful of years later, the United States has now more than doubled all of Russia’s payloads to orbit since 1990.
“Another way to look at it is to analyze the shares of yearly global payload captured by selected spacefaring nations,” the authors write. “Between 1995 and 2012, the US share of global payload collapsed from almost 50 percent to a trough of less than 20 percent, far below Russia and only a few percentage points above China and Europe. Since then, it accelerated rapidly to a peak of over 82 percent in 2024.”

Apple Watch battery replacement: How much does it cost and is it worth it?
Should you replace your Apple Watch's battery or upgrade to a new model?
When you spend a lot of money on one of the best Apple Watch models, you want it to last as long as possible. But inevitably, as with any device that uses lithium-ion batteries, the battery will slowly degrade over time. You'll find it draining faster and faster, and you'll have to recharge it more often. Thankfully, this doesn't necessarily mean you'll have to toss the watch into a recycling bin and buy a new one. Apple Watch batteries can be replaced, which is a consideration worth making to extend the life of the device while also helping the environment.
Spending the $99 it typically costs to fix the watch through Apple can be worth it to get more usage from a wearable that cost you hundreds of dollars — assuming it still has life left it in otherwise. You'll have to determine if that money is better spent on an upgrade for the refined design and exclusive features of a more recent model, keeping watchOS compatibility in mind.
Pricing an Apple Watch battery replacement
You can arrange Apple Watch repairs directly through Apple, and the price is generally a flat fee of $99. Other retailers like Best Buy serve as Apple authorized Apple Watch service and repair providers, offering the same repair or replacement service for an equal fee. Typically, the process will take about a week, and you can schedule it online or in store.
If you have an active AppleCare plan on your device, that covers battery issues, including if the battery capacity drops below 80%. However, it does not cover normal degradation of the battery over time. Chances are, if this is the case, your Apple Watch is long outside of its warranty and extended warranty period anyway. There is an option to get ongoing AppleCare for Apple Watch for a monthly or yearly fee until you cancel. But this still includes service fees and/or deductibles and doesn't cover battery depletion from normal use.
Another option, if you're confident enough to consider it, is a DIY replacement. You'll find batteries offered by companies like iFixit, though the company only sells batteries for the original and Series 1 models. After acquiring a replacement battery for a newer model elsewhere, you can use iFixit's detailed instructional guides on how to swap it out manually. But this is not recommended unless you feel comfortable handling the intricate repair process; there are risks that come with attempting it yourself.
When to replace battery versus get a new watch
While eliminating e-waste and extending the life of tech products is great, there comes a time when an Apple Watch isn't worth bringing back to life with a new battery. First, consider software support. The latest watchOS 27 drops support for many older devices; it's only available for the Apple Watch Series 9, SE 3, and Ultra 2 and newer. That means if you own an Apple Watch Series 8 or older model, you won't get the latest software update. Your watch will continue to work just fine, though.
In fact, many people report still using models as old as the Series 4 today. The previous generation watchOS 26 had wider compatibility, working with models dating back to the Apple Watch Series 6 and second-generation SE. This means the Apple Watch Series 5 and first-generation SE (and older) are no longer supported, with their software end of life dating back to September 2024.
Your iPhone model shouldn't be a concern Apple's iPhone and Apple Watch compatibility page shows that older watchOS versions work fine with modern iOS releases, though you can't use the latest Apple Watch with an iPhone running an old iOS release. For example, an Apple Watch Series 11 (our review) will only pair with an iPhone 11 or newer that's running iOS 26 or later.
Apple Watches don't hold their value for as long as many other Apple products, so you may not recoup the battery investment if you resell the watch. Check what comparable models are selling for first so you know how much profit you could make. If you're handing the watch down to a friend or family member, consider giving it a replacement battery so they can enjoy the wearable for years to come.
To help you decide what's best, consider the age of the watch, software support, cost of the battery, and how much longer the watch will likely be supported. I'd suggest replacing the battery for a Series 6 or 7 and above, which are the oldest models compatible with watchOS 26. But for anything older than five or so years, you're better off upgrading instead.

- The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is one of the latest series of foldable phones showcased by Samsung, the others being the Galaxy Z Flip 8 and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra .
- While the Galaxy Z Flip 8 and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra broadly stick to more conventional form factors, the Z Fold 8 comes with a more square-ish, wider design.
- The Z Fold 8 comes with top-of-the-line hardware, but its design is what makes it perhaps the most innovative foldable we have seen for a while.
Foldable phones started out as being insanely innovative. And then proceeded to become as predictable as the unfoldables. Every year saw foldable devices that were essentially the same as their predecessors, and just like the non-foldies, were “thinner and more powerful than before.” Innovation on the foldable front seemed to be following the “retain design, improve specs, make thinner” formula seen on normal phones, with the addition of a “this time you cannot even see the crease” line!
Which is why the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 comes as a much-needed breath of fresh air in the foldable segment. At last there is something that’s different on the foldable front, beyond the usual slim, specs and crease conversation.
A distinct square-ish look that reminds one of pocketbooks
The Z Fold 8 brings the most basic innovations to the foldable table – it looks different and works differently. Yes, it does also come with flagship-level specs, but we do not think too many people will buy it for its spec sheet. The spec chasers with deep pockets are more likely to be attracted to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, while those on a tighter budget will not extend themselves beyond the relatively affordable Z 8 Flip. But those who want something different will go for the Z Fold 8.
While the Z Fold 8 follows the “open to get a bigger display” tradition of all foldables, it tries to hit the middle ground between the Z Flip 8 and the Z Fold 8 Ultra, attempting to blend the compactness of the Flip form factor with the productivity of the Fold 8 Ultra. It has a 5.5-inch cover display that is larger than the 4.1-inch one of the Z Flip 8 and a 7.5-inch main (internal) display that is slightly smaller than the 8-inch one on the Z Fold 8 Ultra. It, however, retains the Fold series’ quality of opening from the side rather than upwards as in the Flip.
However, unlike Galaxy Fold devices of the past – and most non-flip foldables – the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is actually shorter and wider than most phones. When shut, the Galaxy Z Fold 7 is 123.9 mm tall, which makes it one of the most compact devices out there, beaten only by foldables that flip (the Z Flip 8 itself is 85.7 mm tall). But what is interesting is that at 81.9 mm (when shut), it is one of the widest devices out there – the iPhone 17 Pro Max is 78 mm wide, for comparison.
This gives the Z Fold 8 a very distinct, slightly squarish look, like one of those pocket books that we used to carry around for making quick notes. This squarish appearance was quite the rage once upon a time – Motorola used it in the Moto Charm, Blackberry used it in the aptly-named Passport – but has largely gone out of fashion. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 attempts to bring it back into our lives, with a fold in the middle.
The fold that is just the type for those who like to type
From our limited experience of it so far, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the most comfortable foldable we have used in terms of portability, usability and productivity. The reason for that is its shape. Samsung has marketed the Galaxy Z Fold 8 as one which delivers a reel-friendly 16:10 aspect ratio when shut and opens up to reveal a more book-like 3:2 aspect ratio, making it the perfect device to view content on, but we think that is only part of the appeal of the device.
The wider-than-usual 5.5-inch cover display makes typing on the Z Fold 8 actually easier than even on the Z Fold 8 Ultra, which has a larger, but narrower, 6.5-inch display. In fact, this is perhaps the best typing experience we have had on a phone for a long time, although we do feel that its form factor makes it perfect for writing on – it actually gives us those classic notepad feels.
Time to be square again?
Of course, this does result in our opening the Z8 Fold less often as compared to the Z Flip 8 and the Z Fold 8 Ultra, which makes us wonder if it is time for the square-ish form factor, but that is another story for another day. We will also write more about the entire Fold experience in our detailed review. But as of now, it is safe to state that the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is perhaps the most radical change we have seen in a foldable since they came into existence.
It is also the first foldable we have written about without any mention of its processor, storage, RAM, cameras, or even software. The Z Fold 8 makes all of these seem secondary to the way in which it looks and works. Actually, we do not even think we have mentioned its price either. Which is what tech really should be about. In purely tech terms, we are flipping for this fold.
