The Labor government has pledged a new single-service opt-out register for gambling ads - an idea similar to the Do Not Call register for spam calls - as part of amendments to its wagering ad bill, as well as restrictions on inducements and limiting commissions for agents.
Communications minister Anika Wells has also confirmed gambling companies will face a new levy to pay for the register, a beefed-up measure to curb wagering ads, after concerns were raised through a Senate inquiry that Australians would struggle to find or complete individual opt-out options on each online service.
The measure falls short of calls from some, including Labor and Liberal MPs, for an “opt-in” model for gambling ads, or for a complete ban on online advertising.
The Albanese government’s gambling reforms are expected to proceed quickly through parliament this week, with Labor sources saying they hoped the changes contained in two separate bills would pass both houses before the end of Thursday. A Senate inquiry into the government’s bill will be tabled on Monday afternoon.
Despite Labor’s hopes of passing its gambling legislation this week, the Coalition has not yet publicly committed to supporting the package.
While a further raft of amendments to the bill are likely to outlined tomorrow, Wells on Monday introduced a third bill setting out some changes the government proposes to make to its own legislation.
The bill’s explanatory memorandum says the government’s plans include “restricting the use of inducements by licensed interactive wagering service providers”, as well as plans to prohibit “inducement-based direct marketing and social media advertising to certain customers, restricts attempts to obtain consent to receive such marketing, prohibits certain commission-based referral arrangements”.
“The government has listened carefully to the evidence presented during the recent Senate inquiry and through ongoing stakeholder engagement. We are particularly concerned by evidence about wagering inducements and the role these practices can play in encouraging gambling and exacerbating gambling-related harm,” Wells told parliament in introducing the new bill.
A major change contained in the third bill is a new “Wagering Advertising Opt-out Register”. While neither Wells’ speech nor the explanatory memorandum explains exactly how this would work, the explanation says it would be “a single mechanism through which individuals may opt out of receiving wagering advertising from online content service providers”.
Labor’s initial bill had stopped short of enacting a full ban on wagering ads online, as recommended by Peta Murphy’s landmark 2023 parliamentary report, in favour of establishing a “triple lock” system for ads to be shown online; that online ads could only be shown to users who are logged-in and aged over 18, and provided with an opt-out feature.
But gambling harm advocates and critics of Labor’s bill had criticised this system, saying existing opt-out features on streaming services or social media platforms were often hard to find online, and that only a tiny percentage of users had made use of those features.
The government’s new proposal for a single opt-out register is a compromise to provide an easier avenue for opting out of ads, without enacting a full ban or switching to an opt-in.
Wells told parliament that the register would “provide Australians with a ‘one-stop shop’ to opt out of seeing wagering advertising on online platforms”, and be administered and established by the Australian Communications and Media Authority .
Guardian Australia is seeking information about how the register would operate.
“This Bill enables the ACMA to recover the costs of those activities through a levy imposed on licensed interactive wagering service providers. It is appropriate that the wagering industry, rather than taxpayers, bears the costs of regulating these activities,” Wells said.

There is something oddly magnetic about Kyle Chandler’s eyebrows. They’re disarmingly expressive, and Chandler’s grouchy-yet-charming Hal Jordan, Earth’s one and only Green Lantern, uses them to great effect in the season premiere of HBO’s latest superhero drama. If I were to critique Lanterns solely on eyebrow charisma, I’d give the show five out of five alien-powered super-rings.
Alas, after watching just the first episode, I’m really not sure what to make of it at all. Like most critics, I was given seven episodes as screeners, but I decided to only watch the premiere before penning my recap. This is what audiences will see on Sunday night, after all, and it’s all they’ll have to go on. I might as well have the same experience. It can be fun to watch along with the audience as a reviewer rather than skip ahead. That way you can come up with theories and be part of the discussion. That’s especially true when it’s a mystery.
In any case, there will be spoilers here since this is both a recap and review of the first episode, but I want to talk about expectations before we get into the story itself. I think my reaction to this season premiere has a lot to do with the expectations that were set leading up to the show’s release.
You’ll notice in the headline up above I say that Lanterns is “No True Detective.” Maybe I’ll change my mind about that once I’ve seen more of the season, but it only took one episode of True Detective Season 1 for me to know that this was something special. It was dark and eerie and terrifying and, more than anything, it instantly immersed us in the Southern Gothic swamps and bayous of rural Louisiana. The sense of place, whether or not it was at all realistic, was palpable and felt at once authentic and grounded, but also disturbingly surreal. We were lost in that fever dream from start to finish.
And the two detectives – Matthew McConaughey’s Rust Cohle and Woody Harrelson’s Marty Hart – were the perfect pair, totally incompatible in almost every way, yet somehow perfect for each other. Was this a deconstruction of the buddy cop genre or a full-throated embrace of its conventions? Whatever it was, it set the bar high. Too high for subsequent seasons and too high for most shows in the detective genre writ large. “What are some detective shows like True Detective?” has to be an incredibly common Google search. Certainly forum threads and listicles aplenty have been written pointing hungry fans of that perfect season of television toward other contenders. We are often disappointed.
So it was a rather ballsy move to market Lanterns as a superhero detective story inspired by True Detective Season 1. And perhaps not altogether wise. The season premiere has plenty going for it, but Lanterns is nothing like True Detective so far. Yes, it has two major timelines that the story will unfold across, similar to Rust and Marty’s investigation (which took place across several timelines). It has two detectives whose personalities mix like water and vinegar. It’s a mystery, though the nature of the mystery is not made particularly clear in the pilot beyond having to do with aliens and the origin of the Green Lantern powers. It has all these components present but it lacks the hook. I’m not sure, 57 minutes in, why I’m supposed to care.
True Detective opens to a field of fire. It opens to a horrific crime scene . A young woman’s body discovered amidst the charred sugarcane next to a tree, antlers attached to her like some grotesque crown, her kneeling corpse in a prayerful pose. There’s something haunting and ritualistic about all of it. You can’t look away. You don’t want to look, but you can’t look away. I’ll never forget those opening moments, when I first met Dora Lange.
Lanterns opens to a group of kids watching a news program about Hal Jordan. We meet our young protagonist, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre as an adult) who is clearly fascinated by this ex test-pilot turned superhero. His brothers are worried because their dad is coming home soon and apparently they’re not supposed to be watching TV. When their father comes home, in military fatigues, he takes the boy outside and plays William Tell with an apple and his military issue sidearm. John doesn’t even flinch. It’s certainly a bizarre way to introduce these characters.
The rest of the episode is similarly odd. We skip forward twenty years, from 1996 to 2016. John is now a trainee under Hal Jordan. The two men don’t like one another very much, which is common enough in the buddy cop genre. There isn’t much banter, however, because while Hal is very chatty and funny and a bit of a rake, John is very much the strong and silent type. He says “Yes sir,” a lot and Hal asks sarcastically why each time he says “Yes sir” it sounds more like “bleep you”.
Hal is training John as a backup in case anything ever happens to him, though he insists he will never retire and John will never become a Green Lantern, since only one Green Lantern is assigned to earth. We know that by the time Superman takes place, Nathan Fillion’s Guy Gardner has the ring, but in 2016 it’s Hal Jordan and he’s training John and has a very . . . peculiar style of mentorship, including placing his ring on the dashboard and leaping out of the car as it careens off a cliff. John puts on the ring as the car heads toward impact and, we learn later but don’t see, conjures bubble wrap all around him to save himself.
A Green Lantern ring works like this: Whoever wears it can simply conjure into being whatever they can imagine, it’s just always a bright green color, like Nickelodeon slime green. You can use them to fly and do other neat stuff, but Hal doesn’t really care to teach John much, and John resents him for it. On his walk to the taco stand where Hal told him to meet back up, a “backup copy” of Hal pops out of the ring and relays a message to give to himself: It’s hailing in Rushville, Nebraska.
When Hal hears this, he flies off, leaving John to fend for himself. He ends up flying to Nebraska where he meets up with Hal and finds a grim scene. A football game ended in tragedy, several people shot dead. The local sheriff, Kerry Kane (played by Kelly Macdonald, but also my mom’s name is Kerry Kain so . . . that was a bit surprising) – in any case, the sheriff seems to have history with Hal and doesn’t want him anywhere near the crime scene. He thinks the whole thing has to do with aliens and she seems exasperated by his presence. When they apprehend a suspect, Kerry won’t let Hal interview him, so he gets in a fight at a local bar with some local yokels (enraging them by playing the song Brand New Key over and over and over again on the jukebox) so that he can take a trip to the local jail and have a word with the “alien” in custody.
One thing leads to another and Kerry doesn’t put him in the cells but rather in a closet for the night and the next morning he goes in front of a judge to get bail, which all seems a bit much for a bar fight in a redneck Nebraska town like Rushville where he was clearly the victim, but whatever. The point is, he’s bailed out by a mysterious benefactor who happens to be Kerry’s father-in-law, William Macon (played by the always charming Garret Dillahunt). The Green Lantern and his trainee go to visit Macon for lunch and learn that he’s running a pretty major militia out in the Nebraska backcountry, though he’s just the steward of the operation. An NDA, he tells Hal, prevents him from revealing his benefactor.
A few things happen quite quickly: John sleeps with a mysterious woman who, it turns out, is Zoe Macon (Poorna Jagannathan), William’s wife. William pulls strings with his daughter-in-law and Hal gets to question the man in custody, and the man in custody turns out to be an alien, after all, and tries to blow everyone up to get “revenge” over something we don’t know about yet. Hal saves the day with his ring and then we jump ahead to 2026, where John Stewart returns to Rushville in a snowstorm and the whole thing feels very Fargo-like.
He meets up with Kerry and the two of them head back to the football stadium where they find Hal Jordan’s frozen corpse sitting in the stands.
It’s a bit of a messy opener for this new DC show. Not bad, necessarily, but not super great either. Not something I’m going to go around telling everyone to watch, but not something I’ll warn you away from.
The inspirations creators Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof and Tom King and other producers and writers on the show have listed go beyond True Detective to Slow Horses, Fargo, The Right Stuff, No Country For Old Men and the buddy-cop genre more broadly. But these are all pretty outstanding, critically acclaimed shows and movies, and at least judging by this opening salvo, Lanterns isn’t that. Not yet, anyways, no matter how charming Kyle Chandler’s eyebrows might be (he honestly reminds me of a younger Kurt Russell a lot of the time) or how piercing Aaron Pierre’s eyes are. The cast is solid, the show is interesting enough, but this season premiere needed to wow, and it did not wow. Maybe it’s just silly to think a show about “magic” rings could ever live up to True Detective (hey, just ask Rings Of Power!)
My curiosity is piqued, but nothing more. Hopefully the rest of the season is better and my doubts are ill-founded. We shall see. I’ll keep watching and reviewing each week’s episode here on this blog as well as on my YouTube channel.

What I Saw in Sinaloa
The U.S. is trying to destroy Mexican cartels. But so far, a turf war has only deepened.
Sign up for our newsletter about national security here.
Last Tuesday night, I was eating sushi with a Mexican police chief in downtown Culiacán, a city that had momentarily flickered back to life amid a bloody cartel turf war. At the table next to us was a birthday party. The police chief ordered a salmon roll. Through the window, I could see groups of families and friends walking on the sidewalk, past car dealerships and strip malls, after months of self-imposed lockdown.
Among them were three influencers who pulled up to a KFC down the street. They were dressed as food-delivery workers, carrying insulated bags on their backs, joking with one another and livestreaming everything with their phones. César Gastélum, the group’s front man, had become famous for such innocuous pranks. Even as thousands were murdered by the cartels, Gastélum, a stocky, bearded 24-year-old, posted videos of himself dancing in pajamas, dressing as a priest, sipping iced coffee. He had more than 700,000 followers on TikTok.
It was this kind of incongruity that had drawn me to Culiacán, the capital of Sinaloa. The city is the center of the fiercest and most consequential battle between armed groups in Mexico, and I wanted to untangle what was behind the surge of violence. From afar, it was difficult to tell whether someone like Gastélum was proof that the mundane and the horrific could coexist here, as they have for decades across Mexico, or whether he was a symbol of something else—the way drug cartels had quietly co-opted even the city’s least likely protagonists.
At about 8 o’clock, Gastélum and his friends were recording themselves waiting for their fried-chicken orders when two men on a motorcycle drove past. “Those guys scare me,” Gastélum said. He then seemed to regain his calm, joking about his skinny jeans in front of the camera when the motorcycle returned. It stopped momentarily in front of the three young men. The driver, wearing a black helmet with a face shield, raised a gun about two feet from Gastélum’s head and fired. The livestream captured the moment of the bullet’s impact and then went dark.
Someone on the city’s ambulance team texted me when the 911 call came in, and I ran across the street to the KFC. I got to the scene as police were arriving. Gastélum’s body lay at the drive-through’s exit, a ribbon of blood streaming toward the sidewalk. A cluster of soldiers gathered nearby, some of them scrolling through Gastélum’s TikTok feed. A small group of crime photographers were taking photos and uploading videos.
“As you can see, they have killed another influencer here in Culiacán,” José Ángel Beltrán of Luz Noticias said, narrating on Facebook Live.
Culiacán, for years the axis of Mexico’s drug wars, is now the focus of a U.S. effort to demolish drug cartels—something President Trump has said he’s willing to use military force to achieve. It is in many ways an understandable target: The Sinaloa cartel, which has administered the state for decades, is responsible for trafficking millions of kilos of fentanyl, meth, and cocaine into the United States. The Justice Department has indicted both the Sinaloa governor and the Culiacán mayor for cooperating with the cartel. Several of its leaders are serving life sentences in the U.S., and others have been targeted by Mexican security forces using intelligence from the United States.
And yet, so far, these actions have only deepened the civil war between two Sinaloa-cartel factions, one run by the children and supporters of Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán (the Chapitos), and the other run by allies of Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada García (the Mayos). In 2022, there were 476 homicides in Sinaloa. In 2025, it had 1,657. Government action against organized-crime groups in Mexico has almost always had such an effect—increasing violence without significantly altering the flow of drugs into the United States. But the current Sinaloa turf war—la narcopandemia, locals call it—has created new categories of victims, far from the foot soldiers and hit men targeted in previous spasms of violence. Now influencers and content creators are recruited by cartels to distribute their messages online. And university and vocational students have been kidnapped, presumably because their skills are needed by criminal groups. Each time a young person here is killed or vanishes, there are immediate questions about whom he or she might have been working for. When drug traffickers allegedly subsidize TikTok dances, a victim’s innocence can be almost impossible to discern.
As forensic police arrived at the KFC, Beltrán told me that another TikToker had been killed a few blocks away months earlier. A fitness influencer, El Tata, was murdered while leaving a shopping center. The body of a YouTuber, El Pinky, was found showing signs that he had been gagged and bound. About a dozen other influencers in Sinaloa have been killed, kidnapped, or attacked. Each time, the Mexican government investigated whether the influencers had somehow been linked to one group and targeted by the other. Last year, an unidentified plane dropped thousands of flyers over Culiacán that accused a number of influencers and musicians of having ties to the Chapitos (Gastélum was not on the list).
Standing in front of the crime scene as the forensic police hovered around Gastélum’s body with flashlights, I asked Beltrán why he thought a goofy livestreamer would be a target in a cartel turf war.
“Did you see that he was wearing a cowboy hat?” Beltrán asked me.
Cowboy hats have become a symbol of the Mayos faction of the cartel. The implication was that Gastélum, while performing juvenile pranks, had been making a subtle nod to one group’s power. Online commenters rushed to make the same point.
Beltrán filmed one last video of Gastélum’s body as it was taken away, and then he tapped me on the shoulder. Another victim had been found half a mile away: a man shot in the city’s botanical garden after a screening of a Lady Gaga documentary. I went with him to cover it. When we got there, it was dark, and the body was lit by a streetlight. Beltrán took his phone out again and started streaming.
“Hello again, everyone,” he said. “It’s another rough night in Culiacán.”
The next day, I drove 30 minutes from downtown Culiacán to a neighborhood called Costa Rica, on the outskirts of the city. I passed several motorcyclists who had their face covered by a ski mask. These punteros, as they’re called, have for years worked as low-level informants for the cartel. Even before the fracture of Sinaloa, the cartel was famous for its capacity to monitor every inch of Culiacán. In addition to deploying the punteros, it placed hundreds of cameras across the city and set up surveillance teams in residential neighborhoods.
The Mexican government has surged hundreds of soldiers and national guardsmen across the city, ostensibly to disrupt the criminal groups who have terrorized it. But the military presence is overwhelmingly performative. On the road to Costa Rica, I watched as punteros and soldiers nonchalantly drove past one another.
I pulled up to the squat house of Marta Pérez Guzman, whose son, David Antonio Ruelas Pérez, had been kidnapped by armed men along with his classmate José Isaías Ibarra Duarte. There were 2,154 disappearances in Sinaloa last year, but the kidnapping of Ruelas, 22, and Ibarra, 23, had received more attention than most. The men were students at an aviation school in Culiacán, and many here suspected that they had been abducted to work on cartel aircraft. There was another notable fact: Ibarra is a U.S. citizen, born in Los Angeles.
His mother, Graciela Duarte Valdez, had wondered whether that would be enough to nudge the U.S. government to act. After all, Trump had articulated in Truth Social posts and Fox News interviews his desire to intervene in Mexico. She had traveled to the closest U.S. consulate, in the neighboring state of Sonora, and made her case. Not only was her son still missing, but the Mexican attorney general’s office had obtained surveillance footage of the kidnapping and showed it to her. Through tears, Duarte described seeing footage of four men who wore ski masks and carried rifles getting out of a minivan and forcing her son and Ruelas into a second car. It all took only a few seconds.
She felt abandoned by the Mexican government’s investigators, who asked questions suggesting that the boys had been working for a cartel faction before the kidnapping. When she went to the U.S. consulate, officials took notes and thanked her for coming (when I asked the State Department about the case, a spokesperson told me in a statement that it was “aware of reports of the kidnapping of a U.S. citizen in Mexico” but did not elaborate). Duarte was despairing; she knew that just a small fraction of disappeared people were later found alive in Sinaloa. One day last year, she heard that Governor Rubén Rocha Moya was visiting her neighborhood. She ran to meet him.
“Please help,” she told the governor, as she held a missing-person poster with her son’s photo and name on it. Rocha told her he would try.
A few months later, Duarte was skimming her Facebook feed for information about missing people and recovered bodies when she saw a news story that said Rocha had been indicted by the United States for colluding with the cartel. The U.S. government had acted, but she could not bring herself to see the move as productive or helpful. Rocha temporarily resigned and fled Culiacán. The Mexican government announced that it would support him until the U.S. showed more evidence of his collusion.
“All I could think was that I had begged that man for help,” Duarte said. “But of course, he did nothing. He had been working for the cartel the whole time.”
About a third of Mexico is controlled by organized criminal groups, according to a U.S.-government analysis. Culiacán—even during its most peaceful stretches—has been a prime example. The cartel presence here has never been subtle. One man in his early 20s told me that his childhood friends had been recruited to work in fentanyl labs and would return smelling like chemicals for weeks. The children of cartel kingpins enrolled in the city’s top prep schools. In one cemetery, families of deceased cartel operatives erected graves the size of suburban homes. Each time the cartel’s fractures sent the city into spirals of violence—in 2010 and 2017—they ended the same way: not with the disintegration of organized crime but with one faction emerging as the victor.
The Trump administration believes that it can avoid repeating this pattern, partially by going after Mexican politicians who support the cartel—“all the government officials that are part of the ‘Culiacán clan,’” Sara Carter, the director of the White House’s Office of National Drug Control Policy, told a journalist earlier this year. The U.S. has also continued its decades-long strategy of targeting top cartel operatives, largely by funneling intelligence to elite Mexican-military units who have conducted a number of successful operations. That partnership is deeper than it has been in years. But I didn’t meet anyone in Culiacán who believes that the strategy will reduce violence here. So far, it hasn’t reduced drug flows, either. Even officials in the Mexican government who are in favor of attacking criminal groups privately dismiss the Trump administration’s absolutist goal of eliminating cartels, given the enormous demand for drugs in the United States.
“On Day one, President Trump designated major cartels—including Sinaloa—as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, unlocking powerful sanctions, asset seizures, and enhanced prosecutorial tools to crush their operations. We will not allow cartels to profit off of poisoning our children and grandchildren,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, told me in a statement.
As César Gastélum’s body was buried last week, some of the city’s influencers posted tributes to him, as if describing a fallen comrade. “We need to take care of ourselves,” one wrote to his 2.3 million followers. Even Mexico’s president weighed in, promising to find the assailants. Duarte had followed the news. Gastélum was just a year older than her son.
But she was following another story more closely. The government had detained a dozen young alleged cartel operatives in a rural area outside Culiacán. It published photos of the boys and men, their faces blurred. Many of their T-shirts were off, revealing skinny frames. Duarte zoomed in on one of them. It was hard to tell, but he looked at least a little bit like her son.

Aid shortages and fears of starvation as Indonesia reels from deadly earthquake
- Published
Aid disruptions and aftershocks across the Indonesian island of Flores are fuelling fears among thousands of survivors who were displaced by a 7.7 magnitude earthquake on Saturday.
Refugees are sleeping outdoors through sweltering days and frigid nights for fear that more buildings may collapse. Tents set up amid the rubble of collapsed hospitals are serving as makeshift emergency rooms for injured patients. And as landslides sever access roads and supplies dwindle in several parts of the island, there are growing concerns about how much longer survivors can hold out.
At least 53 people were killed and some 5,000 displaced by the initial quake, which struck shortly before 06:00 Saturday (23:00 GMT Friday) at a depth of just 15km.
It is the country's deadliest earthquake since 2022, when hundreds of people were killed in West Java.
"We heard that medical assistance would be provided, but nothing has arrived yet," Rista Mari, a public relations officer at the Ruteng Regional General Hospital in Manggarai Regency, told the BBC. "We hope that assistance will arrive soon."
Early data from Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency indicates that more than 1,000 houses have been damaged, along with dozens of health facilities, schools and government offices.
But the full scale of the disaster is still being uncovered.
In Flores' westernmost town of Labuan Bajo, the gateway to Komodo National Park and one of Indonesia's most popular tourist destinations, many survivors have been sleeping outdoors, fearful that if the tremors continue they might be crushed in their sleep.
"The shaking was very scary. My house almost collapsed," said one farmer named Anastasia Imad, from a green emergency tent erected next to her damaged home. "We were worried that the aftershocks would collapse the house while we were sleeping."
Herry Kabut, editor-in-chief of local publication Floresa Media, told the BBC that "each resident has set up their own evacuation post" amid blackouts, landslides and roadblocks.
"So far, many basic necessities such as [basic foodstuffs] and clean water are in great demand," he said. "People have no idea where to evacuate. There's been no government advice. Many have fled to the hills and are starving."
Health services across the island have similarly been forced to move outside and set up emergency tents due to damaged facilities. Ruteng Regional General Hospital's operating room, delivery room, pharmacy, and laboratory were all rendered defunct after the building's roof collapsed.
Elsewhere, in Ngada Regency, local resident Charles Abar told the BBC that health facilities and equipment had been severely damaged and that, as of Sunday night, no medical assistance had arrived.
He believes the government's response hasn't been swift enough.
"I think facilities like emergency tents need to be provided immediately, but I also see that district and regional governments are struggling due to budget constraints, limited supplies, and so on," he said.
Meanwhile, he added, villages have been cut off from aid and displaced people whose homes were damaged or destroyed have been forced to seek higher ground, as hundreds of aftershocks continue to rattle the island.
"The community is still traumatised," he stressed.
Indonesia is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity, lying along the meeting point of three major tectonic plates.
On Sunday night, rescuers successfully reached a village on Palue Island, just north of Flores's mainland, that had been cut off for nearly two full days after the initial quake.
Rescuers were only able to reach Nitung Village after a two-hour overland journey from the coast.
"Our challenge was the road, which was still prone to landslides," said Sikka Deputy Police Chief Commissioner Marselus Yugo Amboro, who led the rescue mission. "It was a life-threatening route."
Yugo said hundreds of homes in Nitung Village were severely damaged by the earthquake, and that residents had been sheltering in makeshift shelters. Electricity and communication lines were completely cut off following the earthquake, he added.
"They haven't received aid yet because Nitung Village was isolated for nearly two days after the quake," he said, noting that efforts were underway to rush aid to the survivors.
"This is likely the village in Sikka Regency that suffered the worst damage from the earthquake."
Additional reporting by Eliazar Robert in Sikka Regency, East Nusa Tenggara

Extreme heat, humidity, cold weather and changes in routine can make periods harder to manage. But persistent changes in cycle length, bleeding or pain should not simply be blamed on the weather; medical attention should be sought
A period arriving a few days earlier or later than expected can be unsettling, particularly during a heatwave, a spell of heavy rain or a sudden change in routine. The menstrual cycle is primarily regulated by hormonal signals between the brain and ovaries. Weather does not directly control menstruation, but extreme conditions can place physical stress on the body and affect sleep, hydration, physical activity, appetite and stress levels. These changes may, in turn, affect ovulation and the symptoms experienced around a period.
How it works
Sandhya Vasan, director and senior consultant, gynecology, SIMS Hospital, Chennai, says extreme weather can act as a physiological stressor. The body’s stress response involves hormones such as cortisol, which can affect the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis that regulates ovulation and menstruation. If this hormonal signalling is disrupted, ovulation may be delayed, occur earlier or, in some cases, be skipped, resulting in a longer, shorter or irregular cycle.
The evidence linking weather directly to menstrual changes, however, remains limited. Much of the effect may come from the changes that extreme weather brings to everyday life rather than from temperature itself.
Heat can amplify symptoms
Extreme heat can make an already uncomfortable period harder to manage. Dehydration, fatigue and poor sleep can add to the physical stress of menstruation and may make cramps, headaches, dizziness and premenstrual symptoms more noticeable.
P.M. Gopinath, director of reproductive medicine, Kauvery Hospital, Vadapalani, Chennai, says heat causes blood vessels to dilate as the body attempts to lose heat. At the same time, sweating leads to fluid and electrolyte loss. Together with heat-related fatigue and disturbed sleep, these changes can make menstrual symptoms feel more intense.
Pavithra Ramakrishnan, consultant, obstetrics, gynecology and reproductive medicine, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, OMR, Chennai, says some women may notice heavier or lighter bleeding, fatigue and headaches during extreme heat. Dehydration and physical stress can also affect the timing of ovulation, potentially shifting the next period.
However, a change in bleeding should not automatically be considered a response to temperature. Persistent or significant changes require assessment for other causes.
Some women may be more vulnerable to the effects of extreme weather. These include adolescents whose cycles are still becoming regular, women with PMOS (previously PCOS) or thyroid disorders, athletes, outdoor workers and those with limited access to water and rest. Women approaching perimenopause, or those prone to migraines or low blood pressure, may also find symptoms more difficult to manage.
Cold weather effects
The relationship between cold weather and menstruation is less clear. Cold can cause blood vessels to constrict and muscles to tighten, which may make cramps feel worse for some women. Reduced physical activity during colder weather can also contribute to discomfort.
Heavy rain and flooding create a different menstrual health concern. When transport is disrupted or access to toilets, clean water and menstrual products is limited, maintaining menstrual hygiene becomes more difficult. The problem is therefore not only physical discomfort but also access to basic facilities needed to manage menstruation safely.
Humidity and hygiene
Hot and humid conditions can also increase sweat and moisture around the genital area. This can contribute to irritation, chafing and skin infections, particularly when tight synthetic clothing or damp clothes are worn for long periods.
Dr. Gopinath recommends changing menstrual products regularly, wearing breathable cotton underwear and keeping the area clean and dry. Scented products that can irritate sensitive skin should be avoided. Cloth pads should be washed thoroughly and dried completely before reuse.
Managing periods
Managing the effects of extreme weather largely involves reducing the additional physical stress on the body.
Adequate fluid intake is important, particularly during hot and humid weather. There is no single amount of water that everyone needs each day; requirements vary with temperature, physical activity and individual health. Water-rich foods such as cucumber, watermelon and citrus fruits can also contribute to fluid intake.
A balanced diet, including iron-rich foods, can help maintain energy levels, particularly for women who have heavy menstrual bleeding. Light physical activity such as walking, stretching or yoga may help with cramps. During extreme heat, strenuous exercise can be shifted to cooler parts of the day, with adequate rest and fluids.
Keeping a menstrual calendar can help distinguish an occasional change from a persistent pattern. Recording the dates of periods, duration of bleeding, flow and associated symptoms can also provide useful information during a medical consultation.
When to seek help
The most important distinction is between a temporary change during extreme weather and a persistent menstrual problem.
A period that is slightly early or late after a period of heat, poor sleep or disrupted routine may not indicate an underlying disorder. But repeated irregularity should not be explained away as a weather-related effect.
Doctors recommend medical evaluation if cycles remain irregular for about three cycles, bleeding becomes unusually heavy or pain is severe. Periods lasting more than seven days, fainting, significant dehydration, fever or foul-smelling discharge also warrant medical attention. Severe pain that does not improve with usual measures should not be ignored.
Conditions such as PMOS (previously PCOS) and thyroid disorders can cause irregular periods and abnormal ovulation independently of weather. If such conditions are suspected, appropriate evaluation and treatment may be needed.
Weather can therefore influence menstrual health, particularly by adding physical stress or worsening existing symptoms. But it should not become an easy explanation for persistent changes that warrant medical attention.

The blaze has mushroomed to 3,000 hectares two days after breaking out in the High Fens park, an area of boggy peatlands and pine forests popular with hikers.
Area firefighting chief Luc Burette warned that “if we cannot contain the fire” there was a risk it could spill over the German border just a stone’s throw to the east.

The Iran war’s mental toll on US sailors
Sailors are sounding the alarm about conditions on the USS Lincoln.
Welcome to The Logoff: The cracks are starting to show in President Donald Trump’s Iran campaign.
What’s happening? Conditions on a US warship deployed in the Middle East have grown so dire, multiple sailors have reportedly tried to go overboard (at least one did so but was rescued safely, according to CNN).
The attempts to jump overboard comes as family members of sailors are raising concerns with Democratic lawmakers about deteriorating mental health on the ship amid sanitation issues and shortages of food and basic supplies.
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier has been deployed for more than 250 days, starting last November, including a stretch of more than 200 days at sea — a modern record. Its deployment was supposed to end months ago, in May, but has continued as Trump’s Iran war stretches on.
How is the administration responding? Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday that reports about conditions on the Lincoln are “completely misrepresented.” Help is on the way for the Lincoln, though, with another US aircraft carrier en route to the area to replace it (according to the Wall Street Journal, the replacement was already planned, and not in response to deteriorating conditions on the Lincoln).
Why does this matter? Conditions on the Lincoln are not the only recent stumbling block for the US war with Iran. Earlier this month, we learned more about the US’s increasingly serious shortages of key offensive and defensive missiles, including THAAD and Patriot interceptors used to protect US troops and allies. On top of that, the Washington Post reported Thursday that the US has run through around a quarter of its Reaper drones, which cost tens of millions of dollars apiece.
It’s the latest example of how the math of the war is starting to slant against the US: Reaper drones and Patriot missiles are incredibly expensive, while Iran has figured out how to mass-produce attack drones on the cheap. And with no end in sight, shortages and situations like the Lincoln will only become a larger problem.
And with that, it’s time to log off…
Here’s some good news from my colleague Adam Clark Estes: As wrecked as your attention span may feel, it’s not permanently degraded. He talked with attention experts to figure out how to repair his, and how we can all do the same. You can read his full story here with a gift link — and then, for all of our brains’ sake, let’s log off. We’ll see you back here tomorrow.

Keeper Bihina stars as Cameroon upset Morocco to make Wafcon final
- Published
Michaely Bihina was the heroine as the Cameroon goalkeeper saved an extra-time penalty and three more spot-kicks in a shootout to send her side though to the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations final at the expense of host nation Morocco.
The 22-year-old pushed away Fatima Tagnaout's attempt from 12 yards in the 118th minute to ensure the game in Rabat finished 0-0 after 120 minutes.
Bihina then brilliantly kept out efforts from Kenza Chapelle, Maryame Atiq and Sakina Ouzraoui to leave the Moulay Hassan Stadium in stunned silence.
Teenage Cameroon defender Myriam Nyadjou held her nerve to secure a 3-1 win on penalties for the Central Africans.
The Indomitable Lionesses will face Malawi in Sunday's final (19:00 GMT) after the southern Africans beat Algeria 3-1 earlier on Wednesday.
Cameroon's run to the final is all the more remarkable given they were knocked out in qualifying and only progressed to the finals on the strength of their world ranking after the Confederation of African Football decided to expand the tournament to 16 teams midway through the preliminary process.
Morocco suffer heartbreak again
While the first Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon) semi-final was littered with chances and incident, the late game in the capital was a far tighter affair.
Morocco created little to reflect their dominance of the ball against an organised and disciplined Cameroon side who grew in confidence in the latter stages of the second half.
The Atlas Lionesses came close to an opener in the 14th minute when Sanaa Mssoudy diverted Hanane Ait El Haj's right-wing cross against the right-hand upright, and the forward also thrashed into the side-netting on the hour mark.
A flurry of late chances came at the end of regulation time, with Imane Saoud shooting straight at Bihina, Mssoudy heading wide and Michaela Abam firing over the Morocco bar.
Abam then had a shot blocked towards the end of the first period of extra time and Morocco defender Atiq headed over in the second half.
The match's key incident came right at the end of extra time when Morocco were presented with a glorious chance to win the tie following a video assistant referee (VAR) review, with Togolese official Vincentia Amedome deciding Nyadjou had caught Ouzraoui in the face with her arm.
Ait El Haj had converted from the spot in the quarter-final win over South Africa but substitute Tagnaout assumed responsibilities and the winger's tame left-footed effort was palmed away by Bihina.
There was more to come from the Cameroon keeper, who joined Portuguese giants Benfica in February and had previously made a remarkable nine stops in her side's quarter-final upset against 10-time champions Nigeria.
Chapelle put her effort too close to Bihina but two stunning stops followed to deny Atiq and Ouzraoui.
Khadija Er-Rmichi had kept her side in the shootout by saving an effort from Grace Mendoua, but the Morocco keeper had little answer to Bihina's heroics.
A semi-final defeat comes as a big blow to Morocco, who have invested heavily in football in recent years and hired Spain's Women's World Cup winning manager Jorge Vilda in an attempt to claim a maiden continental crown.
The Atlas Lionesses were runners-up in 2022 and reached the final of the delayed 2024 Wafcon last July, but threw away a 2-0 half-time lead against Nigeria and were forced to settle for second place again.
Cameroon, meanwhile, return to the final for the first time since losing to Nigeria as tournament hosts in 2016.
The Indomitable Lionesses have lost three previous finals and coach Valentine Nguele, who only took charge in June, will need to nullify the threat of the Chawinga sisters Tabitha and Temwa when her side come up against Malawi on Sunday.
Whoever comes out on top, it will be a new name on the trophy.
On Thursday Ivory Coast take on Ghana (17:00 GMT) and Nigeria meet South Africa (20:00 GMT) in African play-offs for the chance to go into an inter-continental qualifier for the 2027 Fifa Women's World Cup.

Turn on these settings to protect your Android phone from theft
Google has added some smart theft-detection features to Android in recent years.
For years, Android anti-theft protection was more reactionary than proactive. Users are all too familiar with traditional warnings and protocols, like shielding your phone when entering your PIN, utilizing location services and avoiding easily guessed passwords. Fortunately, anti-theft tools are finally getting better at preventing theft with the help of AI and Google's built-in Theft Protection suite.
If your phone is snatched out of your hand, for instance, new motion-sensing theft detection will quickly lock it down. If a thief kills your connection by pulling your SIM card or switching to Airplane Mode, the Offline Device Lock feature triggers a countdown, locking the screen in short order. These are nifty new features that avoid annoying false positives with usage limitations and active use checks.
Even better, you don't have to dig deep into your device settings to find and activate theft protection measures. As long as your device is running Android 10 or newer, the feature is bundled into Google Play Services. Keep in mind that some entry-level or budget smartphones running Android Go Edition with low RAM, Android tablets and devices lacking the full range of Google Play Services may not have some or all of Google's security suite features.
How to Enable Anti-Theft Features On Android?
The primary settings to look for are under Google's Theft Protection menu. Settings menus aren't universal with Android phones, so there may be a degree of variation between devices. For Samsung users, the order is typically Settings → Security and Privacy → Lost Device Protection → Theft Protection.
Google Pixel phones are similar, but slightly different: Settings → Security & Privacy → Device Unlock → Theft Protection. The most prominent feature is Theft Detection Lock, and it's best to start there. This uses motion and sudden disconnection indicators (like your phone being snatched and moved quickly) to lock down your phone screen automatically. After you turn it on and confirm, your device will now respond to aggressive or sudden movement.
Next, enable Offline Device Lock so your screen stays protected if a thief disables your mobile data or Wi-Fi by switching Airplane Mode on. The lock will kick in shortly after disconnect and doesn't require a local connection to do so. Last but not least, set up Remote Lock. This lets you lock your phone from anywhere by visiting android.com/lock, entering your phone number and following the prompts. Google's Find Hub app is no longer your sole fallback option, and Remote Lock works even if the thief moves the phone to another network.
How Can You Prevent Thieves from Turning Off Your Device?
You'll never fully take advantage of the Theft Protection features if you don't use a PIN, biometrics and a more complicated password than your first name. Besides, Google explicitly requires a screen lock for Identity Check and other device-protection tools, so you may as well set it up properly. On Pixels and newer Android phones, Identity Check can periodically re-verify using your biometrics or PIN, especially when you're off your regular beaten path and away from work or home.
Enable Theft Detection Lock and Offline Device Lock so your phone auto-locks and remains that way, even if the thief yanks it offline. If they try to power it down or keep it in Airplane Mode, your data remains secure behind the screen lock, completely shielded. On Samsung Galaxy phones, there is a dedicated Theft Protection page that ties into Samsung's own lost-device tools as well.
Make sure Remote Lock is enabled and your phone number is verified, so you can lock your phone down from any browser the moment you realize your phone is gone and you didn't leave it on top of the car or inside the refrigerator. Hey, it happens.

Australia slows down ‘backpacker visas’ in fresh migration crackdown
The visas, which allow people to work and travel in Australia for a set period of time, are popular with European and Japanese citizens
“They are still being processed, but they are being processed more slowly than they were previously,” Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said on Sunday.
The visas allow people to come to Australia to work and travel for a set period of time, and are popular with European and Japanese citizens.
Applications for people from 24 nations with an annual cap are “paused” for the current financial year, which began in July, according to the department’s website. Processing times for people from nations with no cap have started to get longer since July, The Sydney Morning Herald reported.
The Minister had been planning to announce new migration curbs at a speech earlier this month, but that was cancelled at the last minute and the new policy was currently “going through a cabinet process,” Burke said on Sunday, declining to say when the new policy would be announced.

Mumbai: With the Ganpati Festival approaching, several mandals across Mumbai have raised concerns over potholes, hanging cables, unauthorised parking and traffic bottlenecks along idol procession routes.
According to a Hindustan Times report, a meeting was held on August 14 to discuss these issues. Mumbai Mayor Ritu Tawde and Mumbai Traffic Police Joint Commissioner Satyanarayan Choudhary were also present at the meeting.
Mandals seek urgent action
The Brihanmumbai Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Samanvay Samiti has sought urgent action from the BMC and Mumbai Traffic Police, including road repairs and safety measures, before idol arrival and immersion processions begin.
The committee has sought immediate repairs to potholes along key routes, including the Andheri-Kurla Link Road between Marol and Ghatkopar. It has also raised concerns over hanging overhead cables along procession routes, particularly around the Sakinaka-Andheri signal area, Sagar Tech Plaza and the road towards Kurla, which could obstruct tall idols and procession vehicles.
The committee also highlighted a fatal cable-related accident during last year’s idol immersion and urged authorities to ensure that all overhead cables are secured at a safe height.
Traffic arrangements sought in Ghatkopar
It has also sought special traffic arrangements at Jagruti Nagar Metro Junction in Ghatkopar West, stating that the existing one-way system could lead to severe congestion during the festival.
With the immersion lake in Aarey reportedly unavailable, the committee expects more mandals to use the Jogeshwari-Vikhroli Link Road towards Shyam Nagar Lake. It has urged the Traffic Police to make appropriate arrangements to manage traffic movement along the route.
Safety concerns over structures
Concerns were also raised over dilapidated railway bridges and other structures that could pose risks during the festival. The committee pointed out that rainwater leaks from structures beneath flyovers and monorail bridges, particularly along routes in Lalbaug used for idol arrivals.
Following the concerns raised by the mandals, Mayor Ritu Tawde assured that the administration would address the issues at the earliest.

Families with teenagers in education know the private, hidden pain of exam season. But this year, what might have been a summer of quiet family anxiety has erupted in several countries into public unrest.
Exam-related turmoil has led to mass student protests in Mexico after nearly 60,000 university applicants were forced to resit tests amid suspected cheating, while Portugal’s disastrous attempt to digitise school exam marking sparked the country’s worst education crisis in decades.
By far the largest and most ground-shaking incident was in India, however, where an exam paper leak affected millions of students and was linked to more than a dozen students taking their own lives. The scandal forced the education minister to resign, and challenged the government’s hold over its 1.4 billion citizens.
Why does this exam season seem to be particularly tense and volatile? Experts say the growth of AI cheating and attempts by academic institutions to digitise examinations are at the heart of the issue. When coupled with the high stakes of good grades in an increasingly precarious global economy, the result can be explosive.
“It would seem that exams are getting more fraught on a global scale,” said Dr Sarah Eaton of the Werklund School of Education at the University of Calgary. “The pressure on young people has absolutely changed.
“We’ve seen the economic situation change around the world in the last decade. And the results of one examination determining a person’s entire future really creates untenable pressure on young people,” said Eaton, a leading expert on academic ethics. “This is a tragedy when young people are dying by suicide because of an examination outcome.”
When a single test can determine a young person’s entire future, cheating is no longer just about individuals but becomes a systematic issue, said Eaton. This is compounded when illicit commercial industries, known as the “education mafia”, exploit student desperation by stealing and then selling exam papers, something that has become widespread in India and elsewhere.
Students from across India joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party, a youth-led protest campaign that began as an online satirical joke and grew into a nationwide outcry that poses an unprecedented challenge to Narendra Modi’s government.
“When you get large-scale fraud combined with systemic failure, there’s almost a guarantee of a breakdown of public trust,” said Eaton. “And once that trust is broken, it’s almost impossible to regain. I can’t imagine how India is going to deal with this, just given the levels of corruption and fraud that we’ve seen.”
In Portugal, the national fallout from a failed push by its education minister, Fernando Alexandre, to fully digitise the exam marking process has landed the government in a crisis. Parents, teachers, and students have been protesting, demanding Alexandre’s resignation after his policy resulted in serious marking errors.
Similar demonstrations took place in Mexico. The National Autonomous University of Mexico (Unam), the country’s most prestigious university, announced that due to abnormally high marks in entrance exam results, which raised suspicions of widespread cheating, approximately 58,000 students would have to retake the exam.
Schools worldwide are rushing to deal with AI use by students, either through bans or teaching AI literacy and ethics to pupils. Denmark announced this month that from the new term, teenagers would have to make a verbal defence of their written essays to combat AI cheating.
Eaton has implemented similar reforms in her class. “AI can generate a perfect essay in seconds. So an essay is no longer a viable way to demonstrate students’ learning,” she said. “We should let it die with dignity and find other ways to assess student learning.”
In Eaton’s view, cheating is a “human problem” and so grading and assessing student learning has historically also been a human responsibility, which she said cannot easily be off-loaded to the latest tech.
But what institutions around the world have been doing instead, she said, is hoping technology can be easily and cheaply used to prevent cheating en masse.
Dr Thomas Lancaster, a computer scientist at Imperial College London who researches the educational use of generative AI, has studied how cheating has gone hi-tech. It is no longer about sneaking notes written on a sleeve, he said, but sophisticated communication.
Lancaster says students have always cheated but it has become far easier, with pupils using earpieces or miniature cameras, and increasingly, communicating with friends or family with access to internet searches.
“I think the number of notes you sneak in, they’re only useful if they’re the right notes and if you can interpret them very quickly,” he said.
“But with any kind of communication technology, you can have that expertise waiting outside for you in a human form. They either know the answers; they’ve got the expertise; or they can look them up online. You can go further than that now and have access to AI to communicate directly during the exam as well,” he added. “It’s spy technology, really.”
Rather than individual student misconduct, Eaton said the failure to properly train educators was forcing students to spend valuable time trying to navigate through these “broken” systems rather than focusing on learning.
“This idea of these mass examinations happening at scale, it sort of dehumanises the learning process and the assessment process,” she said.
This, she said, “sort of perpetuates this idea that examinations are the most important thing for students. I think we’ve lost the thread. Learning should be the most important thing for students.”

Multiple people dead as flooding continues in Indiana
At least six people across multiple counties in Indiana have died related to historic flooding. While some of the worst hit areas are beginning to recover, severe weather is expected to impact the region on Sunday.
Some parts of the state received more than 11 inches of rainfall over three days, beginning Aug. 11, according to a preliminary report issued by the National Weather Service.
Thunderstorms are expected to move across central Indiana late Sunday evening and could cause additional flooding in areas already impacted by the storms, according to the National Weather Service.
Indianapolis Mayor Joe Hogsett on Saturday said on social media that the city is experiencing "its most severe flooding in 30+ years." But flood waters have now started to recede and the city has reopened some of the flood gates, according to the Indianapolis Department of Public Works.
"Engineering will closely monitor our flood-control infrastructure (levees, control gates, etc.) to ensure it continues to operate as anticipated. Crews are working to clear debris blockages of natural flow and monitor flood gates," the department said in a Sunday morning update. "As the water levels recede, crews will continue to complete regular checks on infrastructure, and make further determinations on additional gate openings."
Flooding is expected to continue along the White River in Anderson, Ind., which rose to a record 24.9 feet, and along the Wabash River and the East Fork White River.
More than 128,000 people across the state were without power as of Sunday afternoon, according to NIPSCO, the local power company. 
As crews work to make repairs, communities are coming together to help one another.
On Sunday, hundreds of people gathered at a volleyball court in Rocky Ripple, a town northwest of Indianapolis, with shovels and sandbags to help reinforce the town's levee, according to NPR Member Station WFYI. Margaret Brabant, a resident of Rocky Ripple since 1992, wore a yellow life jacket as she directed cars of people who arrived to help.
"This is pretty overwhelming, because the generosity is just stunning," Brabant told WFYI.
President Donald Trump on Saturday approved an emergency declaration for Indiana, which allows the Federal Emergency Management Agency to assist with recovery efforts from the storm.
Thunderstorms are expected to bring heavy rainfall and possible flooding to West Virginia on Sunday, the National Weather Service also said.
NPR's Laura Sullivan contributed to this report.

Playing at the World Championships is one of the biggest career moments for any sportsperson. Simran Singhi will have more than a few supportive faces in the stands at New Delhi’s Indira Gandhi Stadium on Monday evening when she steps out on court to make her Badminton World Championships debut. “It’s incredible to make my World Championships debut, and it’s even more special that it’s happening in India. My mother will be there, and half of my family is from New Delhi so they will be there as well. Everyone is really excited to see me play,” the 24-year-old tells Sportstar.
There’s one face Simran will be missing, though. That will be Manoj Ramachandran, one of her biggest childhood mentors, who passed away last year. “Manoj uncle was like a second father to me. When I was a kid, he used to accompany me to training and competitions. He was always really supportive of me. He would have been so happy to see me compete at a World Championships. I know he would be so proud of me,” she says.
Simply making it to the World Championships is a career-defining moment for Simran. “If you ask any player, they’ll tell you the same thing. Sab ko toh at least ek baar World Championships khelna hai (Everyone wants to play at the world level at least once). Every player has this dream, but there are times when you wonder if it will be possible or if it’s just something that happens to other people,” says Simran, who will partner Kavipriya Selvam in the women’s doubles against the Spanish pair of Nikol Carulla and Carmen Jimenez, ranked 69th in the world.
Growing up, this hadn’t been something she’d thought about. Simran had grown up in the same Mumbai neighbourhood as international player and USA coach Shlok Ramachandran and India’s top men’s doubles player Chirag Shetty. She studied at the same school, Ryan International, and was a member of the same sports club, Goregaon Sports Club. Yet she came into badminton by chance.
“I’m from a Marwari family. There was no idea about sport. But one day during my summer vacations, my mother took me to a summer sports camp at Goregaon Sports Club. At that time, both Shlok bhaiya and Chirag bhaiya were already training at the Uday Pawar Academy there. Shlok’s father was Manoj uncle, and he suggested that I also start training there,” she recalls.
Simran slowly developed an interest in the sport, and Manoj, already a family friend, made sure her enthusiasm didn’t flag. “He would accompany me to the ground for practice, and he would also travel with me for competitions,” she recalls.
At that early age, Simran appeared a top prospect as a singles player. “I won the National Under-13 championships three years in a row,” she says.
Her form slowly faded, though. As top players from the Uday Pawar academy left to train at the prestigious Gopichand academy in Hyderabad, Simran found herself with fewer partners and fewer options. Moving to another city and living in a hostel was not an option. Instead, she shifted her training base to an academy in Thane.
“It was 1.5 hours from my house. That meant four or five hours of travelling each day. On top of that, I was still in school and having to balance my studies. All that affected my performance,” she says. As the losses mounted, so did the doubts.
“I gave up on singles too easily. Maybe I could have tried harder to move to a different academy and city, but at that time in my life I’m not sure I could have done that,” she admits.
It was around this period that doubles offered Simran a new route. She’d been partners with Ritika Thaker since the U-13 level, and the two started winning domestic tournaments, eventually claiming the junior nationals in 2019. Three years later, they made the Indian senior squad for the Uber Cup.
Although she had finally made an Indian international team, Simran felt the partnership had stopped progressing. “We had been partners from U-13 onwards. It felt strange to walk away from it,” she says.
Taking a risk
She spoke to World Championships doubles medallist Ashwini Ponnappa, who gave her a blunt piece of advice. “She told me, ‘you can’t spend your whole life making everyone happy. Eventually you are going to have to take a decision even if it’s not the easy one’,” she says.
Simran agreed. “I was not happy being an average player. But if you want to take risks, you have to take your decisions,” she says.
The partnership ended in 2024, and Simran was without a partner for two months. Then Kavipriya approached her. “Let’s try for two tournaments. If it works out, we’ll continue,” Kavipriya told her.
It did.
The partnership has given Simran something she had been searching for years: the feeling that she is still improving. There were two quarterfinal finishes at the Guwahati Open and Odisha Open last year. This year at the India Open, the two ran Worlds silver medallists Pearly Tan and Thinaah Muralitharan close in the first game of their opening-round match before eventually going down in straight games.
“We had fought back to nearly level the first game at 19-17 all in the opening game. It would have been great for our self-belief if we had taken that game, but I could feel that we were improving,” she says.
The World Championships is the latest reward for that progress. But getting here has involved another, less visible battle: paying for it.
Financial woes
Simran has spent much of her career outside the very top tier of India’s badminton system, where players receive greater institutional support. Below that level, she says, the economics can become a test of whether a player is willing to continue.
“At some point it becomes a battle of wills over whether you are willing to stick it out. Whatever has come into my account in terms of salary or even prize money has gone out almost simultaneously when I have to pay for my training or my flight tickets,” she says.
There are flights to book, hotels to pay for, tournament expenses and shuttlecocks to buy. “A box of shuttles costs around Rs 3,000, and as a pair, Kavi and I go through two or three boxes a week,” she says. She and Kavipriya have moved from Hyderabad to Nagpur, where they now train under former national coach Arun Vishnu. That brings further expenses in coaching fees and accommodation. Even taking a coach to an international tournament brings another cost. “If you want to bring a coach, then just the accreditation costs 200 USD. You end up playing without someone in your corner,” she says.
She’s had to cut costs even at the World Championships. She has made her own arrangements, taking a late-night flight and staying at an Airbnb rather than the team hotel.
Her sponsorship support has also fluctuated. She had ONGC backing from 2013, when she became U-13 champion, until 2021. A long-term private sponsor withdrew support last year. Her school, Ryan International, has helped fund some tournaments, while Goregaon Sports Club has also supported her at various points. She joined the State Bank of India last year. But the expenses remain.
“I’m mostly managing on my own. Whatever I’ve earned, that’s what I’m spending. I won a silver medal at the 2024 national games, and I was awarded Rs. 10 lakh by the Maharashtra government for that. All of it has gone back into the sport,” she says. “There are months I’ll look into my account, and it’s on the verge of going negative. Badminton’s an expensive sport. I would not recommend playing if you aren’t in that top group,” she says. “At 24, how much do you ask your parents to support you?”
There are days when the pressure to perform can become crushing. But Simran says she tries to keep her focus on badminton and on proving that she and Kavipriya can climb higher.
The pair, currently ranked 42nd in the world, knows it sill has work to do. Simran believes they need to become fitter and more consistent, particularly against the best Asian pairs. “We are handling the rallies, but we are getting tired. For the top Chinese and Koreans, the same pace is like a warm-up,” she says.
The target at the World Championships, she says, is to show that they’ve come closer to the best in the world. “We don’t want to show up at the worlds. We also need to perform and gain confidence. We can’t be scared of who we are playing,” she says.
The ambition now extends beyond the World Championships. The Asian Games is a dream. So is the Olympics, a dream she has carried for years.
But first comes Delhi. After years of wondering whether she would get to play at the highest level, simply walking into the Indira Gandhi Stadium will be an achievement.
“I feel I’ll be making a lot of people proud. But I want to prove I belong at this level,” she says.
